parole.testo: From Old Norse Búi, from búi (“dweller”), from búa (“to dwell”), from Proto-Germanic *būą.

parole.significato: A verb-building suffix that can be added to nouns or adjectives.
parole.testo: From Old Danish -æ, from Old Norse -a, from Proto-Germanic *-ōną.

parole.significato: equivalent of English -ing; suffix for present participle terms
parole.testo: From Old Danish -ændæ, from Old Norse -andi, from Proto-Germanic *-andz, from Proto-Indo-European *-onts.

parole.significato: Used to make adjectives meaning times.
parole.testo: From Old Norse -faldr, from Proto-Germanic *-falþaz. See fold

parole.significato: Used to make adjectives meaning times.
parole.testo: An expansion of -fold. From Old Norse -faldr, from Proto-Germanic *-falþaz.

parole.significato: added to a verb to form a noun for an action or process, the result of or the subject performing such action
parole.testo: From Old Norse -ing, -ung, from Proto-Germanic *-ingō, *-ungō.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives from verbs, having the sense of "may be the object of"; -able.
parole.testo: From Old Danish -likær, -lik, from Old Norse -ligr (“-y, -ly, -like”), from Proto-Germanic *-līkaz (“-like, -ly”), from *līką (“body; corpse, dead body”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“similar, like; image, likeness”). Cognate with English -ly and German -lich

parole.significato: Forms adjectives from nouns with sense of pertaining to
parole.testo: From Old Norse -iskr, -skr, from Proto-Germanic *-iskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos.
From Old Danish -skap, from Old Norse -skapr, from Proto-Germanic *-skapiz.

parole.significato: taking (used only as the second part of compounds)
parole.testo: From Old Norse tekt f (“safety”), cognate of Norwegian Bokmål -tekt and Swedish täkt. A noun derived from the verb Old Norse taka (“to take”), Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”).
From Old Danish at, from Old Norse at, from Proto-Germanic *at.
From Old Norse af, from Proto-Germanic *ab. Related to English of, off and German ab.

From Old Danish aftæn, from Old Norse aptann, from Proto-Germanic *aftanaz, *aftunaz. Cognate with Swedish afton and Norwegian Nynorsk aftan. The West Germanic forms English even, Dutch avond, and German Abend go back to a different form: *ēbanþs. The relation between the two forms is unclear.

From Old Danish akæ, from Old Norse aka (“to drive”), from Proto-Germanic *akaną, cognate with Swedish åka. The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti, which is also the source of Latin agō (whence also Danish agere), Ancient Greek ἄγω (ágō).

From Old Danish akær, from Old Norse akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz, cognate with Swedish åker, English acre, German Acker. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”), which is also the source of Latin ager, Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós), Sanskrit अज्रः (ájraḥ).
From Old Norse akrhœna, composed of akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”) and Old Norse hœna (“hen”).
From Old Danish akærn, from Old Norse akarn (“acorn”), from Proto-Germanic *akraną, cognate with English acorn, German Ecker (archaic), Dutch aker (archaic), Gothic 𐌰𐌺𐍂𐌰𐌽 (akran, “fruit”).

From Old Norse agn, from Proto-Germanic *aganą (“bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱH-ono-, same source as Sanskrit अश्नाति (aśnāti, “to eat”), Sanskrit अशन (aśana, “eating”), Ancient Greek ἄκολος (ákolos, “morsel”).
From Old Danish axul, from Old Norse ǫxull m, from Proto-Germanic *ahsulaz, cognate with Norwegian aksel, Swedish axel. Related to the following word.
From Old Danish axæl, from Old Norse ǫxl f, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō, cognate with Norwegian aksel, Swedish axel, English axle, German Achsel.
Equivalent to alen (“ell”) + bue (“bow”). From Old Norse al(n)bogi, ǫl(n)bogi, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô, cognate with Swedish armbåge, English elbow, German Ellbogen.
From Old Danish aldær, from Old Norse aldr, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą.

parole.significato: cubit, ell (a unit of length of varying value, in Denmark 62.8 cm (equal to 2 feet) until 1907)
parole.testo: From Old Norse alin, ǫln, from Proto-Germanic *alinō (“elbow, ell”), cognate with English ell, German Elle. Compare also albue (“elbow”).
From Old Norse alfr, from Proto-Germanic *albiz.

Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *anadz, cognate with German Ente, Dutch eend. The Germanic noun derives from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts (“duck”), which is also the source of Latin anas, Ancient Greek νῆττα (nêtta), Lithuanian ántis, Sanskrit आति (ātí). The sense of "false story"
From Old Danish annær or annæn, (andræ pl), from Old Norse annarr, from Proto-Germanic *anþeraz (“second, other”).
From Old Danish angær, from Old Norse angr, from Proto-Germanic *angazaz.
From Old Danish andlætæ, from Old Norse andlit, from Proto-Germanic *andawlitją. Cognate with Swedish anlete, Old English andwlite, German Antlitz.
From Old Norse andsvar, from Proto-Germanic *andaswarō, cognate with English answer. A compound of *anda- (“against”) + *swarō (“solemn statement”).

From Old Norse arðr (“plough, ard”), from Proto-Germanic *arþrą, cognate with Swedish årder and Norwegian Bokmål ard (whence (English ard). The Germanic word is related to Latin arātrum (“plough”) and Ancient Greek ἄροτρον (árotron, “plough”).
From Old Danish argh, from Old Norse argr, from Proto-Germanic *argaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃orǵʰ-, *h₃erǵʰ- (“to copulate”).

parole.significato: ark (Noah's Ark or the Ark of the Convenant)
parole.testo: From Old Danish ark, Old Norse ǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *arkō, borrowed from Latin arca (“chest, coffin; ark”).
From Old Norse armr (“arm”), from Proto-Germanic *armaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mo- (“arm”).
From Old Norse armr (“arm, poor”), from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“poor”).
Inherited from Old Norse arfr (“heritage”), from Proto-Germanic *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“to change ownership”).

parole.significato: ash tree (Fraxinus spp.), especially, common ash (tree, Fraxinus excelsior)
parole.testo: From Old Norse askr, from Proto-Germanic *askaz.
From Old Danish askæ, from Old Norse aska, from Proto-Germanic *askǭ. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἄσβολος (ásbolos).
From Old Norse ást, from Proto-Germanic *anstiz.

parole.significato: that (introduces a noun clause functioning as the subject, object or predicative of a verb, or as the object of a prepo…
parole.testo: From Old Norse at. Cognate with Swedish att, Norwegian at. Probably from Proto-Germanic *þat, a demonstrative pronoun used as a conjunction; compare English that, German dass, Dutch dat.

parole.significato: to (infinitive-marker, obligatory when the infinitive functions as noun phrase or an adverbial phrase, but omitted when…
parole.testo: From Old Norse at, cognate with Swedish att, Norwegian å. Originally the same word as the preposition Old Norse at (“at, to”), from Proto-Germanic *at, cognate with English at. Doublet of ad). In the West Germanic languages, a different preposition, *tō (“to”), serves as the infinitive marker, cf En
From Old Norse áttján, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun.
From Old Danish atær, from Old Norse aptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftrą.
From Old Danish thraa, attraa, from Old Norse þrá, from Proto-Germanic *þrawō. Cognate of English throe. The Danish form has been prefixed with the preposition ad.
From Old Danish thraa, attraa, from Old Norse þrá, from Proto-Germanic *þrawōną, derived from the noun. The Danish form has been prefixed with the preposition ad.
From Old Danish aughæ, from Old Norse agi (“fear, discipline”), from Proto-Germanic *agô, form of *agaz (“fear, dread”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂égʰos, from *h₂egʰ- (“to be upset, afraid”).
From Old Norse aga (“frighten, scare”), from Proto-Germanic *agōną
From Old Danish auænd, afund, from Old Norse ǫfund, from Proto-Germanic *abundiz. Cognates include Swedish avund and Icelandic öfund
From Old Norse afl n (“strength, power”), from Proto-Germanic *aflą, cognate with Norwegian avl.
From Old Norse afla, from Proto-Germanic *aflōną, cognate with Norwegian avle.
From Old Danish agnæ pl, from Old Norse ǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *ahanō. Cognate with Latin agna, English awn.
From Old Norse bað, Proto-Germanic *baþą (“bath”), cognate with English bath and German Bad.

parole.significato: to bathe, take a bath, take a swim
parole.testo: From Old Danish bathæ, from Old Norse baða, baðask, from Proto-Germanic *baþōną (“to bathe”). Cognate with English bathe and German baden.

From Old Norse bak n (“back”), from Proto-Germanic *baką, cognate with Norwegian bak, Swedish bak, English back. The preposition is a shortening of Old Norse á bak (“on the back of”), compare English back from aback, from Old English onbæc.
From Old Danish bakæ, from Old Norse baka, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną. Cognate with Swedish baka, English bake, German backen.

parole.significato: baker (person that produces and sells bread and cakes)
parole.testo: By surface analysis, bage (“to bake”) + -er (agent suffix). From Old Norse bakari, from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz, cognate with Swedish bagare (influenced by Danish), English baker, German Bäcker, Dutch bakker.
From Old Danish bakkæ, from Old Norse bakki (“bank; ridge”), from Proto-Germanic *bankô (“bank, embankment; a hill”). Akin to English bank.
From Old Danish barn, from Old Norse barn, from Proto-Germanic *barną. Compare English bairn.

parole.significato: prattle, babble, speak at length and annoyingly
parole.testo: From Old Norse babbla, from Proto-Germanic *bablōną, *babalōną (“babble”). Cognate with English babble.
From Old Norse beit f (“pasturage”), Old Norse beita f (“bait”), from Proto-Germanic *baitō (“food, bait”), cognate with German Beize (“mordant”) (whence Danish bejdse).

parole.significato: to ask, request (to demand something from someone, with the person as an object and with the preposition om + the thing…
parole.testo: From Old Norse biðja, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną (“to ask”). Cognate with Swedish be, bedja, English bid, Dutch bidden, and German bitten. The Germanic verb probably goes back to Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰedʰ-, cf. Polish żądać (“to demand”) and Ancient Greek θέσσασθαι (théssasthai, “to pray”).

parole.significato: to make a halt, take a rest
parole.testo: From Old Norse beita (“to let graze, rest”), from Proto-Germanic *baitijaną, cognate with Norwegian beite (English bait is borrowed from Old Norse). A causative of the verb *bītaną (“to bite”) (cf. Danish bide).

parole.significato: both (each of two; one and the other)
parole.testo: From Old Danish bæggiæ, from Old Norse beggja, from Proto-Germanic *bajjǫ̂, the genitive form of Proto-Germanic *bai (“both”). In Old Norse the other cases have been replaced by the enlargened stem báðir (cf. Danish både).

parole.significato: leg (a limb of a human or an animal used for walking; also, by analogy, the legs of a desk or a chair)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bein (“bone, leg”), from Proto-Germanic *bainą, cognate with English bone, German Bein.
From Old Norse bý, from Proto-Germanic *bijō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰey-. Cognate with English bee.
From Old Norse bit n, from Proto-Germanic *bitą. Derived from the verb *bītaną (“to bite”).
From Old Norse biti m, from Proto-Germanic *bitô, cognate with German Bissen. Derived from the verb *bītaną (“to bite”).

parole.significato: bite (to cut off a piece by clamping the teeth)
parole.testo: From Old Danish bitæ, from Old Norse bíta, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, cognate with English bite, German bissen, Dutch bijten. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”), cf. Latin findō (“to cleave”), fissiō (“breaking up”) (hence fission).
From Old Danish bezæl, from Old Norse beizl, from Proto-Germanic *baitislą.

From Old Norse bíða, from Proto-Germanic *bīdaną (“to wait, await”), cognate with Swedish bida, English bide, abide, German beiten (dialectal). The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydʰeti, which is also the source of Latin fīdō (“to trust”), Ancient Greek πείθω (peíthō, “to persuade”).

From Old Danish bindæ, from Old Norse binda (“to bind, tie”), from Proto-Germanic *bindaną, cognate with English bind and German binden. The Germanic verb derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“bind”), cf. also Sanskrit बन्धति (bándhati, “to bind”) and Latin offendīx (“knot”).

parole.significato: mountain (large mass of earth and rock)
parole.testo: From Old Danish biærgh, from Old Norse bjarg, berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. Cognate with Norwegian and Swedish berg, English barrow, German Berg. From Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“hill, fort”).
From Old Norse bjarga (“to save, help”), from Proto-Germanic *berganą (“to preserve, keep, protect, save”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to hide, protect”).
From Old Danish biært, from Old Norse bjartr, from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer(H)ǵ-tó-s, from *bʰerHǵ- (“to shine”) + *-tós
From Old Danish biørn, biorn, from Old Norse bjǫrn (“bear”), from Proto-Germanic *bernuz, northern form of Proto-Germanic *berô, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“brown, shining”).
From Old Norse blað, from Proto-Germanic *bladą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₃-tó-m, from *bʰleh₃-.
From Old Norse blanda, from Proto-Germanic *blandaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. See English blend.
From Old Danish blek, from Old Norse bleikr, from Proto-Germanic *blaikaz.
From Old Norse bleikja, from Proto-Germanic *blaikijaną, from *blaikaz, whence also bleg.
From Old Danish bliþær, blithær, from Old Norse blíðr, from Proto-Germanic *blīþiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-.
From Old Norse blindr, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz. Related to blænde and blunde.
From Old Norse blesi, from Proto-Germanic *blasį̄, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shine”).
From Old Danish bloth, from Old Norse blóð, from Proto-Germanic *blōþą (“blood”).

From Old Danish blomæ (“flower”), from Old Norse blómi m, from Proto-Germanic *blōmô m (“flower”), cognate with Swedish blomma, English bloom, German Blume f, Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐌼𐌰 m (blōma). Derived from the verb *blōaną (“to bloom”) (cf. German blühen). These words go back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (

Older blomster, from Old Norse blómstr m, in which -r belongs to the root, cf. also Swedish blomster. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *blōstmô, cognate with English blossom, Dutch bloesem. Related to the older "flower" word in Danish, blomme. In Danish -r was taken for a plural ending and omitted in th
From Old Norse blót, from Proto-Germanic *blōtą.

parole.significato: to make a sacrifice (especially a blood sacrifice by heathens)
parole.testo: Revived in the 1800s from Old Norse blóta, from Proto-Germanic *blōtaną, cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐍄𐌰𐌽 (blōtan, “to worship”).
From Old Danish bla, from Old Norse blár (“blue”), from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue”).
From Old Norse blástr (“blast”).
From Old Danish bløthær, from Old Norse blautr, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz. Compare Old Norse blauðr (“weak, timid”).
From Old Norse búa (“to reside”), from Proto-Germanic *būaną, cognate with Norwegian bo, bu, Swedish bo, German bauen, Dutch bouwen, Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌿𐌰𐌽 (bauan).
From Old Norse bót, from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, atonement”), cognate with Swedish bot, English boot, German Buße, Dutch boete. Doublet of bøde.
Inherited from Old Norse bók (“beech, book”), from Proto-Germanic *bōks, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech”).
From Old Danish bokstav, from Old Norse bókstafr, from Proto-Germanic *bōkastabaz.
From Old Danish borth, from Old Norse borð, from Proto-Germanic *burdą. Cognate with English board, German Bord.

From Old Danish borgh, burg, from Old Norse borg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“stronghold, city”), cognate with German Burg (“castle”) and English borough. The Germanic noun is derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise”), which is also the source of Danish bjerg (“mountain”).

From Old Norse bógr (“shoulder”), from Proto-Germanic *bōguz (“arm; shoulder”). Cognate with English bough (“branch”), German Bug (“animal shoulder; ship bow”), and Dutch boeg (“ship bow”). In the maritime sense, the Danish word is influenced by Dutch (like English bow).
From Old Norse bráð, from from Proto-Germanic *brēdô, cognate with German Braten.
From Old Norse bráðr, from Proto-Germanic *brēþaz (“in a hurry”), cognate with Swedish bråd.

parole.significato: fire (large, destructive fire, as in a building)
parole.testo: From Old Danish brand, from Old Norse brandr, from Proto-Germanic *brandaz, compare with Swedish brand, English brand, German Brand.

A merger of two unrelated adjectives: * Old Norse *brantr (east), brattr (west), from Proto-Germanic *brantaz, cognate with Norwegian bratt, Swedish brant, English brant. * Old Norse bráðr (“hasty, sudden”), from Proto-Germanic *brēþaz (“hot, in a hurry, rushed”), cognate with Norwegian brå, Swedish
From Old Danish breth, from Old Norse breiðr, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz. Cognate with Old English brad.
Equivalent to bred (“wide”) + -de (noun suffix), from Old Norse breidd, from Proto-Germanic *braidiþō.
From Old Norse breiða, from Proto-Germanic *braidijaną (“to broaden”).
From Middle Danish brækne, from Old Norse (related to Swedish bräken (“fern”)), from Proto-Germanic *brak- (“bushes, undergrowth”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-.

parole.significato: chest (of a larger animal, especially horses)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bringa, from Proto-Germanic *bringô, which is related to *brinkaz (“edge, hill”). Cognate with Swedish bringa, Old English bringádl (“epilepsy”).
From Old Norse brestr m, from Proto-Germanic *brestuz. Doublet of brøst.
From Old Norse bresta, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną, cognate with Swedish brista, English burst, German bersten.
From Old Norse broddr, from Proto-Germanic *bruzdaz.
From Old Danish brothær, from Old Norse bróðir (“brother”), from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
From Old Norse bróðir (“brother”), from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
From Old Norse brúðr (“bride”), from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz, cognate with English bride and German Braut.
Inherited from Old Norse brot, from Proto-Germanic *brutą, derived from the verb *breutaną (cf. Danish bryde).

parole.significato: a bridegroom or groom (short for bridegroom)
parole.testo: From Old Norse brúðgumi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô.

parole.significato: steward (a man managing another person’s estate)
parole.testo: From Old Danish bryti, brytæ, from Old Norse bryti, from Proto-Germanic *brutjô. Cognate with Old English brytta. Derived from *breutaną (“to break”) (see below).

parole.significato: to break (to cause to end up in two or more pieces or to make an opening in something)
parole.testo: From Old Danish brytæ, from Old Norse brjóta, from Proto-Germanic *breutaną, cognate with Norwegian bryte, Swedish bryta.
From Old Norse bryggja, from Proto-Germanic *brugjǭ. Cognate with English bridge and German Brücke.
From Old Norse brugga (past participle bruginn, from Proto-Germanic *brewwaną. Cognates include English brew and German brauen.
From Old Norse brún, from Proto-Germanic *brūwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰrúHs. Cognate with Ancient Greek ὀφρύς (ophrús).

From Old Norse brjóst, from Proto-Germanic *breustą n (“breast, chest”), cognate with Swedish bröst, English breast. Related to *brusts f (“breast, chest”), in German Brust, Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐍃𐍄𐍃 (brusts). Derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”).
Reborrowed in the late 1800th from Old Danish bra (“eyelid, eyelash”), from Old Norse brá, from Proto-Germanic *brēwō.

parole.significato: to burn (to cause to be consumed by fire)
parole.testo: The Danish verb is a fusion of two related verbs: 1. the intransitive Old Norse brenna, brinna (past tense brann), from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną, and 2. the transitive Old Norse brenna (past tense brenda), from Proto-Germanic *brannijaną. They are still kept apart in Swedish: intransitive brinna (pa
From Old Danish brøth, from Old Norse brauð (“bread”), from Proto-Germanic *braudą, cognate with Swedish bröd, English bread, German Brot.
From Old Norse brestr m, from Proto-Germanic *brestuz. Doublet of brist.

From Old Danish buthæ, bothæ, from Old Norse boða. from Proto-Germanic *budōną (“to proclaim, teach, instruct”), from Proto-Germanic *budą (“message, command, precept”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be awake, perceive fully”).
From Old Danish boghæ, from Old Norse bogi, from Proto-Germanic *bugô. Cognate with Swedish båge, English bow, German Bogen.

parole.significato: belly (the lower part the body of an animal or, by analogy, an aircraft)
parole.testo: From Old Norse búkr, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish buk, German Bauch, Dutch buik.

parole.significato: the male of certain ruminants (deer, goat, sheep)
parole.testo: From Old Danish buk, from Old Norse bukkr, Proto-Germanic *bukkaz (“buck”).
From Old Norse botn, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz.
From Old Danish bunkæ, from Old Norse bunki, from Proto-Germanic *bunkô.

From Old Norse byrja (“to begin”), from Proto-Germanic *burjaną (“to lift”). Doublet of børje. The Old Norse verb is also construed with an infinitive subject in the sense "it is proper". In Modern Danish and Swedish, the verb has a personal subject and an infinitive as the object. The original Dani
From Old Norse buskr, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

From Old Danish biuthæ, from Old Norse bjóða, from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to offer”). Cognate with English bid and German bieten. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to wake, rise up”), which is also the source of Sanskrit बुद्ध (buddha, “awakened, enlightened”) (hence b

parole.significato: barley (cereal of the genus Hordeum (especially Hordeum vulgare), or its grains)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bygg n (“barley”), from Proto-Germanic *bewwą.
From Old Danish byrth, burth, from Old Norse burðr m (“bearing, birth”), byrð f (“ancestry”), from Proto-Germanic *burdiz ~ *burþiz, cognate with Swedish börd, English birth and German Geburt.
From Old Danish byrthæ, byrþi, from Old Norse byrðr, from Proto-Germanic *burþį̄ (“burden”).

From Old Danish bathæ, from Old Norse báðir (“both”), a combination of Proto-Germanic *bai and the demonstrative pronoun þeir, cf. Old English bā þā (English both) and Old High German beide (German beide).

parole.significato: stretcher (simple litter designed to carry a sick, injured, or dead person)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bára, from Proto-Germanic *bērō.
From Old Danish bas, from Old Norse báss, from Proto-Germanic *bansaz. Cognate with English boose, German Banse and Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐍃𐍄𐍃 (bansts).
From Old Danish bælgh, from Old Norse belgr, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz (“bag”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).

parole.significato: to chug (to drink a lot of beer, water, etc. quickly and voraciously)
parole.testo: From Old Norse belgja, from Proto-Germanic *balgijaną, causative of *belganą. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).
From Old Danish bær, from Old Norse ber, from Proto-Germanic *bazją.

From Old Danish bæræ, from Old Norse bera, from Proto-Germanic *beraną, cognate with Swedish bära, English bear, German gebären. The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), which is also the source of Latin ferō, Ancient Greek φέρω (phérō), Sanskrit भरति (bhárati).
From Old Norse bifa, from Proto-Germanic *bibāną, cf. German beben.
From Old Norse bǿta, from Proto-Germanic *bōtijaną, cognate with Swedish böta, German büßen, Dutch boeten, Gothic 𐌱𐍉𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bōtjan). Related to the noun *bōtō (Danish bod).

parole.significato: beech (a tree of the genus Fagus)
parole.testo: From Old Norse bók (“beech”), from Proto-Germanic *bōkō, cognate with English beech, German Buche. The Danish form has the vowel from the old collective noun bøge (in place names), from Proto-Germanic *bōkiją. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech”), which is also the source of
From Old Norse beygja (“to bend”), from Proto-Germanic *baugijaną, cognate with German beugen. A causative of *beuganą, *būganą.
From Old Danish byghil, bøgel, from Old Norse bygill, from Proto-Germanic *bugilaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk bygel, Swedish bygel, German Bügel. Derived from the verb *beuganą (“to bow”).
From Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk bølgje, Swedish bölja, English billow. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (also in Danish bælg).
From Old Norse bœn, from Proto-Germanic *bōniz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“speak”).
From Old Danish bøøn, from Old Norse baun, from Proto-Germanic *baunō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ-, *bʰabʰ-eh₂- (“bean”). The final -e was added under Middle Low German influence.
From Old Norse byrr, Proto-Germanic *buriz (“favorable wind”).

From Old Norse burðr m (“bearing, birth”), byrð f (“ancestry”), from Proto-Germanic *burdiz ~ *burþiz, cognate with Norwegian foster m, burar (“uterus”), Swedish börd, English birth, German Geburt. Doublet of byrd.

From Old Danish byriæ, from Old Norse byrja, from Proto-Germanic *burjaną. Doublet of burde. The word was reintroduced from Swedish börja in the 19th century to replace begynde (a German loanword), but unsuccessfully.
From Old Norse burst, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz.
From Old Danish thē, from Old Norse þeir, from Proto-Germanic *þai. Usage of this word as a gender-neutral third-person singular pronoun is a semantic loan from English they.

From Old Danish degh, from Old Norse deig, from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”). Compare Swedish deg, Norwegian Nynorsk deig, German Teig, West Frisian daai, Dutch deeg, English dough.

From Old Norse deila (“to divide, allot”), from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną, cognate of English deal and German teilen. In older Danish, the verb meant "to take to court”. The present verb has been influenced by Middle Low German dēlen (“to divide”).

parole.significato: the (used before an adjective preceding a noun)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þann, the accusative form of sá, from Proto-Germanic *sa (“that”), from Proto-Indo-European *só (“this, that”).
From Old Norse þar, from Proto-Germanic *þar (“there”), cognate with English there, German da.

parole.significato: breast milk, mother's milk, when sucked from the breast
parole.testo: From Old Danish di, from Old Norse *día, from Proto-Germanic *dijōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”). Cognate with Latin fellō, Sanskrit धयति (dhayati, “to suck”). Compare causative dægge, Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌳𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (daddjan, “suckle”). The noun is derived from the verb.
From Old Danish dikæ, diki, from Old Norse díki, from Proto-Germanic *dīkiją, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ-.
From Old Norse þínn, from Proto-Germanic *þīnaz (“your”).
From Old Norse djarfr, from Proto-Germanic *derbaz. "brave" sense revived in the 18th century.
From Old Norse dómr (“judgement”), from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos.
Compound of dom + hus, from Old Norse dómhús, from Proto-Germanic *dōmahūsą.

parole.significato: a court, court of law (place where justice is administered)
parole.testo: From Old Norse dómstóll, from Proto-Germanic *dōmastōlaz.
From Old Norse dráp (“killing”), from Old Norse drepa (“to hit; to kill”), from Proto-Germanic *drepaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dhrebh-. Compare Icelandic dráp, Swedish dråp.

From Old Danish draghæ, from Old Norse draga, from Proto-Germanic *draganą, cognate with English draw and drag and German tragen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“pull, draw, drag”), cf. Ancient Greek τρέχω (trékhō, “to run”) (Latin trahō (“to pull”) has a problematic t-
From Old Norse drengr (“young warrior”), from Proto-Germanic *drangijaz (“man, servant”).
From Old Norse drif, from Proto-Germanic *dribą, cognate with Swedish drev. Derived from the verb *drībaną (“to drive”).

parole.significato: operation, running (of a company, a service or a mashine)
parole.testo: From Old Norse drift, from Proto-Germanic *driftiz, cognate with Swedish drift, English drift, German Trift, Dutch drift. Derived form the verb *drībaną (“to drive”).
From Old Danish drikkæ, (Western) Old Norse drekka, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną, cognate with Swedish dricka, English drink, German trinken.

parole.significato: to force, drive, impel (to put in motion)
parole.testo: From Old Danish drivæ, from Old Norse drífa, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną, cognate with Swedish driva, English drive, Dutch drijven, German treiben.

From Old Danish drotten (later misinterpreted as the definite singular form), from Old Norse dróttinn, from Proto-Germanic *druhtinaz (“leader, lord”), cognate with Old English dryhten, Old High German truhtin. Derived from the noun *druhtiz (“troop”).
From Old Danish dropæ, from Old Norse dropi, from Proto-Germanic *drupô.

From Old Danish dræpæ, from Old Norse drepa, from Proto-Germanic *drepaną (“to hit, strike”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål drepe and Swedish dräpa. Also cognate with German treffen (“to meet, hit”), whence Danish træffe.

parole.significato: the act of pulling, drawing fish in (using a dragnet)
parole.testo: From Old Norse dráttr, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz. Derived from the ancestor of the verb drage (“drag”).

From Old Danish drøm, from Old Norse draumr, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz (“dream”), cognate with English dream, German Traum. The Germanic noun is derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ- (“to deceive, injure”), hence Sanskrit द्रुह्यति (druhyati, “to hurt”) and also, via Low German, Danish bedra

parole.significato: to dream (to see imaginary events while sleeping)
parole.testo: From Old Danish drømæ, from Old Norse dreyma (“to dream”), Proto-Germanic *draumijaną, cognate with English dream, German träumen. Derived from the noun *draumaz, hence Danish drøm.
From Old Norse drynja, from Proto-Germanic *drunjaną (“to rumble”).

parole.significato: thou, you (2nd person singular subject pronoun, informal)
parole.testo: From Old Danish thu, from Old Norse þú, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂ (“you”). Cognate with English thou, Latin tū, Sanskrit त्वम् (tvam), Avestan 𐬙𐬏𐬨 (tūm), Russian ты (ty).
From Old Danish dughæ, from Old Norse duga, from Proto-Germanic *duganą (“to be useful”), cognate with Swedish duga, German taugen, Gothic 𐌳𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (dugan).
From Old Danish dufæ, from Old Norse dúfa, from Proto-Germanic *dūbǭ, cognate with Norwegian due, Swedish duva, Dutch duif, German Taube, English dove.

From Old Danish duft (“powder”), Old Norse dupt n (“powder”), from Proto-Germanic *duftaz, cognate with Swedish doft (“powder”) and German Duft (“smell”), Middle High German tuft (“fog”). Semantically, the Danish word is influenced by the German word. The Germanic noun is derived from Proto-Indo-Eur
From Old Norse dǫgg (“dew”), from Proto-Germanic *dawwō, *dawwaz (“dew”), cognate with Swedish dagg, English dew, German Tau (“dew”), Dutch dauw.
From Old Norse dokka, from Proto-Germanic *dukkǭ, cognate with Old Saxon dokka, Old High German tocka.
From Old Danish dualæ, from Old Norse dvala, from Proto-Germanic *dwalaz. Related to dvæle and dølge.
From Old Norse dvergr, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz.
From Old Danish diup, from Old Norse djúpr, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-. Compare Swedish djup, German tief.

From dyb (“deep”) + -de. It seems to be a new formation from ca. 1700 rather than an inherited word from Old Norse dýpt, Proto-Germanic *diupiþō, cognate with English depth, Dutch diepte, and Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌹𐌸𐌰 (diupiþa).

From Old Norse dygð (“virtue”), cognate with Norwegian, Swedish dygd, from Proto-Germanic *dugiþō, a variant of *dugunþō in English douth, German Tugend, Dutch deugd. These words are derived from the verb *duganą (“to be useful”), hence Danish du.
From Old Danish dyngjæ (“fertilizer”), from Old Norse dyngja, from Proto-Germanic *dungijǭ.
From Old Norse dýrr, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz, cognate with Swedish dyr, English dear, German teuer, Dutch duur.

parole.significato: feat, deed; an impressive, heroic or otherwise laudable act
parole.testo: From Old Danish dāth, from Old Norse dáð, from Proto-Germanic *dēdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tis, from *dʰeh₁- (“to place, set, put”). Cognate with Old English dǣd (whence English deed).

A merger of two words: 1. Old Norse dáligr, derived from dá n (“coma”), from Proto-Germanic *dawą, related to *dawjaną (“die”); and 2. Middle Low German dōrlik (“foolish”), derived from dōre (“fool”), from Proto-West Germanic *dauʀō, cognate with German Tor (cf. also Danish dåre).
From Old Norse deyja (“to die”), from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål dø, Swedish dö, Icelandic deyja, English die.

From Old Norse deypa (“to dip in water, baptize”), inherited from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną (“to dip”). Cognate with German taufen and Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌿𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (daupjan, “immerse, baptize”). The Christian meaning of the word may have spread from Gothic to the rest of the Germanic languages. The verb is likely

From Old Danish døth, from Old Norse dauðr, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz. Cognate with English dead and German tot. Originally a past participle of the verb Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”) (Danish dø).
From Old Danish døth, from Old Norse dauðr, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz. Cognate with English death and German Tod. Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”) (Danish dø).
From Old Danish døthæ, from Old Norse deyða, from Proto-Germanic *daudijaną. Compare Swedish döda, German töten.

parole.significato: day - the 24 hour period stretching from midnight to midnight.
parole.testo: From Old Danish døghn, from Old Norse dœgn, from Proto-Germanic *dōg- (“daily period, day”), from Proto-Germanic *dōgaz (“daily”). Cognate with Old English dōgor (“day”), Gothic -𐌳𐍉𐌲𐍃 (-dōgs, “age in days”).

parole.significato: to conceal, keep as a secret
parole.testo: From Old Danish dyliæ, from Old Norse dylja, from Proto-Germanic *duljaną, cognate with Swedish dölja.
From Old Norse dynr, from Proto-Germanic *duniz.
From Old Norse daunn, from Proto-Germanic *dauniz. from Proto-Indo-European *dʰowh₂-nis, [Term?]. from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂-.
From Old Norse dyrr, dyr, from Proto-Germanic *durz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door, gate”).
From Old Danish døf, from Old Norse daufr, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-.
From Old Danish ēþ, eth, from Old Norse eiðr, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz.

From Old Danish etær, from Old Norse eitr, from Proto-Germanic *aitrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂oyd-, *h₂eyd-. Cognate with Icelandic eitur, Faroese eitur, Elfdalian ietter, English atter, Dutch etter, and German Eiter.
From Old Danish ikærnæ, from Old Norse íkorni, from Proto-Germanic *aikwernô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer-.

From Old Danish eghæ, from Old Norse eiga (“to own”), from Proto-Germanic *aiganą. Cognate of English owe and related to Danish egen and English own. Older Danish had present tense aa, past tense aatte and past participle aat, which are still used on rare occasions in higher poetry in the 19th centu
From Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aigǭ (“property”). Derived from the verb.

From Old Norse elri (“alder”), cf. ǫlr (compare Icelandic elri, Swedish al, Norwegian Bokmål older), from Proto-Germanic *aluz, *alusō (compare English alder), variant of *alizō, *alisō (compare Dutch els, German Erle), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisos.
From Old Norse elgr (“moose”), from Proto-Germanic *elh-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“red, brown”).
From Old Danish ællær, from Old Norse ella, ellar, from Proto-Germanic *aljaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.
From Old Norse ellifu, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Compare Norwegian Bokmål elleve, Swedish elva, Icelandic ellefu, Faroese ellivu.
From Old Danish ælskæ, from Old Norse elska (“to love”), from Proto-Germanic *aliskōną (“to care for, cultivate, cherish”), from *aliskaz (“dear, precious”).
From Old Norse eimr, from Proto-Germanic *aimaz. Cognates include Norwegian Nynorsk eim and Icelandic eimur.

parole.significato: office (position in the state or in the public administration)
parole.testo: From Old Norse embætti, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtiją, cognate with Swedish ämbete, German Amt, Dutch ambacht, doublet of amt (“county”)). Derived from *ambahtaz (“servant”), which is an old loan from Gaulish ambaxtos (“vassal”), whence also ultimately ambassade (“embassy”).

Perhaps from em, but blended with Norwegian myrja (“mass, ember”). Ultimately from Old Norse eimyrja (“embers”), from Proto-Germanic *aimuzjǭ, equivalent to eimr + yrja. The form emmer seems to have been used originally as a singular, compare the variant emme (“ember”). Compare Old English ǣmyrġe (“
From Old Norse einn, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one, some”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”).

From Old Norse en, earlier an, probably from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then”), like English than, German denn (“than, for”). For the loss of þ-, compare Old Norse at (“that”) from Proto-Germanic *þat (“that”).
From Old Norse enn, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.
From Old Danish ændæ, from Old Norse endi, endir (“end”), from Proto-Germanic *andijaz (“end”), cognate with English end and German Ende.
From Old Danish ændæ, from Old Norse enda, from Proto-Germanic *andijōną (“to end”), cognate with English end and German enden.
From Old Norse endalauss, from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz, equivalent to ende + -løs.
From Old Danish æng, from Old Norse eng, from Proto-Germanic *angijō f, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énkos. Compare German Anger, Latin ancrae, Ancient Greek ἄγκος (ánkos) and Sanskrit अङ्कस् (aṅkas).
From Old Norse æfinligr, an enlargement of earlier *æfinn from Proto-Germanic *aiwīnaz, cognate with Old High German ēwīn, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌽𐍃 (aiweins). Derived from the noun *aiwaz (“age, eternity”).
From Old Norse efni n (“material, ressources, matter”), from Proto-Germanic *abniją, cognate with Swedish ämne (“subject”), doublet of emne (“subject”). Related to the verb.
From Old Norse efna, from Proto-Germanic *abnijaną (“to perform”), cognate with Swedish ämna.
From Old Danish fathær, from Old Norse faðir, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
From Old Danish faghær, from Old Norse fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz, cognate with Norwegian fager, Swedish fager, Icelandic fagur, English fair.
From Old Norse fall, from Proto-Germanic *fallaz, cognate with English fall, German Fall. Derived from the verb *fallaną (“to fall”). The sense "case" is a calque of Latin cāsus.
From Old Danish fallæ, from Old Norse falla, from Proto-Germanic *fallaną. Cognate with English fall, Swedish falla, German fallen.
Inherited from Old Norse faðir, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”).
From Old Danish fara, faræ, from Old Norse fara, from Proto-Germanic *faraną, English fare, German fahren.

From Old Danish *far (“pig”), from Old Norse *farr, from Proto-Germanic *farhaz, cognate with Swedish fargalt, English farrow, German Ferkel, Dutch varken. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos, hence also Latin porcus, Polish prosię (“piglet”).
From Old Danish fastær, from Old Norse fastr, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz; see it for cognates and further etymology.
From Old Norse fasta, from Proto-Germanic *fastǭ (“fast”), cognate with German Fasten. Like the verb, derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *fastuz (“firm”).
From Old Norse fasta, from Proto-Germanic *fastāną (“to fast”). Cognate with English fast and German fasten. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *fastuz (“firm”).

parole.significato: fat (carrying a larger than normal amount of fat on one's body), obese
parole.testo: From Old Danish fet, from Old Norse feitr (“fat”), from Proto-Germanic *faitaz.
From Old Norse feita, from Proto-Germanic *faitijaną (“to fatten”). Derived from the adjective *faitaz (“to fat”) (Danish fed).
From Old Danish fegh, from Old Norse feigr (“near to death”), from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz. Influenced by German feige.
From Old Norse fimm, from Proto-Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe (“five”).
From Old Norse fimti, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô (“fifth”).
From Old Norse fimmtán, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun.
From Old Norse ferskr, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-.
From Old Danish finnæ, from Old Norse finna (“find”), from Proto-Germanic *finþaną. Cognate with English find and German finden.
From Old Norse fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz, from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷrós.
From Old Norse fjórir, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (“four”).
From Old Norse fiskr, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”). Cognate with English fish and German Fisch. The Germanic word is related to Latin piscis, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk- (“fish”).

From Old Danish fiskæ, from Old Norse fisk(j)a (“to fish”), from fiskr (“fish”), from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”), from Proto-Indo-European *peysk- (“fish”), maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep- (“water”).
From Old Norse fiskari, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz. Cognate with Swedish fiskare, Norwegian fisker.

From Old Danish fiat, from Old Norse fet, from Proto-Germanic *fetą, from Proto-Indo-European *pedóm, from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to walk, step”). Related to fod, Swedish fjät, English foot, Ancient Greek πέδον (pédon) and Sanskrit पद (pada).

From Old Danish fiændæ, from Old Norse fjándi, to Proto-Germanic *fijandz, an old present participle of the verb fjá (“hate”), *fijāną. Cognate with English fiend, German Feind, Faroese fíggindi, Norwegian Bokmål fiende, and Swedish fiende.
From Old Danish fiæthær, from Old Norse fjǫðr (“feather”), from Proto-Germanic *feþrō. Cognates include English feather and German Feder. Cf. also fjeder (“a spring”).
From Old Danish fiarthæ, Old Norse fjórði, Proto-Germanic *fedurþô. Compare Swedish fjärde, English fourth, and German vierte.

parole.significato: used adverbially in the prepositional phrase i fjor (“last year”) – yesteryear, last year
parole.testo: From Old Norse fjǫrð (in prepositional phrase í fjǫrð), from Proto-Germanic *ferudi, from Proto-Indo-European *peruti. Cognates include Ancient Greek πέρυσι (pérusi), Sanskrit परुत् (parut), and Old Irish uraid.
From Old Norse fjórtán, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun.

parole.significato: a plank, board (often of poor quality)
parole.testo: From Old Danish fial, from Old Norse fjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *felō.
From Old Danish fiælæ, from Old Norse fela, from Proto-Germanic *felhaną.
From Old Danish fiærtæ, from Old Norse freta, from Proto-Germanic *fertaną, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-. Cognate with English fart.

From Old Norse flatr, from Proto-Germanic *flataz, cognate with English flat. The Germanic adjective goes back to Proto-Indo-European *plat- (“flat”), cf. Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús) (whence, via Latin, Danish plat and plads).
From Old Norse flak (“loose or torn piece”), flakna (“flake or chip”), from Proto-Germanic *flaką (“something flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”).
From Old Norse flaska, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of fiasko and flakon. See English flask, German Flasche, Italian fiasca, and Italian fiasco.

parole.significato: more (in relation to number, with countable nouns)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fleiri, from Proto-Germanic *flaizô, derived from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“full, many”), compare Latin plūs and Ancient Greek πλείων (pleíōn), which are used with both uncountable nouns (quantity) and countable nouns (number).

parole.significato: most (in relation to number, used with countable nouns)
parole.testo: From Old Norse flestr, from Proto-Germanic *flaistaz, derived from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“full, many”), compare Latin plūrimus and Ancient Greek πλεῖστος (pleîstos), which are used with both uncountable nouns (quantity) and countable nouns (number).
From Old Norse flétta, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną (“to plait, weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, braid”). Cognate with Old English fleohtan and Latin plectere.
From Old Danish floth, from Old Norse flóð, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz, from *pleh₃(w)- (“flow”). Compare Swedish flod, Icelandic flóð, English flood, Dutch vloed, German Flut.
From Old Norse flokkr, from Proto-Germanic *flukkaz.
From Old Norse flom, from Proto-Germanic *flaumaz (“flood”).
From Old Danish flughæ, from Old Norse fluga, from Proto-Germanic *flugǭ.
From Old Norse flýja (“to flee”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną, cognate with English flee, German fliehen, Dutch vlieden.

parole.significato: to flow (run from one place to another, of a liquid)
parole.testo: From Old Danish flytæ, from Old Norse fljóta (“to float”), from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną (“to float”). Cognate with Swedish flyta, English fleet, German fließen, Dutch vlieten.
From Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ (“flatfish”). Cognate with English flounder, German Flunder.

parole.significato: move, remove (move a thing or a person from one place to another)
parole.testo: From Old Danish flyttæ, flyttiæ, from Old Norse flytja, from Proto-Germanic *flutjaną. Derived from the verb *fleutaną (“to flow”) (Danish flyde).
From Old Danish flyghæ, from Old Norse fljúga, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, cognate with English fly and German fliegen.

parole.significato: to skin, flay (removing the skin of an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Norse flá, from Proto-Germanic *flahaną. Compare English flay.

parole.significato: raft (a floating timber platform or an inflatable rubber boat)
parole.testo: From Old Danish flodhe, from Old Norse floti, from Proto-Germanic *flutô (“float, raft”), cognate with Norwegian flåte, Swedish flotte, English float, German Flosse (“fin”). In the sense "fleet", the word has been influenced by French flotte (which is itself a loan from Germanic).

parole.significato: to raft, float (to transport something by having it float on a river)
parole.testo: From Old Norse flota, from Proto-Germanic *flutōną, cognate with Norwegian flote, Swedish flotta, English float, Dutch vlotten. Related to the verb Proto-Germanic *fleutaną (“to float”) (Danish flyde).
From Old Norse flengja, from Proto-Germanic *flangijaną (“to beat, whip”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k- (“to beat”). Related to flå. Cognate with Swedish flänga, English fling.
From Old Norse flesk, from Proto-Germanic *flaiski, cognate with English flesh, German Fleisch (“meat”), Dutch vlees (“meat”).

From Old Danish fløthæ, Old Norse flautir f pl (“sour whipped milk”), from Proto-Germanic *flautijǭ, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål fløte, fløyte, Old English flīete f (“cream”). Derived from *fleutaną (“to float”) (Danish flyde).

parole.significato: to raft, float (to transport something by having it flot on a river)
parole.testo: From Old Norse fleyta, from Proto-Germanic *flautijaną, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk fløyte, Norwegian Bokmål fløte, German flößen. A causative of the verb Proto-Germanic *fleutaną (“to float”) (Danish flyde).
From Old Norse flœða, from Proto-Germanic *flōdijaną, cognate with Norwegian flø, Swedish flöda, German fluten. Derived from the noun *flōduz (“flood”) (Danish flod).
From Old Norse fnýsa, from Proto-Germanic *fneusaną.

From Old Norse fótr, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, cognate with English foot, German Fuß, Dutch voet. The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *pṓds (“foot”), which is also the source of Latin pēs, Ancient Greek πούς (poús).
From Old Norse fóðr, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, guard, graze, feed”).
From Old Norse falda, from Proto-Germanic *falþaną (“to fold”).
From Old Norse fólk, from Proto-Germanic *fulką.

parole.significato: Makes verbs from adjectives meaning "to cause to be [adjective]".
parole.testo: From Old Norse for-, from Proto-Germanic *fra-, from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (“before, in front of”).
From Old Danish forbuth, from Old Norse forboð, from Proto-Germanic *furibudą, cognate with Swedish förbud, German Verbot. Verbalnoun of the verb *furibeudaną, see forbyde.

From Old Danish forbiuthæ, forebiuþa, from Old Norse fyrirbjóða, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *furibeudaną. Cognate with Swedish förbjuda, Norwegian Bokmål forby, Norwegian Nynorsk forby, forbyde, forbyda, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌱𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (faurbiudan), English forbid, German verbieten, Dutch verbieden. Equivalen
From for- and Old Danish iate, iætte (“to promise”), from Old Norse játta, from Proto-Germanic *ja(h?)atjaną (“to assent”), cognate with Norwegian jatte, Old English ġēatan.

From Old Danish forta, fortæ (“space around a horse”), the same word as forte. A compound of for- and Old Norse tá n (“path”), from Proto-Germanic *tanhwą. Cf. Finnish tanhua (“stockyard”), which was borrowed from Proto-Norse or Proto-Germanic. The noun itself is derived from the adjective Proto-Ger

parole.significato: to regret (to feel sorry about some past thing)
parole.testo: From Old Danish tryde, from Old Norse þrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *þreutaną (“to harass”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk tryta (archaic), Swedish tryta, German verdrießen. The Danish form with the prefix is influenced by Middle Low German vordrēten.
From Old Danish fostær, from Old Norse fóstr (“rear, raise”), from Proto-Germanic *fōstrą.
From Old Norse frá, from Proto-Germanic *fram. Cognate with English from, Swedish från, Norwegian Bokmål fra, Norwegian Nynorsk frå, Faroese frá, Icelandic frá.

parole.significato: a Frank (a person from the historical Germanic tribe of the Franks)
parole.testo: From Old Norse frakkar pl, from Proto-Germanic *frankô m (“spear”), cognate with Old English franca (“spear”), Franca (“Frank”), German Franke. Borrowed to Medieval Latin Francus, Old French franc (“free, sincere”), Byzantine Greek Φράγκος (Phránkos, “Frank, person from Western Europe”), Arabic إِفْ
From Old Danish frith, from Old Norse friðr, from Proto-Germanic *friþuz, cognate with Swedish fred, frid, German Frieden, Dutch vrede.
From Old Danish frithæ, from Old Norse friða, from Proto-Germanic *friþōną, cognate with Swedish freda, German frieden, Dutch vreden.
From Old Norse freknur pl, s-less variant of Proto-Germanic *sprekalą (“freckle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to strew, sprinkle”), see also Latin spargo (“to strew, spray”).

From Old Danish frælsæ, from Old Norse frelsi, frjálsi, cognate with Norwegian frelse, Swedish frälse. Derived from the adjective frjáls (“free”), from Proto-Germanic *frijahalsaz (“freedom; free”), cognate with Old English frēols, Middle High German vrīhals, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌻𐍃 (freihals) (all nouns).
From Old Danish frelsæ, from Old Norse frelsa, frjálsa, cognate with Norwegian frelse, Swedish frälsa. Derived from the adjective frjáls (“free”), from Proto-Germanic *frijahalsaz, see above.

From Old Danish fram, from Old Norse framr (“forefront”), from Proto-Germanic *fram, from Proto-Indo-European *pr-, *pro-, *perəm-, *prom-, *promo- (“forth, forward”); see *per-. Originally the same word as fra (“from”).

parole.significato: a concubine, mistress of a king or nobleman
parole.testo: From Old Danish frithlæ, from Old Norse friðla, from Proto-Germanic *fridilǭ, feminine form of *fridilaz.
From Old Danish frest, Old Norse frest n, from Proto-Germanic *frestą, related to *fristiz in German Frist f. The modern Danish form is probably influenced by German.
From Old Danish fræstæ, from Old Norse freista, from Proto-Germanic *fraistōną, a North Germanic variant of *fraisōną.

From Old Norse frygð (“magnificence, splendour”). Cognate with Swedish fröjd. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *frewwiþō or *fruwwiþō, a variant of *frawiþō, which is found in Old High German frewida, German Freude, Dutch vreugd. The modern Danish word has been influenced by German.
From Old Danish frysæ, from Old Norse frjósa (“freeze”), from Proto-Germanic *freusaną. Cognate with Swedish frysa, English freeze, German frieren, Dutch vriezen.

parole.significato: saliva that is secreted around the mouth of animals or people.
parole.testo: From western Old Norse froða (which is also the source of English froth), from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ.
From Old Norse frændi, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, a present participle of *frijōną (“to love”). Cognate with Swedish frände, English friend, and German Freund.
From Old Danish fughl, from Old Norse fogl, fugl, from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, cognate with Swedish fågel, English fowl, German Vogel, Dutch vogel, Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌲𐌻𐍃 (fugls).
From Old Danish fuul, from Old Norse fúll, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz. Cognate with Swedish ful, English foul, German faul, Dutch vuil.

From Old Danish fuldær, full, from Old Norse fullr (“full”), from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, cognate with English full, German voll. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós, hence also Latin plēnus.

parole.significato: to be moved around by the wind
parole.testo: From Old Norse fjúka, from Proto-Germanic *feukaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“billow, bulge, drift”). Cognate with Lithuanian pūgà (“gust, blast, storm, blizzard”).
From Old Danish fyllæ, Old Norse fylla, from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄. Cognate with Swedish fylle, German Fülle. Derived from the adjective *fullaz (Danish fuld).
From Old Danish fyllæ, from Old Norse fylla, from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną, cognate with Swedish fylla, English fill, German füllen. Derived from the adjective *fullaz (Danish fuld).

Older form of fyrre. From Old Danish fyritiughu, from Old Norse fjórir tigir, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr tigiwiz (“forty”, literally “four tens”), cognate with Norwegian førti, Swedish fyrtio, English forty, German vierzig, among others. Note that the suffix -tyve in fyrretyve means “ten”, unlike t
From Old Norse fá, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną, cognate with German fangen, Dutch vangen, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (fahan).
From Old Danish fār, from Old Norse *fāʀ (east), fær (west), from Proto-Germanic *fahaz.

From Old Norse fé (“cattle, property”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål fe, Swedish fä, English fee, Dutch vee, and German Vieh. The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *péḱu (“livestock”), cf. Latin pecū (“farm animals”).
From Old Norse fella, from Proto-Germanic *fallijǭ, an alternative form of *fallǭ, the source of Old English fealle, German Falle.
From Old Norse fella, from Proto-Germanic *fallijaną, cognate with English fell, German fällen. Causative of *fallaną (“to fall”).
From Old Danish færth, from Old Norse ferð, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz. Cognate with German Fahrt (“journey, speed”). Doublet of fart (“speed”)).
From Old Norse ferðask, derived from ferð (< færd), from Proto-Germanic *fardiz.
From Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ, cognate with Swedish färja, English ferry, German Fähre. Derived from the verb *farjaną, see below.

parole.significato: to ferry, transport something by ferry
parole.testo: From Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjaną, cognate with Swedish färja, English ferry, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (farjan, “to sail”). Related to the verb *faraną (“to go, travel”).
From Old Danish fæstæ, from Old Norse festa, from Proto-Germanic *fastijaną, cognate with Norwegian feste, Swedish fästa, German festen. Derived from *fastuz (“firm”).

From Old Danish føthæ, from Old Norse fœða f, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijǭ, which is only found in North Germanic. Related words are *fōdīniz (in Middle Low German vōde, Middle High German vüete, Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐌴𐌹𐌽𐍃 (fōdeins)) and *fōdô (in English food).
From Old Danish føthæ, from Old Norse fœða, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną, cognate with Swedish föda, English feed, Dutch voeden.
From Old Norse fyl (“foal”), from Proto-Germanic *fulją. English foal and German Fohlen go back to a different derivation from the same root, Proto-Germanic *fulô (whence Old Norse foli).
From Old Danish fylghæ, from Old Norse fylgja, from Proto-Germanic *fulgijaną (“to follow”), related to Proto-Germanic *fulgāną in English follow and German folgen.

From Old Norse fyrr, from Proto-Germanic *furi, *furiz (“for, before”). Cognates include Swedish före, för, English for, and German für. A different form of the same word, Proto-Germanic *furai, is found in Danish for and German vor.
From Old Danish før, from Old Norse fœrr, from Proto-Germanic *fōriz (“able to go”), a verbal adjective of Proto-Germanic *faraną (“to go”) Danish fare.
From Old Norse fœra, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną, cognate with Swedish föra, German führen, Dutch voeren. A causative from *faraną (“to go”) (Danish fare).
From Old Norse fyrstr, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz, cognate with Swedish först, English first, German Fürst (“prince”, noun). Doublet of fyrste.
From Old Danish gallæ, from Old Norse gall, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.

parole.significato: sorcery, wizardry, spell, incantation (particularly in Old Norse times)
parole.testo: From Old Norse galdr, from Proto-Germanic *galdraz.

parole.significato: to crow (mostly of the sound of the cock)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gala (“to sing, crow, chant”), from Proto-Germanic *galaną, cognate with Norwegian gale, Swedish gala, English gale.

parole.significato: gallows (wooden framework on which persons are put to death by hanging)
parole.testo: From Old Danish galghæ, from Old Norse galgi, from Proto-Germanic *galgô, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“long switch, rod, shaft, pole, perch”).
From Old Norse galti, galtr, gǫltr, from Proto-Germanic *galtuz.

parole.significato: old (having existed for a relatively long period of time)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gamæl, from Old Norse gamall (“old”), from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz, cognate with Swedish gammal, Dutch gammel. The comparative and the superlative are formed from a different stem: ældre, ældst, from Old Norse ellri, ellztr, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô, *alþistaz, cognate with Englis
From Old Danish gamen, from Old Norse gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną.

parole.significato: the act of walking, a walk
parole.testo: From Old Danish gang, from Old Norse gangr, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ- (“stride, step”).
From Old Norse garn, from Proto-Germanic *garną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰorn-, *ǵʰer- (“gut, intestine”).
From Old Norse gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą.

From Old Norse gagn, from Proto-Germanic *gagną, related with the preposition Proto-Germanic *gagin (“against”) in Danish gen- (“re-”), igen (“again”), gennem (“through”). The English noun gain is a loan from Old Norse.
From Old Danish get, from Old Norse geit, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰayd- (“goat”). Cognates include Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍃 (gaits) and Latin haedus.
From Old Danish gømæ, from Old Norse geyma, from Proto-Germanic *gaumijaną, cognate with Swedish gömma, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌿𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gaumjan).

parole.significato: to herd, shepherd, guide, impel (people or animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish genæ, from Old Norse gegna, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną. Compare Old English gegegnian, German begegnen and Icelandic gegna.

parole.significato: through (in space, from one side to the other)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gegnum, dative of the adjective gegn (“right, fitting”), derived from the preposition gegn (“against”), from Proto-Germanic *gagin (“towards”). Compare also Danish igen, English again, against, German gegen, entgegen.
From Old Norse geirr, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰays- (“pointed stick, spear”).

From Old Danish getæ, gitæ (“to be able”), from Old Norse geta (“to get, guess”), from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to acquire”). The Germanic verb is related to Latin prehendō (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“take, seize”).
From Old Danish geldæ, from Old Norse gelda (“to castrate”), from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną.

parole.significato: a gimmer, a ewe between one and two years old (hasn't had offspring yet)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gimmer, from Old Norse gymbr, from Proto-Germanic *gimrį̄. Cognate with Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira).

From Old Danish getse, gitse, getsa (“to guess”), from Old Norse *getsa, *gitsa, from Proto-Germanic *gitisōną (“to guess”), from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to get”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to take, seize”). Cognate with Danish gåde (“a riddle”), Swedish gissa (“to guess”), Saterland Frisia
Inherited from Old Danish gifæ, from Old Norse gefa, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.

Expected form is gælde, now obsolete. The current form originates likely from a Funen dialectal gjalde, gjalle. From Old Danish gællæ, *giallæ, from Old Norse gella, gjalla, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną (“to shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”).
From Old Norse gjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *gerdō. The Old Norse word has been borrowed into English girth.
From Old Danish glath, from Old Norse glaðr, from Proto-Germanic *gladaz

Compound of glar + mester. First word is from Old Danish glar, glaar, from Old Norse glar, Derived from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”). Cognates include Icelandic gler and Faroese gler. Doublet of glas.

From Old Danish glænte, from a verb originally meaning "glide," from Old Norse *glenta, *gletta, from Proto-Germanic *glentaną (“to slide; glide”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰlend- (“to shine; sparkle; look”).
From Old Norse glóa (“to glow”), from Proto-Germanic *glōaną.
From Old Danish glæthæ, from Old Norse gleðja, from Proto-Germanic *gladjaną.
From Old Norse gneisti, from Proto-Germanic *gahnaistô (“spark”), from *ga- + *hnaistô (“spark”), perhaps from the ultimate source of German knistern (“to crackle”).

parole.significato: to laugh or cackle, especially in a mischievous or malevolent way
parole.testo: From Old Danish gnægjæ, from Old Norse gneggja, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną. Cognates include Swedish gnägga, Icelandic hneggja, Faroese gneggja and Norwegian knegge.
Inherited from Old Danish gōþær, gothær, from Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz. Cognate with English good and German gut.

parole.significato: godi (a priest in pre-Christian Scandinavia and in Nordic Neopaganism)
parole.testo: From Old Norse goði, from Proto-Germanic *gudô, a variant of *gudjô, which is the source of Proto-Norse ᚷᚢᛞᛁᛃᚨ (gudija) and Gothic 𐌲𐌿𐌳𐌾𐌰 (gudja, “priest”). Both words are derived from the noun *gudą (“god”) (Danish gud).

Probably from or related to Old Norse geldr (“barren, yielding no milk”), from Proto-Germanic *galdaz, *galdijaz (“barren, unfruitful”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout, cry”). See also Swedish gall (“barren”), German galt, gelt (“yielding no milk, unfruitful”), Old Norse gelda (“to castr
From Old Norse grǫn, from Proto-Germanic *granō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroH-néh₂-.
From Old Danish grannæ, from Old Norse granni, from Proto-Germanic *garaznô (“neighbour”).

From Old Norse grǫf, gröf, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”). Compare Norwegian and Swedish grav, Icelandic gröf, English grave, West Frisian grêf, Low German Graf, Graff, Dutch graf, German Grab.

parole.significato: dig (to move hard-packed earth out of the way)
parole.testo: From Old Norse grafa (“to dig, bury”), from Proto-Germanic *grabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).

parole.significato: a branch, bough (protrusion of wood from the trunk of a tree)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gren, from Old Norse grein (“branch”), from Proto-Germanic *grainō. Maybe related to the verb *grīnaną, if the original meaning was "to yawn". The noun has replaced the older Germanic word for "branch", *astaz.

From Old Danish gripæ, from Old Norse grípa (“to grab”), from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grasp, grab”). Cognate with Swedish gripa, Norwegian Bokmål gripe, Icelandic grípa, English gripe, West Frisian gripe, Low German griepen, Dutch grijpen, German greifen.
From Old Danish grim (“cruel, grim”), from Old Norse grimmr, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaz.
From Old Norse gríma f, from Proto-Germanic *grimô m (“mask; visor”). Cognates include English grime and grimace.
From Old Norse grína, from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną.
From Old Norse gróa, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreH₁-. Related to græs and grøn.
From Old Norse *grynta, from Proto-Germanic *grunnōną (“to grunt”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrun- (“to shout”). Cognate with German grunzen (“to grunt”), English grunt.
From Old Norse grár, from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz.
From Old Norse grátr, from Proto-Germanic *grētaz. Cognate with Norwegian gråt, Swedish gråt, and Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐍄𐍃 (grēts). Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”).
From Old Norse gráðugr, from Proto-Germanic *grēdagaz, cognate with English greedy, Dutch graag (“gladly”). Derived from the noun *grēduz (“desire”).

From Old Norse gráta (“cry”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną, cognate with Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, and Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (grētan). From Frankish *grātan, the verb was borrowed to French regretter (whence English regret). The Danish form has generalized the vocalism of the preterit (cf. Old Norse g
From Old Danish græs, from Old Norse gras (“grass”), from Proto-Germanic *grasą.
From Old Danish grøt, from Old Norse grautr, From Proto-Germanic *grautiz, *grautaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-.
From Old Danish, from Old Norse grœnn, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz (“green”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreH₁- (“grow, become green”).
From Old Norse guð (“god”), from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Cognate with English god and German Gott.

From Old Danish *guld, from Old Norse *gulð, *gulþ (compare Old Swedish guldh), variant of Old Norse gull, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Cognate to gul (“yellow”). Compare Runic Old East Norse: ᚴᚢᛚ (kul /⁠ḡull⁠/), ᛁᚢᛚ (iul /⁠jull⁠/).
From Old Norse golf (“floor”), from Proto-Germanic *gulbą.
From Old Danish gomæn, from Old Norse gómr, gómi, from Proto-Germanic *gōmô. Compare Swedish gom.
From Old Danish giutæ, from Old Norse gjóta, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną, cognate with German gießen, Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (giutan), Latin fundō, Ancient Greek χεῖν (kheîn).
From Old Norse gyðja, from Proto-Germanic *gudjǭ.

parole.significato: to shiver, shudder (due to fear, cold etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjósa, from Proto-Germanic *geusaną.
From Old Norse *gāʀ (East) / gær (West), from Proto-Germanic *gēz (“yesterday”).

parole.significato: farm, estate, land (property in the countryside)
parole.testo: From Old Danish garth, from Old Norse garðr, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål gård, Swedish gård, English yard, Dutch gaard. Related to gærde (“fence, wall”).

From Old Danish gas, from Old Norse gás, from Proto-Germanic *gans, cognate with Swedish gås, English goose, German Gans, Dutch gans. The Germanic noun derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns (“goose”), which is also the source of Latin ānser, Ancient Greek χήν (khḗn), Lithuanian žąsi̇̀s, Sanskrit
From Old Danish giald, from Old Norse gjald n (“payment”), from Proto-Germanic *geldą, cognate with Swedish gäld c (archaic), English yield, German Geld n (“money”).
From Old Danish gialdæ, from Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną (“to pay, have value”), cognate with Swedish gälda, English yield, German gelten.

From Old Norse gjǫlnar f pl, from Proto-Germanic *gelunō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-, cognate with Norwegian gjelle, Swedish gäl (English gill is from Old Norse), and distantly related to Ancient Greek χεῖλος (kheîlos, “snout, beak, lip”).
From Old Norse gestr, from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest”).
From Old Danish giæf, gæf, from Old Norse gæfr (“comfortable”), from Proto-Germanic *gēbiz, cognate with Dutch gaaf (“complete, smooth”). Derived from the verb *gebaną (“to give”).

parole.significato: feed (a portion of food for domestic animals)
parole.testo: From Old Danish giæf, from Old Norse gjǫf (“gift”), from Proto-Germanic *gebō, cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰 (giba). Derived from *gebaną (“to give”). A related word has replaced this word in its central meaning "gift", namely gave, which is probably a loan from Middle Low German gābe, from Proto-Germani
From Old Danish gøræ, from Old Norse gera, gøra, gørva, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną. Cognate with Swedish göra, German gerben (“to tan”). Doublet of garve and gære.
From Old Danish hath, from Old Norse hatr, from Proto-Germanic *hataz, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂d- (“hate”).
From Old Norse hata, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną.
From Old Norse haki, from Proto-Germanic *hakô.
From Old Norse hǫkull, from Proto-Germanic *hakulaz, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål hagel (from Danish), Norwegian Nynorsk hakel, Swedish hake, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌺𐌿𐌻𐍃 (hakuls).
From Old Danish haghæl, from Old Norse hagl, from Proto-Germanic *haglą (“hail”), cognate with Norwegian hagl, Swedish hagel, English hail, German Hagel, Dutch hagel.
From Old Norse halmr, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz.
From Old Norse hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.
From Old Danish half, from Old Norse halfr (“half”), from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.
From Old Norse hamr, from Proto-Germanic *hamaz, *hamô.
From Old Norse hamarr, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱmoros, from *h₂éḱmō (“stone”).
From Old Norse hampr (“hemp”), from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz.
From Old Danish hanæ, from Old Norse hani, from Proto-Germanic *hanô, from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”).
From Old Danish harm, from Old Norse harmr, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz.
From Old Danish harpæ, from Old Norse harpa (“harp”), from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ. Compare Norwegian Bokmål harpe, Swedish and Icelandic harpa, German Harfe, Dutch and English harp.

parole.significato: sea; ocean (large body of salt water)
parole.testo: From Old Danish haf, from Old Norse haf, from Proto-Germanic *habą, cognate with Swedish hav, German Haff (“bay”) (from Low German).
From Old Danish haghi, from Old Norse hagi, from Proto-Germanic *hagô. Cognate with Norwegian hage, Swedish hage, English haw, German Hag, Dutch haag.

From Old Danish hauæ, from Old Norse hafa (“to have, wear, carry”), from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have, hold”), cognate with English have, German haben. The Germanic words are from Proto-Indo-European *kap- and are not related to Latin habeō.
From Old Norse hǫfn (“haven”), from Proto-Germanic *habnō, from Proto-Indo-European *kopno-.

From Old Danish hafræ, from Old Norse hafri, from Proto-Germanic *habrô, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish havre, English haver (dialect), German Hafer (from Low German), Dutch haver. Derived from the noun *hafraz (“he-goat”).

parole.significato: to be called (to have a specific name)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hetæ, from Old Norse heita, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną (“to call”), cognate with Swedish heta, German heißen, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (haitan, “to call”).

parole.significato: whole, entire, complete, full (undivided, with all elements)
parole.testo: From Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, sound”), cognate with English whole, German heil, Dutch heel, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐌻𐍃 (hails).
From Old Norse heill (“omen, happiness”), from Proto-Germanic *hailzą, from the adjective *hailaz (“whole, sound”) (Danish hel). Compare Norwegian hell.
From Old Danish hælgh, hælagh, from Old Norse helgr f, from Proto-Germanic *hailagijō, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish helg. Derived from *hailagaz (“holy”).
From Old Norse heilagr, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz.

From Old Danish hælsæn, helse, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisǭ, cognate with Swedish hälsa. Ultimately derived from the noun *hailaz (“whole, sound”). Doublet of helse (“health”) and hilsen (“greeting”).

From Old Danish hælwitæ, from Old Norse helvíti, from Hel, hel (“the goddess of the realm of the dead”) (itself from Proto-Germanic *haljō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”)) + víti (“punishment”). Compare Norwegian and Swedish helvete, Icelandic and Faroese helví
From Old Danish hæntæ, hæmtæ, from Old Norse heimta, from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.

From Old Norse hestr (“stallion”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhistaz, a Verner alternation variant of *hangistaz, which is the source of the West Germanic word for “stallion”, cf. German Hengst and Danish hingst (a loanword from Low German).

From Old Danish helse, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisōną (“to salute, beseech”), cognate with Swedish hälsa (“to greet”), English halse (“to salute”), Old High German heilisōn (“to predict”).

From Old Danish himæn, himæl, from Old Norse himinn, from Proto-Germanic *himinaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish himmel, English heaven, German Himmel. The modern Scandinavian form with -l is influenced by German.

From Old Danish hin, from Old Norse hinn. The other Germanic languages have a similar, but phonologically distinct pronoun in the same function: Proto-Germanic *jainaz, cf. Old English ġeon, Old High German jēner, and Gothic 𐌾𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (jains).
From Old Norse hind, from Proto-Germanic *hindiz.
From Old Danish hinnæ, from Old Norse hinna, from Proto-Germanic *hinnǭ, cognate with Swedish hinna.
From Old Norse hinna (“to reach”), from Proto-Germanic *hinþaną, cognate with Swedish hinna (“to have sufficient time”), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌷𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌽 (frahinþan, “to take captive”).
From Old Norse hindra, from Proto-Germanic *hinderōną, cognate with English hinder, German hindern. Derived from the adverb and preposition *hinder (“behind”).
From Old Danish hittæ, from Old Norse hitta, from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną, cognate with Norwegian hitte, Swedish hitta, English hit (probably from Old Norse).
From Old Norse hjallr (“scaffold”), from Proto-Germanic *helþaz (“stack, frame”), cognate with Norwegian hjell, Swedish hjälle.
From Old Danish hælm, from Old Norse hjalmr (“helmet”), from Proto-Germanic *helmaz.
From Old Danish hēm, hiem, from Old Norse heimr, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz, cognate with Swedish hem, English home, German Heim, Ancient Greek κώμη (kṓmē).

From Old Danish hiarnæ, hiærnæ, from Old Norse hjarni (“brain”), from Proto-Germanic *hersô (“brain”), genitive *herznaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂s- (“head”). The same Germanic word is the source of Danish isse (“crown of head”), from Old Norse hjarsi, hjassi. A collective formation from this
From Old Danish hiærtæ, hiartæ, from Old Norse hjarta, from Proto-Germanic *hertô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”).
Inherited from Old Danish hion, hiona, from Old Norse hjón, from Proto-Germanic *hīwōnō.
From Old Danish hiorth, from Old Norse hjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *herdō, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hjord, English herd, German Herde.
From Old Danish hiort, from Old Norse hjǫrtr, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hjort, English hart, German Hirsch.

From Old Norse hjól, hvél, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, cognate with Norwegian hjul, Swedish hjul, and English wheel. The Germanic noun originates from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos (“wheel”), which is also the source of Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos) (cf. cyclus) and Sanskrit चक्र (cakrá
From Old Danish hiælpæ, hialpæ, from Old Norse hjalpa, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną. Cognate with Swedish hjälpa, English help, German helfen.
From Old Norse hyrna f, *hyrni n (not attested in Classical Old Norse, but in Middle Norwegian), from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ f, *hurniją n.
From Old Danish haldæ, from Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną, cognate with Swedish hålla, English hold, German halten, Dutch houden.
From Old Norse holmr, from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz.

parole.significato: wood, forest (of any size); (or strictly) coppice
parole.testo: From Old Danish holt, from Old Norse holt (“wood”), from Proto-Germanic *hultą (“wood”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”). Cognate with English holt and German Holz.
From Old Danish hunung, hunigh, from Old Norse hunang, from Proto-Germanic *hunangą.
From Old Norse hopp (“jump”), from the verb hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną.
From Old Norse hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną, cognate with Swedish hoppa, English hop, German hüpfen, Dutch hoppen.

parole.significato: a prostitute (a woman who earns a living by selling herself)
parole.testo: From Old Danish horæ, from Old Norse hóra, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”).
From Old Danish hors, Old Norse hross n, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą, cognate with English horse, German Ross n.
From Old Norse hósti (“a cough”), hósta (“to cough”), from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *kwas- (“to cough”).
From Old Danish hof, from Old Norse hófr, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hov, English hoof, German Huf.

parole.significato: temple (with reference to pre-Christian Norse religion)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hof (“shrine; court”), from Proto-Germanic *hufą, cognate with German Hof (“yard, court, farmyard”), Dutch hof (“yard, court, garden”). Doublet of hof (“court”).

parole.significato: head (the body part with the brain and main sense organs)
parole.testo: From Old Danish howæth, huwæth, from Old Norse hǫfuð, haufuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, cf. English head, dialectal German Haupt, Dutch hoofd. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *káput, cognate with Latin caput (“head”).
From Old Norse hugr, from Proto-Germanic *hugiz.

parole.significato: skin (outer covering of living tissue of a person)
parole.testo: From Old Norse húð, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish hud, English hide, German Haut, Dutch huid.
From Old Danish huvæ, from Old Norse húfa, from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ.

parole.significato: to cut, to hack, to slash, to hew
parole.testo: From Old Danish huggæ, hoggæ, from Old Norse hǫggva, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną (“to hew, forge”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk hogga, Swedish hugga, English hew, German hauen.

From Old Norse hol (“hole”), from Proto-Germanic *hulą, cf. English hole and German Höhle. The noun is derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”) (see below). Related to hule (“cave”).
From Old Norse holr (“hollow”), from Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”).

parole.significato: flesh (as a result of a certain state of nutrition)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hold (“flesh”), from Proto-Germanic *huldą.
From Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognates include Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs, “clement”) and Old High German hold ( > German hold). More at hold.
From Old Norse hundr, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, from *ḱwṓ (“dog”).
From Old Norse hundrað (“hundred”), from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).
From Old Danish hus, from Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”). Doublet of house.
From Old Norse hvat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód, *kʷod.
From Old Danish hwal, from Old Norse hvalr, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”).
From Old Norse hvelpr, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz.

parole.significato: sharp (able to cut easily; able to pierce easily; offensive, critical, or acrimonious)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hwas, from Old Norse hvass, from Proto-Germanic *hwassaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kvass, Swedish vass, Old English hwæs and Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐍃𐍃𐌰𐌱𐌰 (ƕassaba, adverb).
From Old Danish hwætæ, from Old Norse hveiti, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz.
