From Old Norse hverr (“who, each”), from Proto-Germanic *hwarjaz (“which”), *hwarjazuh (“each”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kven (“who”), kvar (“each”), Swedish vars (“whose”), varje (“each”) Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌹𐍃 (ƕarjis, “which”), 𐍈𐌰𐍂𐌾𐌹𐌶𐌿𐌷 (ƕarjizuh, “each”).
From Old Danish hwi, from Old Norse hví, from Proto-Germanic *hwī, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk kvi (archaic), Swedish vi (archaic), English why.
From Old Danish hwit, from Old Norse hvítr, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, cognate with English white and German weiß.

From Old Danish huilk, huilkin, Old Norse hvílíkr, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz (“what kind of, what sort of”), cognate with English which, German welcher, Gothic 𐍈𐌹𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (ƕileiks). A compound of *hwaz (“who”) + *-līkaz (“shaped”).
From Old Norse hvína, from Proto-Germanic *hwīnaną. Cognate with English whine.
From Old Norse hvess, genitive singular of hvo / hvem (“who”), from Proto-Germanic *hwaz (“who”).

From Old Norse hvískra, from Proto-Germanic *hwīskrōną, a variant of *hwistlōną (in Danish hvisle, Old Norse hvísla, English whistle), *hwisprōną (in English whisper, German wispern), and *hwisplōną (in German wispeln).
From Old Danish hwar(æ), huræ, huro, from Old Norse hvar (“where”), from Proto-Germanic *hwar

From Old Danish hwænnær, hwannær, from Old Norse hvénær, a compound of 1. Old Norse hvé (“how”), from Proto-Germanic *hwē, and 2. Old Norse nær (“closer”). An alternative explanation is that is related to (or borrowed from) Middle Low German wannēr (“when”) (cf. Dutch wanneer), which is a compound o

parole.significato: to arch (to shape, build or form something so that it forms an arch)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hwælvæ, from Old Norse hvelfa, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbijaną. Cognate of Icelandic hvelfa, Norwegian kvelva, Swedish välva, Middle High German welben, German wölben, Old Saxon bihwelvian, Gothic 𐍈𐌹𐌻𐍆𐍄𐍂𐌾𐍉𐌼 (ƕilftrjōm), English whelm, Dutch welven.
From Old Danish hwæssæ, from Old Norse hvessa, from Proto-Germanic *hwassijaną, cognate with Norwegian kvesse, Swedish vässa. Derived from the adjective *hwassaz (“sharp”) (Danish hvas).

From Old Danish hyggiæ (“to think”), from Old Norse hyggja (“to think”), from Proto-Germanic *hugjaną (“to think, reconsider”). The modern meaning has been taken over from Norwegian in the 19th century.
From Old Norse hylla, from Proto-Germanic *hulþijaną, cognate with Swedish hylla. Derived from *hulþaz (“gracious”) (Danish huld).
From Old Norse hylja, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną, cognate with Swedish hölja, German hüllen, Dutch hullen.
From Old Norse hirðir, from Proto-Germanic *hirdijaz (“herdsman”), derived from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”) (Danish hjord).
From Old Danish haand, from Old Norse hǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.
From Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą, cognate with English hair, German Haar, Dutch haar.
From Old Danish harth, from Old Norse harðr (“hard”), from Proto-Germanic *harduz (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *kert-, *kret- (“strong; powerful”).
From Old Danish hæthær, from Old Norse heiðr (“honor, worth”), from Proto-Germanic *haiduz.
From Old Norse hæll (“heel”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, cognate with English heel and Dutch hiel.

parole.significato: to happen (with or without an indirect object)
parole.testo: From Old Danish hændæ, from Old Norse henda, from Proto-Germanic *handijaną (“to seize”), cognate with Swedish hända. Derived from the noun *handuz (“hand”).

A merger of two related verbs: 1. Old Norse hengja (“to hang (transitive)”), from Proto-Germanic *hangijaną, cognate with German hängen; and 2. Old Norse hanga (“to hang (intransitive)”), from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną, cognate with English hang and German hangen. In the past tense, Danish still disti

parole.significato: That branch of the armed forces concerned mainly with ground (rather than air or naval) operations; the army.
parole.testo: From Old Norse herr, from Proto-Germanic *harjaz (“army”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“war”).
From Old Danish hærthæ, from Old Norse herðr, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.
From Old Danish hærthæ, from Old Norse herðr, from Proto-Germanic *hardį̄.
From Old Danish hæriæ, from Old Norse herja, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną, cognate with Swedish härja, English harry, German verheeren. Derived from the noun *harjaz (“army”), see hær.
From Old Danish he(e)s, from Old Norse háss, from Proto-Germanic *haisaz.
From Old Norse hetta, from Proto-Germanic *hattijǭ. Related to hat.

parole.significato: to raise, to elevate, to lift
parole.testo: From Old Norse hefja, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyé-, from the root *kap- (“to seize”). Compare Swedish häva, Norwegian Nynorsk hevja, English heave, West Frisian heffe, Dutch heffen, German heben.
From Old Danish høde, from Old Norse hœta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtijaną, cognate with Swedish höta (obsolete) (now replaced by hota), Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ƕōtjan).
From Old Danish høk, from Old Norse haukr (“hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, cognate with Norwegian hauk, Swedish hök, English hawk, German Habicht, Dutch havik.

From Old Danish høgh, from Old Norse (east) *haugʀ, (west) hár, hór, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, *haugaz (“high”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk høg, Norwegian Bokmål høy, Swedish hög, English high, German hoch, Dutch hoog.
From Old Danish høgh, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“height, high place, hill”), cognate with Norwegian haug, Swedish hög, Old High German houc.

Equivalent to høj (“high”) + -de (noun suffix): from Old Danish høgdh, from Old Norse hæð, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō. Other cognates are Swedish höjd, English height and Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌹𐌸𐌰 (hauhiþa). In Danish and Swedish, the noun has been remodelled after the adjective.

parole.significato: a depression in a river or stream or a cavern
parole.testo: From Old Danish hyl n, from Old Norse hylr m, from Proto-Germanic *hulwiją, cognate with Norwegian høl m, Old High German huliwa (“puddle”), German Hüle, Hülbe (“village pond”, dialect).
From Old Norse hǿna, from Proto-Germanic *hōnijǭ, related to *hanjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”), *kana-.

parole.significato: to hear (to perceive with the ears)
parole.testo: From Old Danish høræ, from Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, cognate with Swedish höra, English hear, German hören. The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti, which is also the source of Ancient Greek ἀκούω (akoúō).

From Old Danish høst, from Old Norse haust n, haustr m, from Proto-Germanic *harbistaz, *harbustaz, cognate with Swedish höst (“autumn”), English harvest, German Herbst (“autumn”), Dutch herfst (“autumn”) and Latin carpere.
From Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *en.
From Old Danish æ, e, from Old Norse æ, ei, ey, from Proto-Germanic *aiwi (“forever”), *aiwaz. May always be used as a prefix.

parole.significato: leech (a blood-sucking animal of the subclass Hirudinea)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ígull (“sea urchin”), from Proto-Germanic *igilaz (“hedgehog”), cognate with Swedish igle (“leech”), German Igel (“hedgehog”), Dutch egel (“hedgehog”). The sense is influenced by Middle Low German egel, ile (“leech”), which derives a related noun, *egulaz, which is also the source of

parole.significato: fire (flames from an object that burns)
parole.testo: From Old Danish eld, from Old Norse eldr (“fire”), from Proto-Germanic *ailidaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk eld, Swedish eld, Old Saxon ēld, Old English ǣled.
From Old Danish illæ. Originally the adverb of the obsolete adjective ild, from Old Norse íllr (adverb illa), from Proto-Germanic *ilhilaz, cognate with Swedish illa (only an adverb).
From Old Norse innri, from Proto-Germanic *innarô, cognate with Norwegian indre, Swedish inre, German innerer, English inner. Utilamtely derived from the adverb *in (“in”).
From Old Danish is, iis, from Old Norse íss, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-.
From Old Danish issæ, from Old Norse hjarsi (“crown of the head”), from Proto-Germanic *hersô.

parole.significato: lard, grease; a solid but soft fat from the intestines of certain animals
parole.testo: From Old Danish istær, from Old Norse ístr, from Proto-Germanic *instraz (“intestine”).
From Old Danish iak, iæk, iægh, æk, ak, from Old Norse ek, Old East Norse iak, from Proto-Germanic *ek, *ik (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm, *eǵh₂óm.

parole.significato: second person plural objective case – you, yourselves
parole.testo: Archaic eder, from Old Danish idher, edher, Old Norse yðr, from Proto-Germanic *izwiz, dative/accusative of *jūz (“you (all)”) (see I). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål dere, Swedish er, English you and German euch.

From Old Norse yðvarr, from Proto-Germanic *izweraz, possessive of *jūz (“you (all)”) (see I). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål deres, Swedish er, English your and German euer. In most Germanic languages, it is an inflected adjective, but in modern Danish (and Norwegian), it is uninflected. In archaizing

parole.significato: iron (metallic chemical element having atomic number 26, and symbol Fe)
parole.testo: From Old Danish jarn, from Old Norse járn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, cognate with English iron and German Eisen. The Germanic word is an old loan from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, cf. Irish iarann.
From Old Danish iorþ, iorth, from Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-.

From Old Norse jǫrðber, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją; equivalent to jord (“earth, soil, ground”) + bær (“berry”), as the berries are close to the ground, cognate with Icelandic jarðarber, Old Swedish iordhbær, Old English eorþberġe, Dutch aardbei, and German Erdbeere.
From Old Norse jól, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą, *jeulō.
From Old Norse jótar m pl, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz, cognate with Old English Ēotas, Īotas.

From Old Danish iæthtæ, arisen by rebracketing from iætæn (with the ending -n interpreted as a suffixed definite article), from Old Norse jǫtunn, from Proto-Germanic *etunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.

From Old Danish iafn, iæfn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz (“even, level”), cognate with Swedish jämn, Norwegian Bokmål jevn, Norwegian Bokmål/Norwegian Nynorsk jamn, English even, Dutch even, effen, German eben.
From Old Danish kakæ, from Old Norse kaka, from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ.
From Old Norse kalla (“call”), itself from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“call, shout”).

parole.significato: calf (a young cow or bull, also used of some other large animals, e.g., the offspring of a deer, whale, elephant, or rh…
parole.testo: From Old Norse kalfr (“calf”), from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish kalv, Dutch kalf, German Kalb, and English calf.

From Old Norse kambr, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, Norwegian, Swedish kam, English comb, German Kamm. The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth, peg”), which is also the source of Sanskrit: जम्भः (jámbhaḥ, “tooth”), Ancient Greek γόμφος (gómphos, “peg”), Polish ząb (“tooth”
From Old Danish kastæ, from Old Norse kasta, from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), cognate with Norwegian kaste and Swedish kasta. English cast is borrowed from Old Norse.
Inherited from Old Norse kǫttr, from Proto-Germanic *kattuz.
From Old Danish kænnæ, from Old Norse kenna (“know, feel”), from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną. Cognate with Swedish känna, German kennen, English ken. A causative form of *kunnaną (“to know”).
From Old Danish kiærnæ, kiarnæ, from Old Norse kjarni (“core”), from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”). Cognate with Swedish kärna and German Kern.

From Old Danish kith, from Old Norse kið (“young goat”), from Proto-Germanic *kidją, *kittīną (“goatling, kid”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gʰaydn-, *ǵʰaydn- (“goat”) or Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ- (“kid, goatling, little goat”). Compare Swedish and Norwegian Bokmål kid, English kid, German Ki

parole.significato: spring, fountain, source (a place where water emerges from the ground)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kelda, from Proto-Germanic *kaldijǭ, cognate with Norwegian kjelde, Swedish källa. Derived from *kaldaz (“cold”).
From Old Norse kitla, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną, cognate with Swedish kittla, English kittle, German kitzeln.
From Old Norse kinn, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu- (“cheek”). Compare Swedish kind, Norwegian and Icelandic kinn, Low German and German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin.
From Old Norse kippa (“basket”), from Proto-Germanic *kippǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gey- (“to bend, twist, entwine”). Influenced by Middle Low German kiffe (“hut”).
From Old Norse klappa, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.
From Old Danish klinæ, from Old Norse klína, from Proto-Germanic *kleinijan-, from Proto-Indo-European *gley-.
From Old Norse kló, from Proto-Germanic *klawō
A conversion of klaa(d)e, from Old Danish klathæ, from Old Norse kláði, from Proto-Germanic *klawiþô.
From Old Norse kljúfa, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“to cleave, split”), from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-.
From Old Norse knappr, from Proto-Germanic *knappô.
From Old Danish knif, from Old Norse knífr (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-.
From Old Norse knúi, from Proto-Germanic *knūwan. Compare Swedish knoge; further Danish knoge, German Knochen, Dutch knook, knokkel, English knuckle. Related to knogle and knuge.
From Old Norse knýta, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną.
From Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”).
From Old Norse *kōʀ (east), kýr (west), from Proto-Germanic *kōz.

From Old Danish koddæ, from Old Norse koddi (“pillow”), from Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“bag, sag, purse”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewt- (“pouch, sack”), from *gew- (“to bend, bow, arch, vault, curve”). Cognates include Swedish kudde and English cod

parole.significato: cock (male gallinaceous bird; dialectal, except when speaking about pheasants)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kokr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz.
From Old Danish kald, from Old Norse kaldr, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

From Old Danish komæ, kommæ, kombæ, from Old Norse koma, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, cognate with English come, German kommen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”), cf. Latin veniō, Ancient Greek βαίνω (baínō) (whence also base and basis).
From Old Danish kona, konæ, kunæ, from Old Norse kona, from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

Older konning, from Old Danish kunung, from Old Norse konungr (“king”), from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”), cognate with Swedish konung, English king, German König, Dutch koning. Derived from *kunją (“kin, clan”) (Danish køn).
From Old Norse konungdómr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz. Equivalent to konge + -dømme.

parole.significato: A nation having as supreme ruler, a kingdom.
parole.testo: From Old Norse konungríki, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to konge (“king”) + rige (“realm”). Compare Norwegian kongerike, Swedish kungarike, Dutch koninkrijk, German Königreich.

From Old Norse korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Related to kerne (“kernel, core”), from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“kernel, core”). Possibly also related to kærne (“(butter) churn”), from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ (“churn”) (see that entry for more).
From Old Norse kraptr, krǫptr, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz, cognate with English craft, German Kraft, Dutch kracht and West Frisian krêft.
From Old Norse krǫf f, from Proto-Germanic *krafō, related to Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”) (see kræve).
From Old Danish krok, from Old Norse krókr (“hook”), from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.
From Old Norse kroppr, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz. Cognate with Swedish kropp, English crop and German Kropf.

parole.significato: to crawl, creep (to move slowly or carefully)
parole.testo: From Old Danish krypæ, from Old Norse krjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål krype, Swedish krypa, English creep, Dutch kruipen.
From Old Norse krás, Proto-Germanic *krēsō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gras-, see also Ancient Greek γράω (gráō, “to eat, gnaw”). The Danish form is influenced by the verb, see kræse.

parole.significato: to serve something delicious, to give a treat
parole.testo: From Old Danish kræsæ, from Old Norse kræsask, from Proto-Germanic *krēsijaną, derived from the noun *krēsō (= Old Norse krás, Danish kræs). See kræs (“something delicious”), which shares the same root.
From Old Danish krævæ, kræviæ, from Old Norse krefja, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”), cognate with Swedish kräva, English crave.
From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, cognate with Swedish kol, German Kohle, Dutch kool, English coal.
From Old Norse kúla (“swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ, cognate with Swedish kula (“bump”), German Kaule (dated), Kuhle (“hollow”, from Low German), Dutch kuil (“pit”).
From Old Danish kunnær, kundær, from Old Norse kunnr, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz. Cognate with English couth.

parole.significato: to be able, can (with an infinitive)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, cognate with English con, German können. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”), which is also the source of the Danish words kende (“to know”), kunde (“customer”), kundskab (“knowledge”), kunst (“art”).
From Old Danish kwal, from Old Norse kvǫl, from Proto-Germanic *kwalō. Cognate of German Qual, Dutch kwaal, Old English cwalu. Compare origin of kvæle.

From Old Danish quinnæ, kvinnæ, from Old Norse kvenna, the genitive plural indefinite of kona (“woman, wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”). Related to English queen via Proto-Germanic *kwēniz.
From Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną (“to say”), cognate with English quoth (“said”), Gothic 𐌵𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌽 (qiþan, “to say”).

From Old Danish quik, qwegh (“alive, lively”), from Old Norse kvikr, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, cognate with English quick, German quick (from Low German), keck. Doublet of kvik, kæk, and kvaj. The modern use as a noun is an abbreviation of Old Danish qwikfæ, Old Norse kvikfé.
From Old Danish kwæld, from Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kweldą, *kwildiz
From Old Danish kwæliæ, kwælæ, from Old Norse kvelja (“to torment, torture”), from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną. Cognate with Swedish kvälja, English quell and German quälen (“to torture”).
From Old Norse kvirr, kyrr, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz, cognate with Swedish kvar, German kirre, Gothic 𐌵𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍂𐌿𐍃 (qairrus).

parole.significato: a grinder, mill (mechanical or electrical machine that pulverizes or grinds a material into powder)
parole.testo: From Old Danish kwærn, quærn, from Old Norse kvern, from Proto-Germanic *kwernō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerewn- (“millstone”). Compare Old English cweorn.
From Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz (“a kiss”). Probably an onomatopoeia.

parole.significato: to frighten, especially in a deterring way
parole.testo: From Old Norse kjósa (“to choose, influence with magic”), from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-.

parole.significato: to kiss (to touch with the lips)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kyssa, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną (“to kiss”), from *kussaz (“a kiss”).

parole.significato: exuberant, happy in an energetic way
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kátr, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz. Cognate with Swedish kåt.
From Old Norse *koʀ (East), kør (West), from Proto-Germanic *kuzą (“choice”). Cognate with Norwegian kår and Swedish kor. Derived from the verb *keusaną (“to choose”).
From Old Danish kiæft, from Old Norse kjaptr, from Proto-Germanic *kebutaz. Cognate with Swedish käft, Norwegian kjeft, Icelandic kjaftur, and Faroese kjaftur. Related to kæbe and kaje.

parole.significato: to comb with a comb or a fine-tooth comb
parole.testo: From Old Norse kemba, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną.
From Old Norse kjarr, from Proto-Germanic *kerzą (“brushwood”), cf. Swedish kärr.

From Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ, cognate with Icelandic kirna, Swedish kärna, English churn, German Kirne, Karn (regional words). Related to Proto-Germanic *kernǭ in Icelandic kerna (“creme”), Middle Dutch kerne, German Kern (regional word) and the following verb. These words may
From Old Norse *kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną, cognate with Icelandic kirna, Swedish kärna, English churn, German kirnen, Dutch karnen.

From Old Danish køpæ (“buy, purchase”), from Old Norse kaupa, past tense keypta, from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, *kaupijaną, cognate with German kaufen and Dutch kopen. The Germanic verb is probably a loan from Latin caupō (“tradesman”).
From Old Norse kjǫt, from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Cognate with Icelandic kjöt, Faroese kjøt, Norwegian Bokmål kjøtt, Norwegian Nynorsk kjøt and Swedish kött.
From Old Norse kjǫlr (“keel”), from Proto-Germanic *keluz (“keel”), cognate with Norwegian kjøl, Swedish köl. English keel, German Kiel and Dutch kiel are all borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Norse kœla, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną, cognate with German kühlen, Dutch koelen. Derived from the adjective *kōlaz (“cool”).

parole.significato: sex (the biological division in male and female individuals)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kyn (“kin”), from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, descent”). Cognate with Swedish kön, Norwegian Bokmål kjønn, English kin, Latin genus and Ancient Greek γένος (génos).
From Old Norse kœnn (“skilled, capable”), from Proto-Germanic *kōniz (“clever”). Cognate with English keen and German kühn (“daring”).

parole.significato: to drive (to be the driver of a vehicle or to convey somebody in a vehicle)
parole.testo: From Old Danish køræ, from Old Norse keyra, from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, Norwegian kjøre, Swedish köra.
From Old Danish lat, from Old Norse latr, from Proto-Germanic *lataz, from Proto-Indo-European *lē(y)d-.
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþǭ, derived from *hlaþaną (“to load”) (see below).
From Old Danish latæ, from Old Norse láta, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną.
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną.

parole.significato: layer, coat (a coherent mass spread on the top or on the outside of something else)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lag, from Proto-Germanic *lagą. Doublet of lav (“guild”) and lov (“law”).
From Old Norse lax (“salmon”), from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *laks- (“salmon”).
From Old Norse lami, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *lomiti.
From Old Danish lamb, from Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz (“lamb”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁-on-bʰ-os- (“lamb”)

parole.significato: country (a geographical area that is politically independent)
parole.testo: From Old Danish land, from Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, cognate with English land, German Land.

parole.significato: to land (get down to the ground or into the water after a flight or a jump)
parole.testo: From Old Danish lændhe, from Old Norse lenda (“to land”), Proto-Germanic *landijaną, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk lenda, Swedish landa (older lända), English land, German landen (older länden). Derived from the noun *landą (“land”). The verb has taken over the vowel from the noun in Danish.

From Old Danish langer, lang, from Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz (“long”), cognate with Swedish lång, English long, German lang. The adjective goes back to Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos, *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”), which is also the source of Latin longus, Ancient Greek δολιχός (dolikhós).

parole.significato: ling, common ling (the fish Molva molva, similar to the cod)
parole.testo: From Old Norse langa, from Proto-Germanic *langǭ, *langijǭ, cognate with Swedish långa, English ling, Dutch leng, German Leng. Derived from the adjective *langaz (“long”).
From Old Norse lǫstr, from the root of Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to reproach, blame”), see also Old High German lastar (“vice”).

From Old Norse hlátr, from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”). Cognate with Norwegian lått, English laughter and German Gelächter. Derived from the verb *hlahjaną (“to laugh”), cf. Danish le, English laugh, German lachen.
From Old Danish lagh, from Old Norse lágr, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz, cognate with Norwegian låg, Swedish låg. English low is borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Norse lag (“layer”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą. Doublet of lag, [Term?], and layer (the Old Norse plural lǫg lives on in Danish lov and English law).
From Old Norse lé (“scythe”), from Proto-Germanic *lewô, cognate with Norwegian ljå and Swedish lie.

parole.significato: to laugh (show mirth by peculiar movement of the muscles of the face and emission of sounds)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlæja, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną, cognate with English laugh and German lachen.

parole.significato: joint (movable connection between the bones in a body or a minor exterior part of the body; also of joints in a plant)
parole.testo: From Old Danish lith, from Old Norse liðr, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz.

parole.significato: gate (in a fence or at a level crossing)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse hliðr, from Proto-Germanic *hlidą, cognate with Swedish lid (“gate”), English lid, German lid (“eyelid”).
Inherited from Old Norse leiðr (“uncomfortable, tired”), Proto-Germanic *laiþaz, cognate with English loath, German leid (“distressing”), Dutch leed (“sad”).
From Old Danish lethæ, from Old Norse leiða (“to lead”), from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to lead”), cognate with English lead, German leiten. It is a causative of the verb *līþaną (“to go, pass”).
From Old Danish letæ, from Old Norse leita (“to seek, search”), from Proto-Germanic *wlaitōną, cognate with Old English wlātian (“to look upon”), Gothic 𐍅𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍉𐌽 (wlaitōn, “to look around”).

parole.significato: lodestar, star (or different thing) used for navigation
parole.testo: From Old Norse leiðarstjarna (“lodestar”), from Proto-Germanic *laidō + *sternǭ, equivalent to lede + stjerne.
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz, influenced by Middle Low German ledich.
From Old Norse leikr, from Proto-Germanic *laikaz.
From Old Danish lækæ, from Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną (“to jump, play”), cognate with Norwegian leike, leke, Swedish leka, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (laikan).
From Old Danish likum, likomæ, lekomæ, from Old Norse líkami, lík(h)amr, from Proto-Germanic *līkahamô, cognate with Swedish lekamen, German Leichnam (“dead body”), Dutch lichaam.

parole.significato: bed, bedding (anything that someone lies on)
parole.testo: From Old Danish leghæ, læghæ, a merger of two nouns: 1. Old Norse lega f (“lying in bed”), from Proto-Germanic *legǭ; and 2. Old Norse lægi n (“anchorage”), from Proto-Germanic *lēgiją. Both nouns are derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *ligjaną (“to lie”).

From Old Danish leghæ, from Old Norse leiga (“rent”), from Proto-Germanic *laigǭ, cognate with Norwegian leie, Swedish lega. Derived from Proto-Germanic *līhwaną (“to lend”), which is the source of Old Norse ljá and German leihen.
From Old Danish leghæ, from Old Norse leigja (“to rent”), from Proto-Germanic *laigijaną, cognate with Norwegian leie, Swedish leja. Related to the former word.
From Old Danish læghræ, from Old Norse legr, from Proto-Germanic *legrą. Cognate with Swedish läger n, English lair, German Lager n, Dutch leger.

parole.significato: limb (arm or leg in a human or an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Danish lim, from Old Norse limr, from Proto-Germanic *limuz (“branch, limb”), cognate with Norwegian, Swedish lem, English limb, Dutch leem.
From Old Norse hlemmr, from Proto-Germanic *hlammiz (“noice; lid”), cognate with Norwegian lem, Swedish läm, Old English hlemm, Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌼𐌼𐌰 (hlamma).
From Old Danish leer, from Old Norse leir, from Proto-Germanic *laizą, cognate with Norwegian leire, Swedish lera. Probably from the Indo-European root *h₂leyH- (“to smear”).
From Old Danish læt, from Old Norse léttr, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz. Cognate with Swedish lätt, Icelandic léttur, English light, Dutch licht and German leicht.
Inherited from Old Danish lev, from Old Norse hleifr, from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (“bread”), cognate with Swedish lev, English loaf, German Laib, Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃 (hlaifs).
From Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, cognate with Swedish leva, Norwegian leve, Icelandic lifa, Dutch leven, German leben, and English live.

From Old Danish liuær, from Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, cognate with English liver and German Leber. The Germanic word may be an irregular remodelling of the Proto-Indo-European word for "liver", *yókʷr̥, cf. Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar) and Latin iecur.

parole.significato: to leave (not eat or drink all of something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lifna (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *lifnōną, cognate with Swedish lämna (“to leave”), Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐌻𐌹𐍆𐌽𐌰𐌽 (aflifnan, “to remain”). The verb is an inchoative of *lībaną (“to stay”) (cf. also *libjaną (“to live”)).

parole.significato: approach (to draw near, in a figurative sense; to come near to in time)
parole.testo: From Old Norse líða (“to elapse”), from Proto-Germanic *līþaną (“to pass, go through”). Cognate with Middle Low German līden (“to suffer”), see above.
From Old Danish litæl, from Old Norse lítill, from Proto-Germanic *lītilaz, cognate of Swedish liten and Norwegian Bokmål liten.
Inherited from Old Danish lyk, from Old Norse líkr, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
Inherited from Old Danish līk, from Old Norse lík, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

From Old Norse líki, from Proto-Germanic *galīkō, cognate with Old English ġelīca (English like) and Old High German gilīhho (German seinesgleichen). Definite form of the adjective *galīkaz (“same, like”).
From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *galīkê, cognate with English like, German gleich. Adverb from the adjective Proto-Germanic *galīkaz (“same, like”), see lig.

parole.significato: to lie (be in horizontal position; be placed or situated)
parole.testo: From Old Danish liggæ, liggiæ, from Old Norse liggja (“to lie”), from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie down”). Cognate with Old English licgan (modern English lie).
From Old Danish lyst, from Old Norse list, from Proto-Germanic *listiz (“craft, art, guide”).
From Old Danish lif, from Old Norse líf, from Proto-Germanic *lībą.
From Old Norse lokka, from Proto-Germanic *lukkōną, cognate with German locken. Possibly related to *leuganą (“to lie”).
From Old Norse lof, from Proto-Germanic *lubą.
From Old Danish lowæ, from Old Norse lofa, from Proto-Germanic *lubōną, cognate with Swedish lova (“to promise; to praise”), German loben (“to praise”), geloben (“to vow”), Dutch loven (“to praise”).
From Old Danish louæ, from Old Norse lófi, from Proto-Germanic *lōfô.
From Old Danish lughæ, loghæ, from Old Norse logi, from Proto-Germanic *lugô (“flame”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”). Compare German Lohe, Swedish låga, Old English līeġ.

From Old Danish lykkiæ, lykkæ (preterite luktæ), from Old Norse lykja (preterite lukta), from Proto-Germanic *lukjaną (“to close, shut”). The modern Danish form has the vowel of the preterite and the participle. There may also be a contamination with the related strong verb Old Danish lukæ, lughæ (p

From Old Norse lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô (literally “the light organ”), cognate with Norwegian lunge, Swedish lunga, German Lunge, English lung. The noun is derived from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”).

From Old Danish ljunken, from Old Norse *ljumka, *lumka (“to warm”), from Proto-Germanic *hlēwanōną (“to make warm”), *hleumaz, *hlūmaz (“warm”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱal(w)e-, *ḱel(w)e-, *k(')lēw- (“warm, hot”). Cognate with Old Swedish lionkin (“lukewarm”), Old Swedish liumber (“warm, mild, t
From Old Norse lús, from Proto-Germanic *lūs, from Proto-Indo-European *lewH-.

From Old Norse lýti f (“ugliness”), lýti n (“flaw”), from Proto-Germanic *liutį̄ f (“deceit”), cognate with Swedish lyte n (“defect”), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌴𐌹 f (liutei). Derived from the adjective *leutaz (“deceitful”), cf. Old Norse ljótr (“ugly”), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐍄𐍃 (liuts, “dishonest”).

From Old Danish lythæ, from Old Norse hlýða, from Proto-Germanic *hliuþijaną. Cognate with Swedish lyda. Derived from Proto-Germanic *hleuþą (“hearing”), hence Danish lyd (“sound”). The verb originally had a weak conjugation.

parole.significato: heather, ling, (used for several plants in the heather family)
parole.testo: From Old Danish liung, from Old Norse lyng, from Proto-Germanic *lingwą. Cognate with Faroese lyngur, Norwegian lyng, Icelandic lyng, Swedish ljung.
From Old Danish lius, from Old Norse ljóss, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz.
From Old Danish lius, liys, from Old Norse ljós, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsą. Related to lue
From Old Danish lysæ, liusæ, from Old Norse lýsa, from Proto-Germanic *liuhsijaną. Derived from *leuhsaz (“light”, adjective) and/or *leuhsą (“light”, noun).
From Old Norse ljóski, from Proto-Germanic *leuskō, *leuskan- (“groin”), likely related to *leuhsaz (“bright, light”), perhaps originally meaning "light skin."

parole.significato: to desire, to want, to feel like
parole.testo: From Old Norse lysta, from Proto-Germanic *lustijaną, cognate with Swedish lysta, English list (archaic), German lüsten. Derived from the noun *lustuz (Danish lyst).

From Old Danish liughæ, lyffuæ, liffuæ, from Old Norse ljúga, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to tell a lie”). Cognate with Swedish ljuga, Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (liugan), German lügen, Dutch liegen, and English lie.
From Old Norse lok (“lock, lid”), from Proto-Germanic *luką (“lock, opening”), cognate with English lock, German Loch (“hole”).
From Old Norse loka (“bolt”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“to shut”).
From Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish lån, German Lehn (English loan is borrowed from Old Norse). Doublet of len.
From Old Danish lār, Old Norse lær (with ʀ-umlaut), from Proto-Germanic *lahwaz (“thigh”), cognate with Norwegian, Swedish lår, Old English lēow.
From Old Norse láss, from Proto-Germanic *lamsaz.

From Old Norse hlé, from Proto-Germanic *hlewą, cognate with English lee, Dutch lij, and German Lee. The adjective is probably originally a different derivation from the same root: Old Norse hlær, from Proto-Germanic *hlējaz (“warm”), compare also *hlēwaz (“warm”), which is the source of Icelandic h
From Old Danish læpæ, from Old Norse *lepi, from Proto-Germanic *lepô, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“lip”).
From Old Danish læthær, from Old Norse leðr, from Proto-Germanic *leþrą
From Old Norse leggr, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaz (“leg, thigh”). English leg is borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Danish lækæ, from Old Norse læknir, from Proto-Germanic *lēkijaz (“physician”), cognate with English leech, and Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐌺𐌴𐌹𐍃 (lēkeis, “physician”).

From Old Danish lægæ, derived from the noun. It replaced an earlier form with -n-: Old Norse lækna, from Proto-Germanic *lēkinōną (“to heal”), cognate with Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐌺𐌹𐌽𐍉𐌽 (lēkinōn), Old English lǣcnian, Old Saxon lāknon, Old High German lāhhinon. Compare (Western) Old Norse læknir where the opposite

From Old Danish læggiæ, læggia, from Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną (“to lay, place”), cognate with English lay and German legen. A causative from the verb *ligjaną (“to lie”), cf. Danish ligge. The two verbs are often confused in Danish in the infinitive and the present (and among s

parole.significato: to leak; to allow fluid to escape or enter something that should be sealed.
parole.testo: From Old Norse leka, from Proto-Germanic *lekaną.
From Old Norse lend, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄. Cognate with Swedish länd, Norwegian lend, Icelandic lend, German Lende, English lend, possibly related to Latin lumbus.
Equivalent to lang + -de: from Old Danish længth, from Old Norse lengð, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō. Cognate with Swedish längd and English length.

parole.significato: longish building of a larger building complex, typically a farmhouse
parole.testo: From Old Norse lengja (“long strap”), from Proto-Germanic *langijô, derived from *langaz (“long”). Compare Swedish länga with the same meaning as in Danish.
From Old Norse lengjask, a middle voice of the verb lengja (“to lengthen”), from Proto-Germanic *langijaną, derived from *langaz (“long”).

From Old Norse hlekkr, from Proto-Germanic *hlankiz (“chainlink, ring; bond, fetter”), from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“bendsome, flexible”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng-, *klenk- (“to bend; twist; wind”).

From Old Danish las, læs, from Old Norse hlass n, from Proto-Germanic *hlassą (“load”), cognate with Norwegian lass, Swedish lass. The Danish form has taken over the vowel from the verb læsse. The Germanic noun is derived from the verb *hlaþaną (“to load”), hence Old Norse hlaða (“to stack”), Danish
From Old Danish læsæ, Old Norse lesa (“read, collect, gather”), from Proto-Germanic *lesaną (“to gather”). Cognate with German lesen (“to read, gather”).

From Old Danish læssæ, lassæ, from Old Norse hlessa, from Proto-Germanic *hlassijaną, cognate with Norwegian lesse, Swedish lassa. Derived from the noun Proto-Germanic *hlassą (“load”), hence Old Norse hlass, Danish læs.

parole.significato: last (piece of wood used for shaping shoes)
parole.testo: From Old Norse leistr (“sock”), from Proto-Germanic *laistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *leys- (“track, furrow”). Cognate with Swedish läst, German Leisten, English last.
From Old Danish løpæ, from Old Norse hlaupa (“to leap, jump, spring”), Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną, cognate with Swedish löpa, English leap, German laufen, Dutch lopen.

parole.significato: to curdle (to make the milk run together)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hleypa (“to cause to run”), from Proto-Germanic *hlaupijaną, a causative of Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną (“to run”).
From Old Norse *hleypir, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupijaz, cognate with Icelandic hleypir (“rennet”), Norwegian løype, Swedish löpe. The noun derived from the verb *hlaupaną (“to run”).
From Old Danish lyt, from Old Norse litr, from Proto-Germanic *wlitiz, *wlituz (“appearance, look, aspect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to see”). Compare Icelandic litur, and Norwegian let.
From Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *launą n, cf. German Lohn.
From Old Norse hlynr, from Proto-Germanic *hluniz (“maple”).
From Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *laugnaz (“hidden”).
From Old Danish, from Old Norse lauss, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz
From Old Norse leysa, from Proto-Germanic *lausijaną, cognate with German lösen, Dutch lozen. Derived from the adjective *lausaz (“loose”) (Danish løs).

parole.significato: password (secret word used to gain admittance)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lausn, from Proto-Germanic *lausīniz.
From Old Norse lauf, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“peel, break off”). Cognate with English leaf.
From Old Norse matr, from Proto-Germanic *matiz, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish mat (“food”), English meat, German Mett (from Low German).
From Old Danish mathk, from Old Norse maðkr, from Proto-Germanic *maþukaz, diminutive of *maþô.

parole.significato: fellow (one of a pair, or of two things used together)
parole.testo: From Old Norse maki, from Proto-Germanic *makô, *gamakô, cognate with English match.
From Old Danish maghær, from Old Norse magr (“thin, meager”), from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Compare Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós)
From Old Norse mala, from Proto-Germanic *malaną (“to grind”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, rub, break up”). Cognate with Icelandic mala.

From Old Norse mjolka, from Proto-Germanic *melukōną (“to milk, to give milk”), cognate with Norwegian mjölka, Swedish mjölka, English milk. Old Danish molkæ and Old Norse molka go back to a different form, *mulkōną. Germanic also had a strong verb, *melkaną (“to milk”), surviving in Dutch melken an
From Old Norse malmr, from Proto-Germanic *malmaz.

parole.significato: mane (longer hair growth on the back of the neck of a horse)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mǫn, from Proto-Germanic *manō (“mane”).
From Old Danish man, from Old Norse *mannʀ, (west) maðr, from Proto-Germanic *mannz, *man(n)ô, cognate with Norwegian mann, Swedish man, English man, German Mann. Doublet of man.

From Old Norse mangr, from Proto-Germanic *managaz. Cognate with Norwegian mang, Swedish mången, English many, German manch. The Danish common gender form is arisen in a merger with the indefinite article en (which has later been added once more, see below).

parole.significato: field (wide, open space used to grow crops or to hold farm animals)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mǫrk (“wilderness”), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“border, marker”), cognate with German Mark f (“border land, marches”).

parole.significato: mark (unit of currency, in Denmark from the Middle Ages until 1875, in Germany and Finland until 2002)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“border, marker”), cognate with German Mark f (currency), originally the same word as the previous one.
From Old Norse mergr, from Proto-Germanic *mazgą.
Old Norse mǫsurr, from Proto-Germanic *masuraz

parole.significato: stomach, tummy, belly (the organ processing digestion of food)
parole.testo: From Old Danish maghæ, from Old Norse magi (“stomach”), from Proto-Germanic *magô, cognate with Swedish mage, English maw, German Magen (“stomach”).
From Old Danish mæth and Old Norse byrr, Proto-Germanic *buriz (“favorable wind”)

From Old Danish mikin, originally an accusative form of mikil, from Old Norse mikill, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“large, great”). Cognate with Icelandic mikinn, mikill, Norwegian mykjen, mykje, mye, Swedish mycken, mycket, English much and Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌺𐌹𐌻𐍃 (mikils). The older form with l is retained
From Old Norse mjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *melwą, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, rub, break up”). Related to male (“grind, crush”), mølle (“mill”) (via Latin), and to muld (“soil”).
From Old Norse mjǫl, from Proto-Germanic *melwą.
From Old Norse mein, from Proto-Germanic *mainą (“damage, hurt, injustice, sin”).
From Old Danish meneth, from Old Norse meineiðr, from Proto-Germanic *mainaiþaz (“perjury”), from *mainą + *aiþaz. Cognate of Old English mānāþ, German Meineid, Dutch meineed.
From Old Danish meræ, from Old Norse meiri (“more”), from Proto-Germanic *maizô.
From Old Danish mithiæ nat, from Old Norse mið nótt, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts. By surface analysis, mid- + nat. Compare Dutch middernacht, Icelandic miðnætti.

parole.significato: first person singular accusative personal pronoun; me
parole.testo: From Old Norse mik, from Proto-Germanic *mek (see there for more).

From Old Danish mighæ, Old Norse míga, from Proto-Germanic *mīganą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃méyǵʰeti, from the root *h₃meyǵʰ- (“to urinate”). Cognates include Latin mingō, Ancient Greek ὀμείχω (omeíkhō) and Sanskrit मेहति (mehati). The noun is derived from the verb.
From Old Norse mínn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz (“my”), genitive of *ek (“I”).
From Old Norse minni, from Proto-Germanic *gaminþiją, cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌹 (gaminþi).
From Old Norse minna and minnast, from Proto-Germanic *minþijaną. Cognate with Swedish minnas.

From Old Danish mistæ, from Old Norse missa, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną, cognate with Swedish mista, English miss, German missen. Doublet of misse (from English). The Danish form has -t- from the past tense and past participle (older miste and mist).
From Old Danish miøth, mioth, from Old Norse mjǫðr, from Proto-Germanic *meduz (“mead”), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey, mead”).
From Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, cognate with English mood, German Mut.
From Old Norse í mót, i.e. the preposition í (“in”) + the noun mót (“meeting”) (compare i møde), from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, cognate with English moot.

Developed from Old Danish mon. Compare Swedish mogen (“ripe”). Related to Old Norse móa (“digest”), from Old Norse móa (“to digest”), from Proto-Germanic *meuk- or *mūk-, from Proto-Indo-European *mewg- (“slimy, slippery”).
From Old Danish mothær, from Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

From Old Norse munu (“would”), muna (“to remember”), from Proto-Germanic *munaną (“to think, remember”), cognate with Old Saxon munan, Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌰𐌽 (munan). In older Danish, the present tense was mon in the singular and monne in the plural, whereas the past tense was monde. These forms have all coal

parole.significato: mother (woman who has, conceives, gives birth to, or raises a child)
parole.testo: From moder, from Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Old Danish morth, from Old Norse morð, from Proto-Germanic *murþą, *murþrą, cognate with English murder, German Mord. From Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“die”).
From Old Danish morthær, morþare, from Old Norse morðari (“murderer”), from morð (“murder”), from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“die”).

parole.significato: morning (the part of the day after midnight and before midday)
parole.testo: From Old Norse morginn, morgunn, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz. Compare Norwegian Bokmål morgen, Swedish morgon, Icelandic morgunn, English morn, morrow, Dutch morgen, and German Morgen.
From Old Norse mosi, mose, from Proto-Germanic *musą, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.

parole.significato: muzzle (the protruding part of an animal’s head which includes the nose, mouth, and jaws)
parole.testo: From Old Norse múli, from Proto-Germanic *mūlô.

parole.significato: mouth (the opening of an animal through which food is ingested)
parole.testo: From Old Norse muðr, munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, cognate with English mouth, German Mund.
From Old Norse mús, from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
From Old Danish myræ, from Old Norse *mýra, from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *morwís (“ant”), cognate with Icelandic maur. Compare Dutch mier, Serbo-Croatian мрав.
From Old Danish mætæ, from Old Norse meta, from Proto-Germanic *metaną, from Proto-Indo-European *med-. Merged with måle. Cognate with Swedish mäta
From Old Danish mal, from Old Norse mál (“language, speech, matter, affair”), from Proto-Germanic *maþlą. Cognate with Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌸𐌻 (maþl).
From Old Norse mál (“size, measurement, time, meal”) (from Proto-Germanic *mēlą).

parole.significato: moon (a natural satellite of a planet, especially the Earth's moon)
parole.testo: From Old Danish mane, from Old Norse máni (“the moon”), from Proto-Germanic *mēnô, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also måned.
From Old Danish manæth, manaþ, from Old Norse mánaðr, mónuðr, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also måne.
From Old Danish mord, marth, from Old Norse mǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.

parole.significato: must, have to, got to (duty or certainty)
parole.testo: From Old Norse mega (“must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *maganą, cognate with English may, German mögen. The original infinitive was lost and replaced by the past tense (in analogy with the verbs kunne (“could”), skulle (“should”), and ville (“would”), in which the infinitive and the past tense have

From Old Norse mjolk, mjǫlk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, cognate with mjølk, Swedish mjölk, English milk, German Milch, Dutch melk, and possibly Proto-Slavic *melko. The Germanic word ultimately derives from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (“to milk”), which is also the source of the verbs Latin mulge

From Old Norse merr (“mare, female horse”), from Proto-Germanic *marhijō, cognate with English mare, German Mähre. Derived from *marhaz (“male horse”), which is preserved in the word marshall, Danish marskal.

parole.significato: mark, sign, label, tag (some kind of marking on a thing, an animal or a person)
parole.testo: From Old Norse merki, from Proto-Germanic *markiją, cognate with Norwegian merke, Swedish märke. It has supplanted a shorter derivation from the same root, *marką, cf. Old Danish mark, Old Norse mark, English mark.

parole.significato: to mark (to put a mark on something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse merkja, from Proto-Germanic *markijaną, cognate with Norwegian merke, Swedish märka, German merken, Dutch merken.
From Old Norse mær, accusative mey, from Proto-Germanic *mawī (“girl”).
From Old Norse mœta (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną, cognate with Swedish möta, English meet, Dutch moeten. Derived from *mōtą, hence Old Norse mót, English moot.
From Old Danish mør, from Old Norse meyrr, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz. Cognate with English mellow and German mürbe.
From Old Danish myrk, from Old Norse myrkr, from Proto-Germanic *merkuz. Cognate with Norwegian mørk, Swedish mörk, and English murk.
From Old Norse myrkr n, from Proto-Germanic *mirkwiz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk mørker and Swedish mörker. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *merkuz, see Danish mørk.
From Old Norse nagli, from Proto-Germanic *nagalô, derived from *naglaz (“nail; peg”), which is the source of Danish negl, English nail, German Nagel (“nail; spike”).

From Old Danish næglæ, from Old Norse negla, from Proto-Germanic *naglijaną, cognate with English nail (Old English næġl(i)an), German nageln (Old High German negilen), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌲𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ganagljan). Derived from the noun *naglaz (“nail”). The modern Danish form is influenced by the noun and German n

parole.significato: nape; the back of the neck
parole.testo: From Old Danish nakkæ, from Old Norse hnakki, from Proto-Germanic *hnakkô, from Proto-Indo-European *knog-, *kneg- (“back of the head, nape, neck”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“to press, pinch, buckle, kink”). Cognate with English neck.
From Old Danish nat, from Old Norse nátt, nótt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Old Norse nǫf (“nave”), from Proto-Germanic *nabō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“navel”).
From Old Norse nafarr, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz. Cognate with Swedish navare, Norwegian navar and Icelandic nafar.

From Old Norse nafli, from Proto-Germanic *nabalô, cognate with English navel, German Nabel. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₃nobʰ- (“navel, nave”), which is also the source of Latin umbilīcus, Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós), and the Germanic word for "nave", *nabō.

parole.significato: name (word or phrase indicating a particular person, place, class or thing)
parole.testo: From Old Danish nauæn, nafn, from Old Norse nafn, from Proto-Germanic *namô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”).
From Old Danish nithær, from Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include Faroese and Icelandic niður, English nether, Dutch neder, German nieder.
From Old Danish naghæl, nahl, from Old Norse nagl (“nail”), from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
From Old Danish nighæ, from Old Norse hneigja, from Proto-Germanic *hnaigijaną.
From Old Norse næmr (“talented”), from Proto-Germanic *nēmiz (“takeable”).
From Old Norse næmi, from Proto-Germanic *nēmiją, related to the following word.
From Old Danish næmæ, from Old Norse nema, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną (“to take”), cognate with German nehmen.
From Old Norse níu, from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ (“nine”).

parole.significato: . feeling of intense hatred or strong envy.
parole.testo: Old Norse níð, from Proto-Germanic *nīþą. Cognate of Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐌹𐌸 (neiþ), Faroese níð, Icelandic níð, German Neid, Dutch nijd.
From Old Norse nítján, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun.

From Old Danish nokær, nogher, noghen, from Old Norse nǫkkurr, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk nokon and Swedish någon. Grammaticalization of the phrase Proto-Germanic *ne wait ek hwarjaz (“I don't know who = somebody”). For the expression, compare Old English nāthwylc (“somebody”) (from *ne wāt hwyl
From Old Danish north, from Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.

parole.significato: north, northwards, (north from one's immediate position)
parole.testo: From Old Danish northæn, from Old Norse norðan, from Proto-Germanic *nurþanē (“from the north”), cognate with Swedish norden, Old English norþan, Old High German nordan.
From Old Norse norrœnn and norðrœnn, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz.

parole.significato: Norwegian (of or relating to Norway, Norwegians or the Norwegian language)
parole.testo: From Old Danish nornst, cf. Middle Norwegian nornskr. The adjective was probably derived from Old Norse norrœnn (“Norwegian”), from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz (“northern”). Cognate with English northern.
From Old Norse nú (“now”), from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”). Cognate with English now.
From Old Danish ny, from Old Norse nýr, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”).
From Old Danish nytæ, from Old Norse njóta (“enjoy”), from Proto-Germanic *neutaną.
From Old Danish nyræ, niuræ, from Old Norse nýra, from Proto-Germanic *neurô.
From Old Norse hnjósa (“to sneeze”), from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną.
From Old Danish nyt, nøt, nyttæ, from Old Norse nyt, from Proto-Germanic *nutjō, cognate with Swedish nytta, German Nutzen. Derived from the verb *neutaną (Danish nyde).
From Old Danish nytt(i)æ, from Old Norse nytja, from Proto-Germanic *nutjōną, cognate with Swedish nyttja, German nutzen, nützen. Derived from the noun *nutjō, see above.
From Old Norse ná, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwijaną, cognate with Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐍈𐌾𐌰𐌽 (nēƕjan, “to approach”). Derived from *nēhwaz (“near”).

From Old Norse náðir f pl (“peace, security”), from Proto-Germanic *nēþō, *ganēþō, cognate with Swedish nåd, German Gnade, Dutch genade. The Scandinavian word has been influenced by Old Saxon Old Saxon (gi)natha.
From Old Danish naal, from Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin”).
From Old Norse nebbi, from Proto-Germanic *nabją, further unknown.
From Old Norse neita, from Proto-Germanic *niitjaną (“to say no”).
From earlier næp (“small, low”), probably related to Old Norse hneppr (“button”) and hneppa (“pinch”), all from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”).
From Old Danish næsæ, from Old Norse nǫs, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s-.
From Old Danish næstæ, from Old Norse næstr, a superlative of ná (“near”), corresponding to Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”) (compare English next).

parole.significato: nut (a fruit consisting of a hard, dry, lipid-rich seed usually contained within a hard shell)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hnot (“nut”), from Proto-Germanic *hnuts.
From Old Norse nauð, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, *nauþiz.
From Old Danish nøt, from Old Norse naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą.
From Old Norse neyða, from Proto-Germanic *naudijaną, cognate with Old English nīedan, Old High German nōten, Gothic 𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌾𐌰𐌽 (nauþjan). Derived from the noun *naudiz (“need”).

From Old Norse nakinn, nǫkkviðr (“naked”), from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”). Cognate with Swedish and Norwegian naken, Icelandic nakinn, English naked, West Frisian neaken, Low German naakd, Dutch naakt, German nackt.

parole.significato: ball (quantity of string, thread, etc., wound into a spherical shape)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hnykill (“swelling”), derived from the noun Proto-Germanic *hnukkaz, *hnukkô (“hook”), cf. Danish nok (“tap”) (dialect), Icelandic hnokki (“hook”), Old English hnocc (“hook, penis”).

parole.significato: a water-demon, the nixie, the nick; (mostly appearing as a grey horse-like creature with inverted hoofs and forward fet…
parole.testo: From Old Danish nøken, from Old Norse nykr, Derived from Proto-Germanic *nikwiz-, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *nigʷ-. Cognate include Old English nicor (“water-elf, hippopotamus, walrus”) (English nicker), Norwegian Nynorsk nykk, Swedish Näcken, German Nix, Dutch nikker and Ancient Greek νίζω (
From Old Danish nørræ, from Old Norse nyrðri, nørðri, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrizô, a variant of Proto-Germanic *nurþrōzô, the comparative of *nurþraz.
From Old Norse oddr, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz, cognate with German Ort (“place, point”).
From Old Danish ok, from Old Norse ok (“and, also”), from Proto-Germanic *auk. Cognate with Swedish och (“and”), ock (“also”), Dutch ook (“also”), and German auch (“also”).

parole.significato: ox (bovine animal used as a beast of burden or for food, especially a castrated male cattle)
parole.testo: From Old Norse oxi, uxi, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô, from Proto-Indo-European *uksḗn (“ox, bull”).
From Old Norse ǫld, from Proto-Germanic *aldiz, cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌳𐍃 (alds).
From Old Danish um, om, from Old Norse um, from Proto-Germanic *umbi. Cognate with German um (“about”).
From Old Danish ef, em, um, from Old Norse ef, from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”). Cognate with English if, German ob (“if”).

Equivalent to om- + gang, functions as a verbal noun of omgå and omgås. From Old Norse umgangr, from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz, cognate with Swedish omgång, German Umgang. The Danish word is influenced semantically by German.
From om + Old Norse krinkr (“ring, round”), from Old Norse umkring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz.

From Old Danish orth, from Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, cognate with English word, German Wort. The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”), which is also the source of Latin verbum.
From Old Norse ormr, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, cognate with English worm, German Wurm. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis, which is also the source of Latin vermis (“worm”).
From Old Danish oost, Old Norse ostr, from Proto-Germanic *jūstaz, *justaz.

From Old Norse átta, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, cognate with Swedish åtta, Norwegian Bokmål åtte, English eight, German acht. The Germanic numeral goes back to from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw, which is also the source of Latin octo, Ancient Greek ὀκτὠ (oktō).

From Old Norse ótta, from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ, cognate with Norwegian otte (“dawn”), German Uchte (“midnight or morning mass”) (Westphalia), Dutch ochtend (“morning”), Gothic 𐌿𐌷𐍄𐍅𐍉 (uhtwō, “dawn”).
From Old Norse ofn m, from Proto-Germanic *ufnaz, *uhnaz, *ugnaz, cognate with Swedish ugn, English oven, German Ofen, Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌽𐍃 (auhns).
From Old Norse padda, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ (“toad”), cognate with Swedish padda, German Low German Padde, Dutch pad.
From Old Norse pík, from Proto-Germanic *pīkaz, *pikkaz, cognate with English pike. Doublet of pik.
Verbal noun to pikke (“peck”), from Old Norse pikka, pjakka, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną.

From Old Danish plogh, from Old Norse plógr (“plough”), from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz, *plōguz (“plough”). Compare Swedish and Norwegian plog, Icelandic plógur, English plough, West Frisian ploech, Low German Ploog, Dutch ploeg, German Pflug.
From Old Norse pors, from Proto-Germanic *pursaz.
From Old Danish posæ, from Old Norse posi, from Proto-Germanic *pusô.
From Old Norse pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, cognate with English pound, German Pfund. An early loan from Latin pondō (“by weight”).
From Old Norse pota, from Proto-Germanic *putōną. Doublet of pode.
Inherited from Old Norse rǫð, from Proto-Germanic *radō (“row”). Cognate with Norwegian rad and Swedish rad.
From Old Norse raka, from Proto-Germanic *rakōną, cognate with Swedish raka, English rake. Related to *rekaną (“to pile”) and *rakjaną (“to stretch”).
From Old Norse rámr, from Proto-Germanic *rēmaz.
From Old Danish rand, from Old Norse rǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *randaz.
From Old Danish rafn, from Old Norse hrafn, from Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-. Onomatopoeic

parole.significato: to comb (to groom the hair with a toothed implement)
parole.testo: From Old Norse reiða, from Proto-Germanic *raidijaną (“to arange”), derived from *raidaz, see above.
From Old Danish ræghn, from Old Norse regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną.
From regn (“rain”) + bue (“bow”), from Old Danish ræghænbughæ, from Old Norse regnbogi (“rainbow”), from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô.
From Old Danish reknæ, from Old Norse regna, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną, cognate with English rain and German regnen. Derived from the noun *regną, cf. Danish regn.
From regn (“rain”) + vand (“water”), from Old Danish rægnwatn, from Old Norse regnvatn, from Proto-Germanic *regnawatōr

A merger of three related verbs: * The intransitive Old Danish rise, Old Norse rísa, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), related to English rise. * The transitive Old Danish resæ, Old Norse reisa (“raise”), from Proto-Germanic *raizijaną (“to raise”), related to English rear (raise is borrowed

parole.significato: a strip of unplowed land serving as a boundary between estates
parole.testo: From Old Norse rein f, from Proto-Germanic *rainō, cognate with Norwegian rein, Swedish ren, German Rain (English rean is from Old Norse).
From Old Norse hreinn (“clean”), from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz, cognate with Norwegian rein, Swedish ren, German rein, Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (hrains).

From Old Norse renna (“to make run, pour”), from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną, cognate with Swedish ränna, German rennen (“to run”). A causative of the verb *rinnaną (Danish rinde). The Danish verb is probably influenced semantically by German.

From Old Danish rensæ, rænsæ, from Old Norse hreinsa, from Proto-Germanic *hrainisōną. Cognate with Swedish rensa, Old High German reinisōn (English rinse is borrowed from Old French rincer). Derived from the adjective *hrainiz (“clean”).

From Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, cognate with Swedish rätt, rät, English right, German recht, gerecht. The Germanic adjective goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós, hence Latin rēctus (“straight”), Ancient Greek ὀρεκτός (orektós, “stretched out”).

From Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtuz, related to the adjective *rehtaz. The Danish word has been influenced by the German cognates Recht (“right, law”) and Gericht (“court”). The meaning “course of food” is influenced by Middle Low German richte and German Gericht.
From Old Norse rétta, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną (“to right”), cognate with English right, German richten. Derived from the adjective *rehtaz (“right, straight”).

parole.significato: reef (ridge of rock or coral in the sea)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rif, from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib”), cognate with English rib, German Rippe, Dutch rib (English reef, German Riff, Dutch rif come from Old Norse). Doublet of ribbe.
From Old Danish ræfsæ, from Old Norse refsa, from Proto-Germanic *rafsijaną

parole.significato: to ride (to sit on the back of an animal)
parole.testo: From Old Danish rithæ, from Old Norse ríða, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną, cognate with English ride, German reiten.
From Old Danish rik, from Old Norse ríkr (“rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, a derivative of *rīks (“king, ruler”), itself a borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs.
Equivalent to rig (“rich”) + -dom (“state of”), from Old Norse ríkdómr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, cognate with Swedish rikedom, English richdom, German Reichtum.
From Old Danish rikæ, from Old Norse ríki, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją, cognate of German Reich.
From Old Norse hrím, from Proto-Germanic *hrīmą.
From Old Danish rinnæ, from Old Norse rinna (renna), from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną, cognate with Swedish rinna, English run, German rinnen, Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐌰𐌽 (rinnan).
From Old Norse hringr, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz.
From Old Norse risi, from Proto-Germanic *risiz..
From Old Norse hrífa, derived from the verb Old Norse hrífa (“to grip”), from Proto-Germanic *hrībaną (“to grip, snatch”).
From Old Danish riuæ, from Old Norse rífa, from Proto-Germanic *rīfaną, cognate with Swedish riva, English rive. In the sense, "to rake", it is derived from the noun.
From Old Norse róa (“row”), from Proto-Germanic *rōaną (“to row”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁-.
From Old Norse rót, from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds. English root is borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Norse hrogn, from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”).

parole.significato: to shake (to move from side to side)
parole.testo: From Old Norse *rokka, *rukka, from Proto-Germanic *rukkōną (“to move, sway”). Cognate with English rock.
From Old Danish rugh, from Old Norse rugr, from Proto-Germanic *rugiz. Compare Norwegian Bokmål rug, Swedish råg, Icelandic rúgur, Dutch rogge, Low German Rogg, German Roggen, and English rye.
From Old Norse rúm, from Proto-Germanic *rūmą (“room, open space”), cognate with English room, German Raum, Dutch ruim, Gothic 𐍂𐌿𐌼 (rum).
From Old Norse rúmr, from Proto-Germanic *rūmaz (“roomy, spacious, open”), cognate with English room (archaic), German raum (archaic), Dutch ruim, Gothic 𐍂𐌿𐌼𐍃 (rums). Related to the noun.

From Old Danish rythjæ, from Old Norse ryðja, Proto-Germanic *rudjaną, a variant of Proto-Germanic *reudaną (“to clear”) (in Old Norse rjóða) and Proto-Germanic *rudōną (“to clear”) (in German roden).
From Old Norse hryggr, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz. Cognate with Norwegian and Swedish rygg, English ridge and German Rücken (“back”).
From Old Danish rykæ, from Old Norse rjúka, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. Cognate with Swedish ryka, English reek, German riechen.
From Old Norse hrár, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, cognate with English raw, German roh.
From Old Norse rá, from Proto-Germanic *raihô, *raihą, cognate with English roe, German Reh. Cf. Proto-Norse ᚱᚨᛇᚺᚨᚾ (raïhan) written on the 5th-century Caistor-by-Norwich astragalus.
From Old Norse rá, from Proto-Germanic *rahō, cognate with Middle Low German rā, German Rah.
From Old Norse hrópa (“to call out, cry, yell”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną. Cognate with English roop (“to cry”) and German rufen (“to call”).
From Old Norse rot, from Proto-Germanic *rutą. Related to Danish rådden (“rotten”) and rådne (“to rot”).
From Old Danish rathæ, from Old Norse ráða, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną. Cognate with English read and German raten (“advise, guess”).

parole.significato: withered or rotten seaweed and/or any other organic material near the sea, giving off a pungent stench.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hræ, from Proto-Germanic *hraiwą.
From Old Danish ræthæs, from Old Norse hræðast, from Proto-Germanic *hrēdijaną.

From Old Norse rekja (“to unroll”), from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną, cognate with German recken (“to stretch”). The Danish verb is also influenced by the unrelated verb Middle Low German rēken (“to reach, suffice”), German reichen, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną (“to reach”).

From Old Norse hrœpa (“to vilify”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōpijaną (“to call”), cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐍉𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (hrōpjan, “to cry out”). Derived from *hrōpaną (“to call”) (whence Danish råbe (“to shout”)).

From Old Danish røth, from Old Norse rauðr, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, cognate with English red and German rot. The Germanic adjective goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-, cf. Latin ruber, Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós).
From Old Danish røk, from Old Norse reykr, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz. See also ryge.
From Old Norse rœkt f, from Proto-Germanic *rōkiþō. Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną, hence Old Norse rœkja (“to take care”), German geruhen (“to deign”).
From Old Norse reyrr (“reed”), from Proto-Germanic *rauzaz, *rauzą.
From Old Danish røræ, from Old Norse hrœra (“stir, move”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną, cognate with English rear (“to stir”), German rühren (“to stir”).

From Old Norse rauf (“gap, rift, hole”), Proto-Germanic *raubō (“rift”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk rauv, ræv, Swedish röv. The noun is derived from the verb Old Norse rjúfa (“to break, tear”), from Proto-Germanic *reufaną (“to tear”).

From Old Norse reyfa (“to tear”), from Proto-Germanic *raubijaną, *raubōną. The Danish word has been influenced semantically by Middle Low German rōven, German rauben. The Germanic word was borrowed into Old French, French rober, whence English rob.
From Old Norse sǫðull, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sod-tlō-, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).
From Old Danish sak, from Old Norse sǫk, from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Cognate with Swedish sak, Icelandic sök, English sake, Dutch zaak, German Sache.
From Old Norse sǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *sagnō, cognate with Swedish sägen, Old English sæġen (“saying, statement”). Derived from *sagjaną (“to say”).
From Old Norse sax n (“sword”), sǫx n pl (“scissors”), from Proto-Germanic *sahsą (“sword”).
From Old Norse salr, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, cognate with German Saal, Dutch zaal. The Germanic word was borrowed to French salon.
From Old Norse sala (“payment”), from Proto-Germanic *salō, derived from *saljaną (Danish sælge).

From Old Norse salt (akin to Old Saxon salt, Old High German salz, Old Dutch salt, Old English sealt), from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Compare Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish salt.
From Old Norse sannr, saðr, from Proto-Germanic *sanþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sónts (“being, existing”), the present participle of *h₁es- (“to be”).
From Old Norse sandr, from Proto-Germanic *samdaz/

parole.significato: a saw (cutting tool with a toothed blade)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sǫg, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, cognate with Norwegian sag, Swedish såg, English saw, German Säge, Dutch zaag.
From Old Norse saga, from Proto-Germanic *sagōną, cognate with Swedish såga, English saw, German sägen, Dutch zagen. Derived from the noun *sagō (Danish sav).
From Old Danish se, from Old Norse (East) *sēa, (Old Norse (West) sjá), from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną, cognate with English see, German sehen, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”).
From Old Norse seigr, from Proto-Germanic *saigaz, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål seig, Norwegian Nynorsk seig, Swedish seg. Related to the verb *sīganą (“to sink”).
Inherited from Old Norse segl (“sail”), from Proto-Germanic *seglą, cognate with English sail, German Segel.
From Old Danish sighær, from Old Norse sigr (“victory”), from Proto-Germanic *segaz, cognate with Swedish seger, German Sieg, Dutch zege.
From Old Norse sigra (“win”), from Proto-Germanic *sigizōną. Derived from the noun *segaz (whence sejr).
From Old Norse sex, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs (“six”).
From Old Norse sextán, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun.
From Old Danish sialfær, sælf, from Old Norse sjalfr, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz. Cognates include English self and German selbst, selber. The sense "even" is probably influenced by German.
From Old Norse seinn (“late”), from Proto-Germanic *sainaz, *sainijaz, cognate with Old English sǣne.
From Old Danish sændæ, from Old Norse senda, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną. Cognate with English send, German senden.

From Old Norse sina, sin (“sinew”), from Proto-Germanic *senawō, cognate with Swedish sena, English sinew, German Sehne, Dutch zenuw. The word possibly goes back to Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥, which is also the source of Latin nervus, Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron).

From Old Danish sitiæ, sitia, sitæ, from Old Norse sitja, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, cognate with English sit, German sitzen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”), cf. Latin sedeō.
From Old Norse sik, from Proto-Germanic *sik.
From Old Danish sighæ, sæghiæ, from Old Norse segja, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną.

parole.significato: to charge (to make an accusation against)
parole.testo: From Old Danish sæktæ, derived from the noun Old Norse sekt (“penalty”), which is in turn derived from the adjective sekr (“guilty”), from Proto-Germanic *sakjaz.
From Old Norse síld, síl, from Proto-Germanic *sīlą.
From Old Norse sétti, from Proto-Germanic *sehtô (“sixth”).
From Old Danish siældæn, from Old Norse sjaldan (“seldom”), Proto-Germanic *seldanē, cognate with English seldom, German selten (“rare, rarely”).
From Old Norse skabb (“scab, scabies”), from Proto-Germanic *skabbaz.
From Old Danish skapæ, from Old Norse skapa, skepja, from Proto-Germanic *skapjaną. Cognate with German schaffen, Dutch scheppen, English shape.

From Old Danish skathi, skatha (“(oblique case)”), from Old Norse skaði, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô, from Proto-Indo-European *sket- (“to injure”); akin to German Schaden, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌸𐌹𐍃 (skaþis), Ancient Greek ἀσκηθής (askēthḗs, “unhurt, undamaged”), and English scathe.

parole.significato: a handle, a grip, a shaft (long thin handle, on for example a broom, knife, paintbrush, or pipe)
parole.testo: From Old Danish skaft, from Old Norse skapt, skaft, from Proto-Germanic *skaftaz.

From Old Danish skam, from Old Norse skǫmm, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European. Compare Norwegian and Swedish skam, Icelandic skömm, German Scham, English shame, Dutch schaamte.
From Old Norse skamma, from Proto-Germanic *skamāną, cognate with English shame, Dutch schamen, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌽 (skaman).

parole.significato: a host, a crowd; a large number of people
parole.testo: From Old Norse skari, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarō.
From Old Danish skarn (“skarn, filth”), from Old Norse skarn, from Proto-Germanic *skarną.
From Old Danish skarp(ær), from Old Norse skarpr, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
From Old Norse skattr, from Proto-Germanic *skattaz (“cattle, goods, wealth”).

From Old Norse skeið f (“reed, sley”), from Proto-Germanic *skaiþiz (“sheath, covering”), which is also continued by the Danish noun skede (“sheath”) (an old plural, cf. Old Norse skeiðir f pl (“sheath”)). Cognate with Norwegian skje (“spoon”) and skjede (“sheath”), Swedish sked (“spoon”), German Sc

From Old Norse skeiðir (“sheath”), plural of skeið (“reed, sley”), from Proto-Germanic *skaiþiz. The old singular is continued by the Danish noun ske (“spoon”). Cognate with German Scheide, Dutch schede, and English sheath. The anatomical sense is a semantic loan from Latin vāgīna.
From Old Danish skial, sk(i)æl, from Old Norse *skjal n, from Proto-Germanic *skilą (“division”), cognate with Norwegian skjell, Swedish skäl. Related to *skiljaną (see skille).

From Old Norse skip (“ship”), from Proto-Germanic *skipą. Cognate with English ship and German Schiff. The meaning "nave" is influenced by German Schiff, which is a loan translation of Medieval Latin navis (“ship, nave”). It has arisen through a confusion of two Greek words: ναῦς (naûs, “ship”) and

From Old Norse skítr, from Proto-Germanic *skītaz, *skitiz, cognate with Dutch schijt, English shit, German Schiss, Scheiß, Scheiße, German Low German Schiet, Norwegian Bokmål skitt, Norwegian Nynorsk skit, skitt, Swedish skit. Doublet of skejs.
From Old Norse skíta, from Proto-Germanic *skītaną, cognate with Swedish skita, English shit, German scheißen.
From Old Danish skiftæ, from Old Norse skipta, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną.

parole.significato: to separate (divide (a thing) into separate parts)
parole.testo: From Old Danish skiliæ, from Old Norse skilja, from Proto-Germanic *skiljaną (“to separate, limit”), cognate with Swedish skilja, English skill (partly from Old Norse).

parole.significato: skilling (A Scandinavian monetary unit and coin up to the 19th century.)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skillingr, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz, the same source of English shilling.
From Old Danish skin, skyn, from Old Norse skinn, Proto-Germanic *skinþą; from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kenH-
From Old Norse skína (“to shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną (“to shine, appear”).
From Old Norse skífa, from Proto-Germanic *skībǭ.

From Old Danish skiold, from Old Norse skjǫldr, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), cognate with Norwegian skjold, Swedish sköld, English shield, Dutch schild, German Schild. Doublet of skilt (“sign”).
From Old Norse skyrta (“shirt”), from Proto-Germanic *skurtijǭ, cognate with English shirt, German Schürze (partly from Low German). Doublet of skørt.
From Old Norse skjól, from Proto-Germanic *skeulą.

From Old Danish skylæ, skyulæ, from Old Norse skýla, from Proto-Germanic *skeulijaną, cognate with Swedish skyla, Dutch schuilen. Derived from the noun *skeulą. In Danish, the verb has taken over the vocalism of the noun skjul.
From Old Norse skór, from Proto-Germanic *skōhaz, of unclear etymology; possibly a derivative of *skehaną (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”).
From Old Danish skogh, from Old Norse skógr, from Proto-Germanic *skōgaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål skog, Norwegian Nynorsk skog, Swedish skog.

parole.significato: slide, slip, slip (e.g. of a moving vehicle, stocks, or values, also used positively)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skrið, from Proto-Germanic *skridą, cognate with Swedish skred. A verbal noun of *skrīþaną, *skrīdaną (Danish skride).

parole.significato: to skid (to slide uncontrolledly on a surface, e.g. if the surface is slippery or non-rigid)
parole.testo: From Old Danish skrithæ, from Old Norse skríða, from Proto-Germanic *skrīþaną, *skrīdaną, cognate with Norwegian skri, Swedish skrida, German schreiten.
From Old Norse skríkja, from Proto-Germanic *skrīkijaną.

parole.significato: very fine (and expensive) clothing worn on special occasions.
parole.testo: From Old Danish skruth, from Old Norse skrúð, from Proto-Germanic *skrūdą. Cognate with English shroud.
From Old Norse skref, from Proto-Germanic *skribą (“split”).
From Old Danish skut, skot, Old Norse skot, from Proto-Germanic *skutą.
From Old Norse skoða, Proto-Germanic *skuþōn, influenced by schauen.
From Old Norse skulu, from Proto-Germanic *skulaną. Cognate with English shall.
From Old Danish skurth, from Old Norse skurðr, from Proto-Germanic *skurdiz. Compare Swedish skörd
From Old Danish sky, from Old Norse ský, from Proto-Germanic *skiwją (“cloud, cloud cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”).
From Old Danish skiutæ, from Old Norse skjóta, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd-.
From Old Danish skuggæ, skyggi, from Old Norse skuggi, from Proto-Germanic *skuwwô (“shadow, reflection”). The Danish noun has taken over the vowel from the verb, see below.
From Old Norse skuld, from Proto-Germanic *skuldiz, cognate with Swedish skuld, German Schuld. Derived from *skulaną (Danish skulle).

parole.significato: to owe (to have debt, to be in debt)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skylda, from Proto-Germanic *skuldijōną, cognate with Swedish skylla, German schulden, Old English sċyldan.
From Old Danish skyndæ, from Old Norse skynda, skunda, from Proto-Germanic *skundijaną.
From Old Danish skal, from Old Norse skál (“bowl”), from Proto-Germanic *skēlō. Also compare Dutch schaal.
From Old Danish skæpnæ, from Old Norse skepna, from Proto-Germanic *skapnijǭ, from the past participle of *skapjaną.

parole.significato: scale (small plates of keratin on the skin of fish and certain reptiles)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skel f (“shell”), from Proto-Germanic *skaljō, cognate with Norwegian skjell, English shell, Dutch schil, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰 (skalja, “tile”).
From Old Danish skialuæ, from Old Norse skjalfa, from Proto-Germanic *skelbaną.
