From Old Danish skiæmtæ, from Old Norse skemta, from Proto-Germanic *skammatjaną (“to make short, briefen”). Cognate with Icelandic skemmta, Norwegian Nynorsk skjemta, Swedish skämta, and Faroese skemta.

parole.significato: rock, skerry (a rock in the sea, a little under or above the surface)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sker, from Proto-Germanic *skarją, cognate with Norwegian skjær, Swedish skär, German Schäre, Dutch scheer (English skerry is borrowed from Old Norse). Related to the verb *skeraną (“to shear”) (Danish skære).
From the verb skære (“to cut”). Partially also from Old Norse skeri m, from Proto-Germanic *skerô m, a variant of *skarō f in English share, German Schar. Doublet of skare.
From Old Norse skærr, from Proto-Germanic *skairiz, cognate with Norwegian skjær, Swedish skär, English sheer. Related to skinne.

parole.significato: cut (to make a cut with a knife or a sword)
parole.testo: From Old Danish sk(i)æræ, from Old Norse skera (“to cut”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną (“to shear”), cognate with Swedish skära, English shear, German scheren.

From Old Norse skeifr, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz (“crooked”), of disputed ultimate origin. Perhaps from the same source as *skeuhaz (“frightened, shy”). Another possibility is Proto-Indo-European *skeh₂iwos, the source of Latin scaevus (“on the left side”). See also Swedish skev, Dutch scheef, Ge
From Old Norse skyn, from Proto-Germanic *skunją; see skynja. Cognate with Norwegian skjønn, Swedish skön.

From Old Norse skyr (“coagulated milk”), from Proto-Germanic *skurją (literally “split, divided”), derived from the verb *skeraną (“to cut”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk skjør, Icelandic skyr. Doublet of skyr.
From Old Norse slag, slagr from Proto-Germanic *slagą, *slagiz, cognate with German Schlag.
From Old Norse sléttr, from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz, cognate with English slight, German slecht, slicht, with meaning influenced by Middle Low German slicht, slecht.

parole.significato: to delete (from a written text or a digital memory)
parole.testo: From Old Norse slétta (“to even out”), from Proto-Germanic *slihtijaną, cognate with German schlichten (“to smooth, settle”), Dutch slechten (“to smooth, remove”). Derived from the adjective *slihtaz (“even”).
From Old Danish slitæ, from Old Norse slíta, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną. Cognate with Swedish slita, English slit, German schleißen, Dutch slijten.

From Old Danish slik, from Old Norse slíkr, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz (“such”), cognate with Norwegian slik, English such, German solch, Dutch zulk, Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌰𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (swaleiks). A compound of *swa (“so”) + *-līkaz (“-like”).

A merger of two related verbs: 1. the intransitive Old Norse sleppa (past tense slapp), from Proto-Germanic *slimpaną, cognate with Swedish slippa. 2. the transitive Old Norse sleppa (past tense sleppti), from Proto-Germanic *slampijaną, cognate with Swedish släppa. The Danish word is influenced by
From Old Norse sløkkva, from Proto-Germanic *slakwjaną.
From Old Norse slá (“bar, rail”), from Proto-Germanic *slahō, derived from *slahaną (“to hit”).
From Old Norse slá (“to hit, beat, strike”), from Proto-Germanic *slahaną (“to hit, strike, kill”), cognate with English slay, German schlagen.
From Old Norse, from Proto-Germanic *slaihwǭ.
From Old Norse sleggja, from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.

parole.significato: to throw, toss or lay down (in a haphazard or careless manner)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Danish slenghe, earlier Old Danish slængiæ, from Old Norse slængja (variants: slyngja), causative to Old Norse slængva (sløngva), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slangwijaną. Has influenced Norwegian (bokmål) slenge; compare Norwegian Nynorsk slengja, which retains the diphthong f
From Old Norse sláttr, from Proto-Germanic *slahtuz.
From Old Norse sljór, slær, from Proto-Germanic *slaiwaz.
From late Old Norse smalr (“little”), from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Compare with English small.
From Old Norse smiðr, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz. Compare Icelandic smiður, German Schmied, Dutch smid, English smith.

From Old Danish smitæ, from a presumed Old Norse smíta, from Proto-Germanic *smītaną (“to sling; throw”). Cognate with Swedish smita, English smite, German schmeißen, Dutch smijten. The word is unknown in Old Norse sources.
From Old Norse *smíla (“to smile”), from Proto-Germanic *smīlijaną, *smirōną (“to smile”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, be glad, wonder”).
From Old Norse smjúga, from Proto-Germanic *smeuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewk-. Related to smug and smuk.
From Old Norse smeygja, from Proto-Germanic *smaugijaną. Related to smyge.
From Old Norse smjǫr, smør, from Proto-Germanic *smerwą. Cognate with English smear.
From Old Danish, from Old Norse snarr, from Proto-Germanic *snarhaz
From Old Norse snara (“a snare”), from Proto-Germanic *snarhǭ. Cognate with English snare.
From Old Danish snjo, from Old Norse snær, snjór, snjár, from Proto-Germanic *snaiwaz, cognate with Norwegian snø, Swedish snö, English snow, German Schnee.
From Old Danish snæghæl, from Old Norse snigill (“snail”), from Proto-Germanic *snigilaz.

From Old Norse sníða, from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sneyt- (“to cut”). Replaced by snitte, from Low German snitte, essentially from the same root. Compare Icelandic sníða, Dutch snijden, German schneiden, dialectal English snithe.

From Old Norse sníkja, from Proto-Germanic *snīkaną, cognate with Norwegian snike, Swedish snika, English sneak. In Old West Norse, the verb has a weak conjugation, but it is a strong verb in the continental Scandinavian languages and in Old English.
From the Old Norse snókr (“a snake”) or snákr (“only in poetry; a snake”), from Proto-Germanic *snakô; cognates include the Swedish and Norwegian snok, Icelandic snákur (“a snake”), English snake.
From Old Danish snytæ, from Old Norse snýta (“to blow one's nose”), from Proto-Germanic *snūtijaną. Cognate with Swedish snyta, German schnäuzen, Dutch snuiten.
From Old Norse sýr, from Proto-Germanic *sūz, from Proto-Indo-European *sū-.
From Old Danish sokn, from Old Norse sókn, from Proto-Germanic *sōkniz. Compare Swedish socken.
From Old Danish sol, from Old Norse sól, from Proto-Germanic *sōl (“sun”).
From Old Norse sáld, from Proto-Germanic *sēdlą (“sieve”).

parole.significato: as, like (introduces comparisons, both noun phrases and dependent clauses)
parole.testo: From Old Norse som, sem (“as, like”), cognate with Norwegian som, Swedish som. Probably a weakened form of Proto-Germanic *samą, *samô (“same, in the same way”), compare Old High German sama, samo, sam (“so, likewise”).
From Old Danish somær, sumær, from Old Norse sumarr, sumar, from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“summer”).
From Old Danish sorg, sorgh, from Old Norse sorg, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”).
From Old Danish swart, swartær, from Old Norse svartr (“black”), from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”).
From Old Danish so(o)t, from Old Norse sótt, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz. Cognate with Norwegian sott, Swedish (archaic) sot, German Sucht. Derived from the verb *seukaną.

From Old Danish souæ, from Old Norse sofa, from Proto-Germanic *swefaną. Cognate with Swedish sova. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *swep- (“sleep”) (whence also Sanskrit स्वपिति (svapiti)). From the same root also comes Danish søvn (“sleep”). Unrelated to English sofa.

parole.significato: a puncheon bridge (placed over a small waterstream/watercourse)
parole.testo: From Old Norse spǫng, from Proto-Germanic *spangō (“brooch, clasp”)
From Old Norse spara, from Proto-Germanic *sparāną, cognate with Swedish spara, English spare, German sparen.
From Old Norse spilla, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną.
From Old Norse spinna, from Proto-Germanic *spinnaną. Compare Swedish and Icelandic spinna, Norwegian Bokmål spinne, English spin, Dutch and German spinnen.
From Old Danish spir, spiræ, from Old Norse spíra (“reed; stalk; thin tree-shoot”), from Proto-Germanic *spīrǭ (“peak; point; tip; stalk”)
From Old Danish spolæ, from Old Norse spóla, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ. Cognate with Swedish spole, German Spule, Dutch spoel.
From Old Norse spor, from Proto-Germanic *spurą, from Pre-Germanic *spr̥Hom, derived from or related to *spurnaną (“to kick”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sperH- (“to trample”).
From Old Danish spottæ, from Old Norse spotta, from Proto-Germanic *sputtōną. Cognate with German spotten.
From Old Danish springæ, from Old Norse springa, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, cognate with English spring and German springen.

parole.significato: to blow up, to cause to explode
parole.testo: From Old Norse sprengja, from Proto-Germanic *sprangijaną, cognate with German sprengen. A causative from the verb *springaną, see springe.
From Old Norse spǫrr, from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *sperg- (“sparrow”).

From Old Norse spýja, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”). Compare Swedish and Norwegian Bokmål spy, Icelandic spýja, English spew, Dutch spuwen, German speien.
From Old Norse spá, from Proto-Germanic *spahōną, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish spå. A variant of *spehōną, which is the source of German spähen (“to spy”) (and, via French, English spy).
From Old Norse spónn, from Proto-Germanic *spēnuz.
From Old Norse spenna, from Proto-Germanic *spannijaną, cognate with Norwegian spenne, Swedish spänna. Doublet of spæne (“to sprint”).
From Old Norse sperra, from Proto-Germanic *sparrijaną.
From Old Norse spætr, from Proto-Germanic *spihtaz (“woodpecker”).
From Old Norse spyrja (“ask”), from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną. Cognate of German spüren (“to sense”), Dutch speuren (“to search thoroughly”), Scottish English speer.
From Old Danish stapæl, from Old Norse stǫpull, from Proto-Germanic *stapulaz. Cognate with German Staffel and English steeple.
From Old Danish stath, from Old Norse staðr (“place, city”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz. Originally the same word as sted (“place”).
From Old Norse stakkr, from Proto-Germanic *stakkaz.
From Old Danish stall, stoll, from Old Norse stallr, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz. More at stall.
From Old Danish standæ, from Old Norse standa, from Proto-Germanic *standaną. Cognate with English stand. Earlier used in a suppletive paradigm with stå (“stå”).

From Old Norse staðr (“place; city”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz. Cognate with German Statt and English stead, which are both restricted in their use. The meaning "city" is found in the cognates Danish stad, Swedish stad (“city”), and German Stadt (“city”). The Danish form sted has its vowel from t

parole.significato: step- (a prefix indicating the individual being referred to is related through the marriage of a parent)
parole.testo: Older stif-, from Old Danish stiup-, styp-, stib-, from Old Norse stjúp-, from Proto-Germanic *steupa- (“bereft, step-”), cognate with Swedish styv-, English step-, German stief-. In modern Danish influenced by the noun sted (“place, stead”) (virtually = "instead").
From Old Norse steik f (“roast”), from Proto-Germanic *staikō. Related to the verb *stikaną (“to stick”). English steak is borrowed from Old Norse.
From Old Danish stekæ, from Old Norse steikja, derived from steik (“roast”), from Proto-Germanic *staikō. Related to the verb *stikaną (“to stick”).
From Old Norse stemma, from Proto-Germanic *stammijaną (“to stop”).
From Old Norse stigi, stegi, from Proto-Germanic *stigô, derived from the verb *stīganą (“to ascend, climb”), see stige.
From Old Danish stighæ, from Old Norse stíga, from Proto-Germanic *stīganą, cognate with Swedish stiga, German steigen, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌴𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽 (steigan).

From Old Danish stiærnæ, from Old Norse stjarna (“star”), from Proto-Germanic *sternǭ, cognate with Swedish stjärna, English star, German Stern, Dutch ster, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌽𐍉 (stairnō). The word derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr, which is also the source of Latin stēlla, Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (ast
From Old Norse stertr, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz.
From Old Norse stokkr, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“stick”).
From Old Danish stoll, from Old Norse stóll, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāl- (“frame, rack, stand”).
From Old Norse stórr (“big, large, tall, great”), from Proto-Germanic *stōraz, cognate with English stour.
From Old Danish storm, from Old Norse stormr (“storm”), from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).
From Old Norse strengr, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ-.
From Old Danish strithæ, from Old Norse stríða, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaną.

From Old Danish strykæ, from Old Norse strjúka, from Proto-Germanic *streukaną. Cognate with Swedish stryka. The similar verbs English stroke and German streichen go back to an unrelated word, *strīkaną.
From Old Danish stra, from Old Norse strá (“straw”), from Proto-Germanic *strawą. Compare Old English strēaw.

From Old Norse straumr (“stream”), from Proto-Germanic *straumaz, cognate with English stream and German Strom. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”), cf. Ancient Greek ῥέω (rhéō) and Sanskrit स्रवति (srávati).
From Old Norse stútr, from or related to Proto-Germanic *stautōną (“to push”).

parole.significato: an undetermined amount of time, a while
parole.testo: From Old Danish stund, from Old Norse stund, from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“point in time, hour”), from the same root as stande, probably from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”) (see stå).
From Old Norse styggr, from Proto-Germanic *stugjaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål stygg (“ugly”), Norwegian Nynorsk stygg (“ugly”), Swedish stygg (“bad”), Dutch stug (“stiff”).
From Old Norse stykki, Proto-Germanic *stukkiją. Cognate with German Stück and Dutch stuk.
From Old Norse stýri (“rudder, helm”), from Proto-Germanic *stiuriją, cognate with German Steuer n, Dutch stuur n. Doublet of styr.

parole.significato: to head, govern, rule, manage, control
parole.testo: From Old Norse stýra, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną, cognate with English steer, German steuern, Dutch sturen. Doublet of styr.
From Old Norse stál, from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, from Proto-Indo-European *stak- (“to stay, be firm”). Compare Swedish and Norwegian stål, Icelandic stál, Dutch staal, German Stahl, English steel.

parole.significato: starling (a songbird, in particular Sturnus vulgaris)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stari, from Proto-Germanic *staraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tern- (“starling”).
From Old Norse starkr, from Proto-Germanic *starkuz, from Proto-Indo-European *sterg-.

From Old Norse steypa (“to cast, pour”), from Proto-Germanic *staupijaną (“to tumble, plunge”), cognate with Norwegian støype, Swedish stöpa (English steep is borrowed from Old Norse). The Germanic verb is related to the adjective *staupaz (“steep”) and the verb *stūpijaną, *stūpēną (“to stand out”)

From Old Norse steytr, from Proto-Germanic *stautiz. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk støyt, Swedish stöt, German Stoß, and Dutch stoot. The noun is related to the verb *stautijaną, *stautōną, cf. Danish støde, German stoßen.

From Old Danish støtæ, from Old Norse stauta, steyta, from Proto-Germanic *stautōną, *stautijaną, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk støyta, Swedish stöta, German stoßen, and Dutch stoten. The verb is related to the noun *stautiz (Danish stød).
From Old Norse stynja, from Proto-Germanic *stunjaną.
From Old Norse súga, from Proto-Germanic *sūganą, from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-.
From Old Norse súla, súl, from Proto-Germanic *sūliz, cognate with English sile (dialectal), German Säule, Dutch zuil. Doublet of søjle.
From Old Norse sund (“swimming, sound”), from Proto-Germanic *sundą, derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *swimmaną (“to swim”).

parole.significato: sour (having an acid, sharp or tangy taste)
parole.testo: From Old Danish, from Old Norse súrr (“sour”), from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, from Proto-Indo-European *súHros.
From Old Norse svala, from Proto-Germanic *swalwǭ. Cognate with English swallow.

A mix of the inherited Old Danish swan, from Old Norse svanr, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”); and the borrowed Middle Low German swane, from Old Saxon swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan. Cognates include German Schwan, Dutch zwaan and
From Old Norse svárr, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, cognate with Swedish svår, German schwer, Dutch zwaar. Doublet of svær. The Danish form with a is influenced by Middle Low German swār.

parole.significato: to answer, reply, respond (give a reply to a question; with a noun phrase or a noun clause as its object, with or witho…
parole.testo: From Old Norse svara (“to answer”), from Proto-Germanic *swarōną, cognate with Norwegian svare, Swedish svara, Middle English swaren. Derived form the noun *swarō (“solemn statement”).

parole.significato: Swedish (relating to the country, people or language of Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Norse svænskr, from Proto-Germanic *swihaniskaz (“Swedish”), cognate with Swedish svensk. Derived from *swihô (“Swede”).
From Old Norse svíða (preterit sveið), from Proto-Germanic *swīþaną.
From Old Danish swikæ, from Old Norse svíkja, svíkva, from Proto-Germanic *swīkwaną. Related to svigte.

parole.significato: (member of family Suidae) hog, pig, swine
parole.testo: From Old Norse svín, from Proto-Germanic *swīną, from an adjectival form of Proto-Indo-European *sū-.
From svippe (“to smack; crack a whip”), from Old Norse svipa (“to move swiftly; whip”), from Proto-Germanic *swipōną (“to move”). Compare Old English swipu (“a scourge, whip”). More at swipe.
From Old Danish swælghæ, from Old Norse svelgja, svelga, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą
From Old Norse svǫrðr m, from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind, turf”), cognate with Norwegian Bokmål svor, Swedish svål, English sward. The Danish form has the vowel of the plural (sverðir).

From Old Danish swar, from Old Norse svárr, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, cognate with Swedish svår, German schwer, Dutch zwaar, Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌴𐍂𐍃 (swērs). The vowel of the modern Danish form is probably due to German influence. Doublet of svar.
From Old Danish swærth, from Old Norse sverð, from Proto-Germanic *swerdą (“sword”), cognate with English sword, German Schwert, Dutch zwaard.
From Old Danish swæriæ, from Old Norse sverja, from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną, cognate with Swedish svär(j)a, English swear, German schwören, Dutch zweren.
From Old Danish swærm, from Old Norse svarmr (“swarm”), from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”).
From Old Danish swepæ, from Old Norse svipa f, from Proto-Germanic *swipǭ, related to the following verb.
From Old Danish swepæ, from Old Norse sveipa, from Proto-Germanic *swaipaną, cognate with Swedish svepa, English swoop, sweep, German schweifen.
From Old Norse svimma, svima, from Proto-Germanic *swimmaną.

From Old Norse sýja, from Proto-Germanic *siwjaną, cognate with Swedish sy, English sew. The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *syewH- (“to sew”), which is also the source of Latin suō, Sanskrit सीव्यति (sī́vyati), Lithuanian siū́ti.
Inherited from Old Danish suth, from Old Norse suðr, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą.

From Old Danish siuk(ær), syk, from Old Norse sjúkr (“sick”), from Proto-Germanic *seukaz. Cognate with Swedish sjuk, Norwegian syk, sjuk, English sick, German siech, Dutch ziek, West Frisian siik, Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐌿𐌺𐍃 (siuks).
From Old Danish syugæ, siwgæ, cognate with Swedish sjuka. Derived from Old Norse sjúkr (“sick”), from Proto-Germanic *seukaz.
From Old Danish siun, sȳn, from Old Norse sýn, sjón, from Proto-Germanic *siuniz. Related to se.
From Old Norse synd, from Proto-Germanic *sundī; compare Old English synn (modern English sin).

parole.significato: sing (to produce harmonious sounds with one’s voice)
parole.testo: From Old Danish siungæ, from Old Norse syngja (“to sing”), from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.

parole.significato: employment, occupation, enterprise (especially a quiet, non-binding, or less strenuous task)
parole.testo: From Old Danish sysæl, syslæ, from Old Norse sýsl, Proto-Germanic *seuhslō, from Proto-Indo-European *sewg-. Compare Old English susl.
From Old Norse sjaután, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun.
From Old Norse sjau, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ (“seven”).
From Old Norse sjaundi, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô. Derived from the cardinal number syv.

parole.significato: so (with adjectives, to the extent (that), often with a following dependent result clause introduced with the conjuncti…
parole.testo: From Old Norse svá, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, cognate with English so, German so, Dutch zo.
From Old Norse sá, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, cognate with English sow, German säen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-, which is also the source of Latin serō.
From Old Norse sár, from Proto-Germanic *sairą, cognate with English sore, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐍂 (sair). Derived from the following adjective.
From Old Norse sárr, from Proto-Germanic *sairaz, cognate with English sore, German sehr (“very”), Dutch zeer.

From Old Danish særæ, from Old Norse særa, from Proto-Germanic *sairijaną, cognate with Swedish såra. Derived from *sairaz (“wounded”). The modern Danish form has reintroduced the vowel of the noun sår.
From Old Danish sæth, from Old Norse sáð (“seed”), from Proto-Germanic *sēdiz. Related to så (“sow”).
From Old Danish sith, from Old Norse siðr, from Proto-Germanic *siduz, from Proto-Indo-European *swedʰ- (“custom, habit”).
From Old Danish sæte, from Old Norse sæti, from Proto-Germanic *sētiją, cognate Swedish säte, English seat, German Gesäß. Derived from the root *sitjaną (“to sit”).
From Old Danish sæc, from Old Norse sekkr, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic.
From Old Danish siæl, sial, from Old Norse selr (“seal”), from Proto-Germanic *selhaz.
From Old Danish sæliæ, from Old Norse selja (“sell”), from Proto-Germanic *saljaną, cognate with Swedish sälja, English sell.
From Old Danish sættæ, sætiæ, from Old Norse setja, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną, cognate with English set, German setzen. A causative of the verb *sitjaną (“to sit”) (Danish sidde).

parole.significato: lake (a large body of fresh water)
parole.testo: From Old Danish sio, syo, from Old Norse sær, sjór, sjár, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz. Cognate with Norwegian sjø, Swedish sjö, English sea, German See, Dutch zee.

From Old Danish supæ, from Old Norse súpa, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną. Also attested as søbbe, syb(b)e. Influences on the vowel likely included the older past tense søb (Old Norse saup) and the noun søbe (“pap”, Old Norse sopi).

From Old Norse sœtr, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, cognate with Swedish söt, English sweet, German süß, Dutch zoet. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂dus, which is also the source of Latin suāvis, Ancient Greek ἡδύς (hēdús), Sanskrit स्वादुः (svādúḥ).
From Old Norse sǿkja, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, cognate with Swedish söka, English seek, German suchen.

parole.significato: to nail (to fix with a nail)
parole.testo: From Old Norse seyma (“to stud”) (rare), from Proto-Germanic *saumijaną (“to sew, seam”), cognate with German säumen, Dutch zomen. Derived from the noun *saumaz (“stitch, seam”) (Danish søm).

From Old Danish sømæ, from Old Norse sœma (“to honour, be content, beseem”), from Proto-Germanic *sōmijaną (“to fit”), cognate with Old English sēman (“to reconcile”) (English seem is borrowed from Old Norse). Derived form the adjective *sōmiz (“suitable”). The modern Danish reflexive construction m

parole.significato: son (a male person in relation to his parents)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Danish sun, Old Norse sonr, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, cognate with Swedish son, English son, German Sohn. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *suHnús, which is also the source of Sanskrit सूनु (sūnú), Lithuanian sūnùs.
From Old Norse sundra, from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną, cognate with Swedish söndra, English sunder, German sondern, Dutch zonderen. Doublet of sondre.

From Old Danish sørghiæ, syrghia, from Old Norse syrgja, from Proto-Germanic *surgijaną, *surgāną (“to worry”). Cognate with Swedish sörja (“to mourn”), English sorrow and German sorgen (“to care”). The construction at sørge for noget is influenced by German für etwas sorgen.

From Old Danish syfn, from Old Norse svefn, from Proto-Germanic *swefnaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk svevn, søvn, Swedish sömn, English sweven (archaic). The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *swépnos (“sleep”), which is also the source of Latin somnus and Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpno

From Old Danish tapæ, from Old Norse tapa (“to lose”), cognate with Norwegian Bokmål tape and Swedish tappa. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *tapōną, *tappōną, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂p (“to sacrifice, lose”), cf. Latin damnum (“loss”) = Old Norse tafn (“sacrificial meat”).
From Old Norse þak (“thatch, roof”), from Proto-Germanic *þaką, cognate with Swedish tak, English thack, thatch, German Dach, Dutch dak.
From Old Danish takæ, taghæ, from Old Norse taka, from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”). Cognate with Norwegian ta, Swedish ta, and Dutch taken. English take is an early loan from Old Norse.
From Old Norse þǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz, cognate with English thank, German Dank.
From Old Danish thackæ, from Old Norse þakka, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną.

From Old Norse *þǫx, from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk svintoks, Swedish tax (“dachshund”), German Dachs, Dutch das. The Danish word may be a younger loan from German Low German Tacks (perhaps itself borrowed from Frisian, cf. Saterland Frisian Taks).
From Old Norse tal, from Proto-Germanic *talą (“number”), cognate with Norwegian Bokmål tall, Swedish tal, Dutch tal.
From Old Danish talæ, from Old Norse tala, from Proto-Germanic *talō.
From Old Danish talæ, from Old Norse tala, from Proto-Germanic *talōną, also from *talō.
From Old Danish tam, from Old Norse tamr, from Proto-Germanic *tamaz, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
From Old Danish tan, from Old Norse tǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.
From Old Danish tapp, from Old Norse tappi, from Proto-Germanic *tappô.
From Old Danish tharf, from Old Norse þǫrf (“need”), from Proto-Germanic *þarbō. Cognate with German Bedarf.

From Old Norse tjá, from Proto-Germanic *tīhaną (“to show”), cognate with Icelandic tjá, Faroese tíggja, Swedish te, German zeihen (“to accuse”). The verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”), which is also the source of Latin dīcō (“to say”), Ancient Greek δείκνυμι (deíknumi, “to sho

From Old Norse teikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną, cognate with English token and German Zeichen. The noun is derived from the verb *tīhaną (“to show, accuse”) (cf. Danish te (“to behave”), German zeihen (“to accuse”)).
From Old Danish thæghæn, from Old Norse þegn, from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz.
From Old Norse teikna, from Proto-Germanic *taiknijaną, cognate with German zeichnen and Dutch tekenen. Derived from the noun *taiką (“sign”), cf. Danish tegn.
From Old Norse þeisti, from Proto-Germanic *þaistô. Likely onomatopoeic.

Inherited from Old Norse tíu, from Proto-Germanic *tehun, cognate with Norwegian ti, Swedish tio, English ten, German zehn. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ (“ten”), which is also the source of Latin decem, Ancient Greek δέκα (déka).
Inherited from Old Danish tith, from Old Norse tíð, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis.
From Old Norse þegja, from Proto-Germanic *þagjaną, cognate with Swedish tiga, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (þahan). The Germanic verb is probably cognate with Latin taceō (“to be silent”).
From Old Norse tíundi (“tenth”), from Proto-Germanic *tehundô (“tenth”).
From Old Danish thiggiæ, from Old Norse þiggja, from Proto-Germanic *þigjaną. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to reach out the hand”).

parole.significato: to, towards (the direction or goal of a physical movement)
parole.testo: From Old Norse til, from Proto-Germanic *tilą (“goal”), cognate with Swedish till (“to”), English till, German Ziel n (“goal”). The preposition has arisen from an adverbial use of the noun, lit. "(with) the goal of something". In Old Norse, the preposition governs the genitive, a usage which is pres

From Old Norse tími, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), cognate with Swedish timme, English time. From Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y-, specifically Proto-Indo-European *deh₂imō. The Germanic noun *tīdiz (“time”) is derived from the same root.

From Old Norse þing n (“assembly, council, business”), from Proto-Germanic *þingą, cognate with Icelandic þing (“assembly, parliament”), Swedish, Norwegian Bokmål ting (“thing”), English thing, Dutch ding, German Ding.
From Old Norse títt (“often”), the neuter form of the adjective tíðr (“frequent”), from Proto-Germanic *tīdijaz. Derived from the noun *tīdiz (“time”).

parole.significato: to serve (a master, a country, a purpose)
parole.testo: From Old Danish thiænæ, from Old Norse þjóna, þéna, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną (“to serve”), cognate with German dienen. The verb is ultimately derived from the noun Proto-Germanic *þewaz (“servant”).
From Old Danish thiænæstæ, from Old Norse þjónusta, þénasta, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz.

parole.significato: a people, nation (of tribes in prehistoric Europe)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þjóð f (“people, nation”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō, cognate with Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰 (þiuda).

From Old Norse tjald (“curtain”), from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål tjeld (“curtain, tent”), Swedish tjäll (“hut”), and German Zelt (“tent”). The modern Danish word telt was borrowed from Low German (like English tilt and Swedish tält (“tent”)).
From Old Danish tiæræ, from Old Norse tjara, from Proto-Germanic *terwą, cognate with Swedish tjära, English tar, and German Teer.
From Old Norse þyrnir m, from Proto-Germanic *þurnijaz, *þurnijǭ, cf. Old English þyrne f. Derived from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz (“thorn”) (Danish torn).

From Old Norse tveir, from Proto-Germanic *twai, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”). The modern Danish form is a merger of the original East Old Norse accusative masculine twā and the nominative/accusative feminine twāʀ (West tvær). The neuter tū (West tvau) is preserved in the adverb itu.
From Old Danish thwa, from Old Norse þvá (“wash”), from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną.
From Old Norse tolf, from Proto-Germanic *twalif. Compare Norwegian and Swedish tolv, Faroese tólv, Icelandic tólf.
From Old Norse tómr, from Proto-Germanic *tōmaz (“empty”).

parole.significato: inch (a unit of length equal to one-twelfth of a foot, in Denmark 2.62 cm until 1907; in English-speaking countries 2.5…
parole.testo: From Old Danish thumæ, Old Norse *þumi, from Proto-Germanic *þumô, *þūmô (“thumb”). Cognate with Swedish tumme (“thumb”), German Daumen (“thumb”), and English thumb. As a measurements, it is originally equal to the width of a thumb. An old diminutive of this word is found in Danish tommel, tommelfin
From Old Norse toppr, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz.
From Old Danish thordyn, thordun. Made up of Old Danish *thor, from Old Norse þórr (from Proto-Germanic *þunraz) + dynr (“drone, noise, din, boom”). Compare Swedish tordön (“thunder”).
From Old Danish thorn, from Old Norse þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”).

parole.significato: A solitary farm, distant from other settlements.
parole.testo: From Old Norse þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, whence also German Dorf, German Low German Dörp, Dorp, Daarp, Dutch dorp and English thorp.
From Old Norse tog, taug, from Proto-Germanic *taugō.
From Old Danish thretiughæ, from Old Norse þrír tigir, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz (“thirty”, literally “three tens”).
From Old Norse þriði, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô (“third”).
From Old Norse þrettán, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun.
From Old Norse trúa, from Proto-Germanic *trūwāną (“to trust”), cognate with English trow and German trauen. Derived from the adjective *trūaz (“trustful”), see below.
From Old Norse trúr, from Proto-Germanic *trūaz (“trustful”), related to Proto-Germanic *trewwaz (“loyal, trustworthy”).

parole.significato: troll (supernatural being of the male gender)
parole.testo: From Old Danish troll, trǫll, from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą, from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂-.

parole.significato: thrush one of several species of songbirds of the family Turdidae
parole.testo: From Old Norse þrǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *þrasduz, from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. .

From Old Norse þrúga, Proto-Germanic *þrūgōną, cognate with Swedish truga. The verb is related to Danish trykke and German drücken (“to press”) (= *þrukkijaną), but apparently not to German drohen (“threaten”) (= *þraujaną) or English threaten (= *þrautōną).
From Old Danish tryg, from Old Norse tryggr (“true”), from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz.
From Old Danish thrykiæ, from Old Norse þrykkja, from Proto-Germanic *þrukkijaną. The meaning "to print" is influenced by the German cognate drucken (“to print”) (vs. drücken (“to press”)).

parole.significato: to evoke or produce events or changes through sorcery
parole.testo: From Old Danish tryllæ, from Old Norse trylla, from Proto-Germanic *truzlijaną (“to perform magic, conjure”).
From Old Danish trodhe, trædhe, Old Norse troða, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną (“to tread”). See under træde.
From Old Danish thraath, from Old Norse þráðr (“thread”), from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”).
From Old Danish trodhe, trædhe, Old Norse troða, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną (“to tread”). See under træde.

From Old Norse tré (“tree”), from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree, wood”), from pre-Germanic *dréu̯om, thematic e-grade derivative of Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”). Cognates From the same Proto-Germanic root: Swedish trä (“wood”), träd (“tree”), Norwegian tre (“tree”), Icelandic tré (“tree”), Engl

From Old Danish trodhe, trædhe, from Old Norse troða, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną (“to tread”), cognate with Norwegian Bokmål tre, Swedish träda, English tread, German treten. The modern Scandinavian form with e-vocalism is influenced by Middle Low German treden. The o-vocalism is retained in Norwe
From Old Norse *þræða, from Proto-Germanic *þrēdijaną (“to thread”), cf. also Icelandic þræða, Norwegian træ, Swedish träda. Derived from the noun tråd, Proto-Germanic *þrēduz (“thread”).
From Old Norse tregr, from or related to Proto-Germanic *tregô (“sadness, sluggishness”).

From Old Danish thræl, from Old Norse þræll, from Proto-Germanic *þragilaz, *þrahilaz, *þrēhilaz, from the root *þreh-, *þreg-, *þrag- ‘to run’, from Proto-Indo-European *trāgʰ- (“pull, drag, race, run”).

parole.significato: to need, want (normally with the preposition til)
parole.testo: From Old Danish thrængia, from Old Norse (east) þrengja, (west) þrøngva, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwijaną (“to press, push”), cognate with Norwegian trenge, Swedish tränga, German drängen. A causative of *þrinhwaną (“to press, to push”).

parole.significato: tired (in need of rest and/or sleep)
parole.testo: From Old Danish thræt, from Old Norse þreyttr, a past participle of þreyta (“to tire”), from Proto-Germanic *þrautijaną, a causative of *þreutaną (Danish fortryde).
From Old Danish træuel, trefflæ, from Old Norse trefill (“thread, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *trabilaz, derived from *trabō (“fringe”).
From Old Norse tún, from Proto-Germanic *tūną, from Proto-Celtic *dūnom.
From Old Danish thung, from Old Norse þungr, from Proto-Germanic *þunguz, from *tengʰ- (“to pull back, be heavy”), cf. Lithuanian tingùs (“heavy”), Russian тя́жкий (tjážkij, “hard”).

From Old Danish tungæ, Old Norse tunga, Proto-Germanic *tungǭ, cognate with English tongue, German Zunge, Gothic 𐍄𐌿𐌲𐌲𐍉 (tuggō). The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”), cf. Latin lingua, Sanskrit जिह्वा (jihvā́).
A merger of two unrelated verbs: 1. Old Norse þora (“to dare”), of unknown origin, and 2. þurfa (“to need”), from Proto-Germanic *þurbaną, related to German dürfen.
From Old Danish thusændæ, thusænd, thusind, thusand, from Old Norse þúsund, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī.
From Old Norse tve-, tví-, from Proto-Germanic *twi-, *twī-.
From Old Danish twennæ, from Old Norse tvennir, from Proto-Germanic *twinaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.
From Old Norse tvinna, from Proto-Germanic *twiznōną, *twiznāną (“to thread”).
From Old Danish thwængæ (“thong”), from Old Norse þvengr, from Proto-Germanic *þwanguz, *þwangiz, cognate with English thong, German Zwang. Doublet of tvang. Related to the following verb.
From Old Danish thwingæ, from Old Norse þvinga, from Proto-Germanic *þwinhaną, cognate with Swedish tvinga, German zwingen, Dutch dwingen.

From Old Danish thwær, from Old Norse þverr (“transverse, adverse, obstinate”), from Proto-Germanic *þwerhaz (“cross, adverse”), cognate with Swedish tvär, German quer, Dutch dwars, Gothic 𐌸𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌷𐍃 (þwairhs).

From Old Norse þvers, from Proto-Germanic *þwerhas (“across”), cognate with Swedish tvers, Swedish tvärs, Old English þwēores, Middle High German twerhes, Middle Low German dwers (adjective), Dutch dwars (adjective). An adverbial genitive of the adjective *þwerhaz (“cross, adverse”) (Danish tvær).

From Old Norse þýða (“to make friends”), Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną, cognate with Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐌸𐌾𐌰𐌽 (þiuþjan, “to bless”). It may originally be the same verb as *þiudijaną (“to interpret”), which is the source of Old Norse þýða (whence Danish tyde) and German deuten.

From Old Norse þýða, from Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną (“to interpret”), cognate with Swedish tyda, German deuten, Low German düden, Dutch duiden. Possibly the same verb as *þiudijaną (“make friend with”), continued by Danish ty (“to resort”).

Maybe from an (incorrect) abbreviation of Old Danish thjanestehjon (“household”), or related to þý (“female thrall”), from Old Norse þjóna, þéna, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną (“to serve”). The verb is ultimately derived from the noun Proto-Germanic *þewaz (“servant”). See modern Danish træl (“thral
From Old Norse tyggva, tyggja, from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną. Cognate with English chew and German kauen (“to chew”).
From Old Danish thiøc, thyk, from Old Norse þykkr, þjukkr, þjokkr, from Proto-Germanic *þekuz.

Old Danish thykk(i)æ, from Old Norse þykkja (“to seem”), from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną (“to seem, to appear”), cognate with Swedish tycka, English think, German dünken. Related to Danish tænke. In the modern standard language replaced by synes.
From Old Danish thun, from Old Norse þunnr, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”).
From Old Norse þyngd, from Proto-Germanic *þungiþō, derived from *þunguz (“heavy”).

From Old Danish thiur, from Old Norse þjórr (“bull”), from Proto-Germanic *þeuraz. The West Germanic languages have a form with s-: English steer, Dutch stier and German Stier. These Germanic words seem to be related to Latin taurus (“bull”) and Ancient Greek ταῦρος (taûros, “bull”), which may go ba
From Old Danish thiuf, þiufær, from Old Norse þjófr, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.
From Old Norse tuttugu, tjogu, from Proto-Germanic *twai tigiwiz.

parole.significato: toe (part of a foot; also part of a sock, stocking or shoe)
parole.testo: From Old Danish ta, from Old Norse tá, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ.
From Old Danish thokæ, from Old Norse þoka, from Proto-Germanic *þukōną.

parole.significato: to put up with, bear, endure, stand, tolerate
parole.testo: From Old Danish tholæ, from Old Norse þola, from Proto-Germanic *þulāną, cognate with English thole.

parole.significato: tear (drop of clear salty liquid from the eye)
parole.testo: From Old Norse tár n, from Proto-Germanic *tahrą, cognate with English tear, German Zähre. The Danish form is originally a plural; the old singular has developed a new meaning, see tår (“drop”). The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru (“tear”), which is also the source of Ancient G
From Old Norse þekja, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Cognate with English thatch, Swedish täcka, Old English þeċċean, German decken, Dutch dekken.
From Old Norse telja (“to count”), from Proto-Germanic *taljaną, cognate with English tell, German zählen.
From Old Danish tæmmæ, from Old Norse temja (“to tame”), from Proto-Germanic *tamjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”).

parole.significato: to kindle, ignite, set fire to
parole.testo: From Old Danish tændæ, from Old Norse tenda, from Proto-Germanic *tandijaną, cognate with Norwegian tenne, Swedish tända, English tend (dialect) (a different ablaut form in German zünden).

From Old Danish thænkiæ, þænkiæ, from Old Norse þenkja (“to know, recognise”), from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną. The Old Danish form is influenced in its form and its semantics by the Middle Low German cognate denken (“think, remember”), like Swedish tänka, Norwegian Bokmål tenke, and Norwegian Nynors

parole.significato: thrash, thresh (to separate the grain from the straw or husks by mechanical beating, with a flail or machinery)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þreskja, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną.

From Old Danish thræskyldæ, from Old Norse þreskǫldr, þreskjǫldr, þrepskjǫldr, from Proto-Germanic *þreskwaþluz. Related to tærske (“to thrash, thresh”), in a dated sense "to stamp, stump". Cognate with Norwegian terskel, treskel, Swedish tröskel.

parole.significato: close (with a little or no distance)
parole.testo: From Old Danish thæt, from Old Norse þéttr (“tight, watertight”), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. Cognate with Swedish tät, English tight, Dutch, German dicht. Doublet of tight.
From Old Norse þeyja, from Proto-Germanic *þawjaną. Cognate with German tauen.
From Old Danish tyghel, from Old Norse tygill, from Proto-Germanic *tugilaz.
From Old Norse tjóðr, from Proto-Germanic *teudrą.
From Old Norse taumr, from Proto-Germanic *taumaz, cognate with Swedish töm (“rein”), German Zaum (“bridle”), English team.
From Old Norse tœma, from Proto-Germanic *tōmijaną, cognate with Swedish tömma, Old Saxon tōmian (“to free”). Derived from the adjective *tōmaz (“empty”) (Danish tom).
From Old Danish tymbær, timbær, from Old Norse timbr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą.
From Old Danish thur, thyr, thiur, from Old Norse þurr (“dry”), from Proto-Germanic *þurzuz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk tørr, turr, Swedish torr, German dürr.

parole.significato: in-, un-, non-; (prefix meaning not, reversing the meaning)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ú-, ó-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-, a prefix use of the particle *né (“not”). Doublet of a-.
From Old Danish ut, from Old Norse út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt.
From Old Danish utæn, utan, from Old Norse útan, from Proto-Germanic *ūtanē
Compound of ud + gang, from Old Norse útgangr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz.
From Old Danish ukæ, uku, wiku, from Old Norse vika, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”).
From Old Danish ugglæ, from Old Norse ugla (“owl”), from Proto-Germanic *uwwulǭ (“owl”).

From Old Danish ull, from Old Norse ull, from Proto-Germanic *wullō, cognate with English wool and German Wolle. The Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂, which is also the source of Latin lāna, Ancient Greek λῆνος (lênos), Sanskrit ऊर्णा (ū́rṇā), Hittite: 𒋠𒀸 (ḫulanaš).
By surface analysis, u- (“un”) + lig (“like”). From Old Norse úlíkr, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz, cognate with Swedish olik, English unlike, Dutch ongelijk, German ungleich.

parole.significato: to wish, grant, not grudge (to find joy in a fortune enjoyed by another; to feel that another has deserved something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse unna, from Proto-Germanic *unnaną, cognate with Norwegian unne, Swedish unna, German gönnen. Related to the Danish words yndig, ynde, gunst.
From Old Norse undir, from Proto-Germanic *under, cognate with English under, German unter.
From Old Norse undr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą, cognate with English wonder, German Wunder.
From Old Norse undra, Proto-Germanic *wundrōną, cognate with Swedish undra, English wonder, English wundern.
From Old Norse ungr, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós, from *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”). Compare Swedish ung, Icelandic ungur, Dutch jong, German jung, English young.
Equivalent to u- (“un-”) + ret (“right”). From Old Norse óréttr, úréttr, from Proto-Germanic *unrehtaz, cognate with English unright, German unrecht, Unrecht, Dutch onrecht.
From Old Norse urt, from Proto-Germanic *wurtiz, cognate with Norwegian urt, Swedish ört, English wort. A variant of *wrōts (“root”) (Danish rod).
From Old Norse óskaddr (“unharmed”). Composed of u- (“un-”) + the past participle of a verb corresponding to Old Norse skeðja, from Proto-Germanic *skaþjaną.
Equivalent to u- + vejr. From Old Norse óveðr, úveðr, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą, cognate with Swedish oväder, English unweather, German Unwetter.
From Old Norse vað, from Proto-Germanic *wadą (“shallow water, ford”), from Proto-Indo-European *wadʰom.
From Old Norse val, from Proto-Germanic *walą. The g is due to influence from the verb vælge.
From Old Norse valka, from Proto-Germanic *walkaną. Cognate with Old English wealcan, Middle English, Middle Dutch, German walken, English waulk, walk.
Learned borrowing from Old Norse valkyrja, from Proto-Germanic *walakuzjǭ.

parole.significato: giving the sense of wrong, bad; mis-, dys-, mal-
parole.testo: From Old Norse van-, from Proto-Germanic *wanaz (“lacking, deficient”). Compare Old Norse vanr (“lacking, wanting”).
Metathesis of Old Danish watn, wan, wand, from Old Norse vatn, from Proto-Germanic *watōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).
From Old Norse vatna, from vatn (“water”), from Proto-Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“wet”).

parole.significato: only used in blive var (“become aware”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse varr, from Proto-Germanic *waraz, cognate with English aware.
From Old Norse vara f, from Proto-Germanic *warō (“attention, care”), cognate with Swedish vara, English ware, German Ware. Derived from Proto-Germanic *waraz (“cautious, aware”) (cf. Danish var).

From Old Norse vari m, from Proto-Germanic *warō (“attention, care”), originally the same word as the previous one. The phrase tage vare is influenced by Middle Low German warnemen, compare German wahrnehmen (“to perceive”), Dutch waarnemen.

From Old Norse vara, from Proto-Germanic *warōną (“to watch, protext”), derived from Proto-Germanic *waraz (“cautious, aware”) (cf. Danish var) Cognate with English ware (“to guard”) and German wahren (“to protect”).
From Old Norse vargr, from Proto-Germanic *wargaz.
From Old Danish wærmæ, from Old Norse verma, from Proto-Germanic *warmijaną.

From Old Danish waskæ, from Old Norse vaska (“to wash”), from Proto-Germanic *waskaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wod- (“wet; water”). Cognate with Swedish vaska, German waschen, Old English wæscan (English wash).
From Old Danish with, withær, wethær, from Old Norse við, from Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against”). Cognate with Swedish vid, English with, Norwegian Bokmål ved, and German wider (“against”).

parole.significato: wood (the material of the inner parts of the trunk and branches of a tree)
parole.testo: From Old Danish with, from Old Norse viðr, from Proto-Germanic *widuz. Compare Norwegian Bokmål ved, Norwegian Nynorsk ved, Swedish ved, Icelandic viður, English wood.
From Old Danish wegh, from Old Norse veikr, from Proto-Germanic *waikwaz.

parole.significato: road (strip of land made suitable for travel, the path or route one takes)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wægh, from Old Norse vegr (“way”), from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, cognate with English way and German Weg. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to transport”), cf. Latin vehō and vector.

From Old Danish wæghæ, from Old Norse vega (“to weigh”), from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to carry, move, weigh”). Cognate with English weigh and German wiegen (“to weigh”), German bewegen (“to move”) (whence Danish bevæge). The Germanic verb is related derived from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰe-, *weǵʰ-
From Old Norse vega (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *wiganą (“to fight”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to overcome”), related to Latin vincō (“to win”).
From Old Danish wæthær, from Old Norse veðr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, cognate with Swedish väder, English weather, German Wetter.
From Old Danish wæl, wel, from Old Norse vel, from Proto-Germanic *wela (“well”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.
From Old Danish win, from Old Norse vinr, from Proto-Norse ᚹᛁᚾᛁᛉ (winiʀ), from Proto-Germanic *winiz, cognate with Swedish vän. rom Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to seek, desire, love, win”).
From Old Danish wændæ, from Old Norse venda, from Proto-Germanic *wandijaną (“to turn”).
From Old Danish wenstræ, winstræ, from Old Norse vinstri, from Proto-Germanic *winistraz.
From Old Danish wæntæ, from Old Norse vænta, vætta, from Proto-Germanic *wēnatjaną, related to *winiz (“friend”).

From Old Danish wærldæn, originally singular definite form of wæræld, wærild, wærælde, from Old Norse verǫld, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz, cognate with Swedish värld, English world, German Welt, Dutch wereld. The original indefinite form in Old Danish was rarely used, to the extent that the defini
Inherited from Old Norse vestr, from Proto-Germanic *westrą.
From Old Norse vér, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy, plural of *éǵh₂.
From Old Danish with, from Old Norse víðr, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz (“broad, wide”), cognate with English wide and German weit.
From Old Danish wit, from Old Norse vit, from Proto-Germanic *witą.

parole.significato: to know (be certain or sure about (something))
parole.testo: From Old Danish witæ, from Old Norse vita (“to know”), from Proto-Germanic *witaną, cognate with Swedish veta, German wissen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *wóyde, originally a perfect form of *weyd- (“see”).
From Old Norse víða (“widen”), verbalization of víðr (“wide”), from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz.
From Old Danish witæ, from Old Norse víti, from Proto-Germanic *wītiją.

parole.significato: a withe, wicker, a withy, an osier (long, thin and flexible (willow) branch, typically used for weaving fences, baskets…
parole.testo: From Old Norse viðja, from Proto-Germanic *wiþjǭ. Cognate with Swedish vidja, Faroese viðja.

parole.significato: witness (one who has a personal knowledge of something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse vitni, Proto-Germanic *witniją (“witness”), derived from the verb *witaną (“to know”).

parole.significato: dedicate something to someone or towards a cause
parole.testo: From Old Norse vígja, from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną.
From Old Norse vík, from Proto-Germanic *wīkō (“village; inlet”), cognate with Norwegian, Swedish vik, English wick, Dutch wijk. Borrowed from Latin vīcus.
From Old Danish wikæ, from Old Norse víkja, from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną, cognate with Swedish vika, German weichen.
From Old Danish wild, from Old Norse vild, from Proto-Germanic *wiliþō. Compare Swedish väld.
From Old Danish williæ, from Old Norse vili, from Proto-Germanic *wiljô. Cognate with Norwegian vilje, Swedish vilja, English will, German Wille, Dutch wil, Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌻𐌾𐌰 (wilja).

parole.significato: to want to, be willing to
parole.testo: From Old Danish wiliæ, willæ, from Old Norse vilja, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, cognate with English will, German wollen. The Germanic verbs goes back to Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-, which is also the source of Latin volō.
From Old Danish wind, from Old Norse vindr, from Proto-Germanic *windaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“blowing”), present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
From Old Danish winnæ, from Old Norse vinna (“to accomplish”), from Proto-Germanic *winnaną.
From Old Norse vinda, from Proto-Germanic *windaną.
From Old Danish wintær, from Old Norse vintr, from Proto-Germanic *wintruz (“winter”).

From Old Norse vís (in ǫðru vís(i) "otherwise"), from Proto-Germanic *wīsō, *wīsǭ (“manner”). Cognate with Norwegian vis, Swedish vis, English wise, Dutch wijze and German Weise. Another variant of the same word is Danish vise (“song”), Swedish visa, from Old Norse vísa.
From Old Norse víss, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“wise”). Cognates include Norwegian vis, Swedish vis, English wise, and German weise.
From Old Norse viss, from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz, cognate with Norwegian viss, Swedish viss, German gewiss.
From vis (“wise”) + -dom, from Old Norse vísdómr (“wisdom”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsadōmaz.
From Old Danish wisæ, from Old Norse vísa f, from Proto-Germanic *wīsō, *wīsǭ (“manner”), the same word as Danish vis, -vis, English -wise, German Weise.

From Old Danish wisæ, from Old Norse vísa, from Proto-Germanic *wīsōną, a variant of *wīsijaną, whence German weisen, Dutch wijzen. Both are derived from the Proto-Germanic adjective *wīsaz (“wise”), whence Danish vis.
From Old Danish visk m, Old Norse visk f, from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz, *wiskō (“bundle of hay”), cognate with German Wisch, Dutch wis.
Probably a convergence of two related Old Norse words vaðr (“fishing line”) (from Proto-Germanic *wadaz) and váð (“cloth, fishing net”).

parole.significato: carriage, coach (wheeled vehicle, generally drawn by horse power)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wagn, waghæn, from Old Norse vagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz (“cart, wagon”). Cognate with German Wagen and English wain (waggon is borrowed via French wagon from Dutch wagen). The Germanic noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to transport”), cf. Danish veje (“to weigh”)
From Old Danish wox, wax, from Old Norse vax, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą.
From Old Danish waxæ, from Old Norse vaxa, from Proto-Germanic *wahsaną. cognate with Swedish växa, English wax (poetic), German wachsen, Dutch wassen.
From Old Norse vald, from Proto-Germanic *waldą, cognate with Swedish våld, German Gewalt.
From Old Norse vǫllr, from Proto-Germanic *walþuz (“forest”), cognate with German Wald. Doublet of val.
From Old Norse valda (“to wield, rule, cause”), from Proto-Germanic *waldaną (“to rule”), cognate with Swedish vålla (“to cause”), German walten (“to rule, exercise”). Doublet of valte.

parole.significato: to become, get (go from one state into another, with a predicative)
parole.testo: From Old Danish warthæ, from Old Norse verða, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną (“to become, happen”), cognate with obsolete English worth, Faroese verða, Icelandic verða, Norwegian Nynorsk verta, Swedish varda, German werden, Dutch worden.

From Old Danish wrang (“wrong”), from Old Norse rangr (“awry”), from earlier *wrangr, from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz (“crooked, twisted, turned awry”), from Proto-Indo-European *werk'- (“to twist, weave, tie together”), *werg'-, *wrengh-, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate with
From Old Danish wrethæ, from Old Norse vreiði, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþį̄, related to vred, from Old Norse vreiðr, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz.
From Old Danish writhæ, from Old Norse vríða, from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną, cognate with Norwegian vri, Swedish vrida, English writhe.

From Old Norse vaga, from Proto-Germanic *wagōną (“to move, stir”), cognate with Swedish vagga, English waw (obsolete), wag, German wagen (“to dare”), Dutch wagen (“to dare; to move”). Doublet of vove. The modern Danish form has been influenced by the previous noun.

Older vurde, from Old Norse virða, from Proto-Germanic *wirþijaną (“to value”). Derived from the adjective *werþaz (“worth”). The modern Danish form is extended with the suffix -ere after Middle Low German werdēren, a derivation from the same adjective.
From Old Norse vápn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną.
From Old Danish watær, wat, from Old Norse vátr (“wet”), from Proto-Germanic *wētaz, cognate with Norwegian våt, Swedish våt.

From Old Danish wathæ, from Old Norse váði (“danger, peril”), cognate with Norwegian våde, Swedish våda. A derivation of vá (“disaster”), from Proto-Germanic *waiwô (“misery”), cognate with English woe, German Weh (Danish ve is borrowed from Low German).

From Old Danish wagh (“heavy sea”), from Old Norse vágr (“sea‚ bay”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“wave”), cognate with Norwegian våg (“inlet”), Swedish våg (“wave”), English waw (obsolete), Dutch waag f, Old Norse vágr (“sea; bay”). Doublet of vove.

parole.significato: a scale (device for measuring weights or masses)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wagh, from Old Norse vág, from Proto-Germanic *wēgō. Cognate with Icelandic vog.
From Old Norse vǫk, from Proto-Germanic *wakwō, cognate with Norwegian Bokmål våk, Norwegian Nynorsk vok, Swedish vak, German Wake.

parole.significato: buzzard (bird of prey of the genus Buteo)
parole.testo: From Old Norse vákr, from Proto-Germanic *wanakaz, cognate with Norwegian våk. Maybe related to Lithuanian vãnagas (“hawk”).
From Old Danish waghæ, from Old Norse vaka, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną, cognate with Swedish vaka, English wake, German wachen.

From Old Norse vakinn, originally a past participle of Proto-Germanic *wakaną (“to awake”), whence also English wake. The Old Norse verb vaka (“to be awake”) (Danish våge) comes from a different variant of the same verb, *wakāną.
From Old Norse vakna, from Proto-Germanic *waknaną. Cognate of Swedish vakna and English waken. From the root of våge (“to be awake”). Equivalent to våge + -ne

From Old Danish war, from Old Norse vár n, from Proto-Germanic *wazrą, cognate with Norwegian, Swedish vår. The word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥, which is also the source of Latin vēr, Ancient Greek ἔαρ (éar).
From Old Danish wædhæ, from Old Norse veðja (“to bet”), from Proto-Germanic *wadjōną, cognate with Swedish vädja, Dutch wedden, German wetten, English wed.

From Old Danish wæthær, from Old Norse veðr (“ram”), from Proto-Germanic *weþruz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål vær, Swedish vädur, English wether, German Widder, Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌸𐍂𐌿𐍃 (wiþrus), Latin vetus, Ancient Greek ἔτος (étos) and Sanskrit वत्स (vatsá).
From Old Norse væta, Proto-Germanic *wētijǭ (“moisture”). Derived from the adjective *wētaz (“wet”) (Danish våd).
From Old Norse væta, from Proto-Germanic *wētijaną (“to wet”). Derived from the adjective *wētaz (“wet”) (Danish våd).

From Old Danish wæg, from Old Norse veggr m (“wall”), from Proto-Germanic *wajjuz. Cognates include Swedish vägg, Norwegian vegg, Faroese and Icelandic veggur, Old English wāg (“wall”), and Gothic *𐍅𐌰𐌳𐌳𐌾𐌿𐍃 (*waddjus).

parole.significato: to wake up (to cause someone to stop sleeping)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wække, from Old Norse vekja, from Proto-Germanic *wakjaną (“to wake”), cognate with Swedish väcka, English watch, wake, and German wecken.
From Old Norse vǫxtr, from Proto-Germanic *wahstuz, cognate with Norwegian vokster, vekst, Swedish växt, English waist, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌷𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (wahstus). Derived form the verb *wahsaną (whence Danish vokse).
From Old Danish wæliæ, from Old Norse velja, from Proto-Germanic *waljaną (“to choose, select”).

A merger of two related verbs: Old Norse velta (intransitive, strong conjugation), from Proto-Germanic *weltaną. 2. Old Norse velta (transitive, weak conjugation), from Proto-Germanic *waltijaną, cognate with German wälzen, English welt (obsolete). They are both related to the verb *waltaną in Germa

From Old Danish wæn. From Old Norse vænn. From Proto-Germanic *wēniz, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁-, the same root as vinr. Related to Icelandic vænn, Faroese vænur, Norwegian Nynorsk ven, Swedish vän.
From Old Danish wæniæ, from Old Norse venja, from Proto-Germanic *wanjaną. Cognates include Swedish vänja, German gewöhnen, and English wean.

parole.significato: worth (the inner worth of a person)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wærth, from Old Norse verð n (“price”), from Proto-Germanic *werþą, cognate with Norwegian verd, Swedish värde, English worth, German Wert m, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸 (wairþ).

parole.significato: worth (only used in a predicative position, with possible complements placed before the adjective)
parole.testo: From Old Norse verðr (“worth, worthy”, adjective), from Proto-Germanic *werþaz., cognate with Norwegian verd, Swedish värd, English worth, German wert.

parole.significato: to be (expresses identity between the subject and a predicative)
parole.testo: All forms except the present are from Old Danish wæræ, waræ, from Old Norse vera, vesa, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell, live, reside”). The present tense is derived from a different root: Proto-Germanic *izum, *izud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-

parole.significato: guardian (of a child or incompetent adult)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wæriæ, from Old Norse verja, from Proto-Germanic *warjǭ. Cognate with Norwegian verje, Swedish värja, värjo. Derived from the verb *warjaną, see below. Another derivation, *warīniz, is found in German Wehr and Danish værn.
From Old Danish wæriæ, from Old Norse verja, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną, cognate with English wear (“to guard”) and German wehren.

parole.significato: work (the product of someone's or something's actions)
parole.testo: From Old Danish wærk, from Old Norse verk n, from Proto-Germanic *werką, cognate with Swedish värk, English work, German Werk and Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon).
From Old Norse verkr m, from Proto-Germanic *warkiz, cognate with Swedish värk.
From Old Danish wærn f, from Old Norse vǫrn f, from Proto-Germanic *warīniz. Cognate with Swedish värn n, German Wehr f and Dutch weer f. Derived from the verb *warjaną, see værge.
From Old Danish wærpæ, Old Norse verpa, from Proto-Germanic *werpaną. Cognate with English warp and German werfen (whence Danish verfe). See also varpe
From Old Danish wærræ, from Old Norse verri (“worse”, comparative), from Proto-Germanic *wirsizô.
From Old Danish wæt, wættæ, from Old Norse véttr, vættr, from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz (“thing”). Cognate with Swedish vätte, English wight and German Wicht.
From Old Norse vefr m, from Proto-Germanic *wabją n, cognate with Swedish väv, English web, Dutch web. Derived from the verb *webaną (“to weave”) (Danish væve).
From Old Norse vefa, from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to weave”). Compare veve, Swedish väva, Faroese veva, Icelandic vefa.
From Old Norse ýta, from Proto-Germanic *ūtijaną, cognate with Old English ȳtan (“to put out, expel”), derived from the adverb *ūt (“out”).
From Old Norse yndi (“joy, delight”), from Proto-Germanic *wunjō (“joy, delight, pleasure, lust”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”).
From Old Danish ønke, from Old Norse aumka, from Old Norse aumr (“miserable”), from Proto-Germanic *arbumaz. see Danish øm. Cognate with Swedish ömka.
From Old Norse yppa, from Proto-Germanic *uppijaną (“to raise, lift”).

parole.significato: river, creek, stream (only used of rivers in Denmark)
parole.testo: From Old Norse á (“river”), from Proto-Germanic *ahwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”), related to Latin aqua (“water”).
From Old Norse á, from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on, onto”). Cognate with Swedish å, English on, and German on.
From Old Norse opinn (“open”), from Proto-Germanic *upanaz, cognate with Swedish öppen, English open, Dutch open, German offen.
From Old Danish opnæ, from Old Norse opna, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną, cognate with English open, German öffnen. Derived from *upanaz (“open”).
From Old Norse ok, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm (“yoke”).

From Old Norse okr, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz, related to German Wucher. The short vowel of the Danish and Old Norse word is surprising (also Swedish ocker. It may a borrowing from Middle Low German wōker, but that doesn't explain the vocalism.
From Old Norse ǫnd, a variant of andi (related to anda (“breathe”)), from Proto-Germanic *anadô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe”).
From Old Danish aar, from Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *jērą, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁r-. Compare Norwegian and Swedish år, English year.
From Old Danish athræ, Old Norse ædr, from Proto-Germanic *ēþrǭ (“vein”). Related to German Ader.
From Old Danish aare, Old Norse ár, Proto-Germanic *airō (“oar”). Related to English oar.
From Old Danish aaz, from Old Norse áss, from Proto-Germanic *ansaz.
From Old Danish ætæ, from Old Norse eta, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, cognate with Swedish äta, English eat, German essen. The Germanic verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-, cf. Latin edō.

From Old Norse egg n (“egg”), from Proto-Germanic *ajją, cognate with Norwegian egg, Swedish ägg, German Ei (English egg is a loan from Old Norse). The Germanic noun derives from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”), cf Latin ōvum, Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión), and Polish jajo.
From Old Norse egg f (“edge”), from Proto-Germanic *agjō, cognate with English edge and German Ecke (“corner”).
From Old Norse elli, from Proto-Germanic *alþį̄.
From Old Norse erendi, ørendi, eyrendi (“errand”), from Proto-Germanic *airundiją. Cognate with Swedish ärende, Norwegian ærend.

From Old Danish, from Old Norse ætt, átt (“family, race, direction”), from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz (“possession, property”), cognate with Old English ǣht, Old High German ēht, and Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (aihts). Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *aiganą (“to possess”).
From Old Norse ey, from Proto-Germanic *awjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”), see å.

parole.significato: desolate, deserted (with no or few people in it)
parole.testo: From Old Norse auðr, eyði, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaz, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk aud, Swedish öde, German öde, Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍃 (auþeis) and Latin vanus.
From Old Norse eyða, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaną, cognate with Swedish öda, German veröden. Derived from *auþijaz, see above.
From Old Danish øk, from Old Norse eykr m, from Proto-Germanic *jaukijaz, cognate with Norwegian øyk, Swedish ök.
From Old Norse auka, from Proto-Germanic *aukaną, cognate with Swedish öka, English eke.

From Old Danish øghæ, from Old Norse auga, from Proto-Germanic *augô, cognate with Swedish öga, English eye, German Auge. The Germanic noun ultimately goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”), cf. Latin oculus (“eye”).
From Old Norse øx (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *akwisī, from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷs-ih₂- (“axe”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).
From Old Norse ǫl, from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut- (“beer”).
From Old Danish usk, ønsk, ynsk, Old Norse ósk (“wish”), from Proto-Germanic *wunskaz, *wunskō (“wish, desire”). Remodelled after the verb.
From Old Danish yske, ønskæ, from Old Norse œskja (“wish”), from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”). The 'n' stems from influence from Middle Low German wunschen, cf. also Swedish önska.
Sense 1 from Old Norse aurr, from Proto-Germanic *auraz (“wet sand or earth, mud”). Sense 2 from Old Norse eyrr, related to aurr.
From Old Norse ǿrr, from Proto-Germanic *wōrijaz, probably cognate with English weary.
From Old Danish øræ, from Old Norse eyra, from Proto-Germanic *auzô, cognate with English ear, German Ohr. From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows- (“ear”), cf. Latin auris.
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃or-no- (“eagle”). More at erne.
Earlier øster, from Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą. The modern form without -r- is influenced by Middle Low German ōst.

parole.significato: upper, top, topmost (placed at the highest point of something, at the top of something, especially a page or an image)
parole.testo: From Old Norse øfstr, from Proto-Germanic *ubistaz, a superlative of the adverb *ub (“up”).

parole.significato: upper (at a higher level, or more to the north, or upstream)
parole.testo: From Old Norse øfri, from Proto-Germanic *ubizô, a superlative of the adverb *ub (“up”). Compare øverst.
